title: Washington joins coalition supporting challenge to unlawful immigration arrests
description:
Circuit in support of litigation challenging the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) policy and practice of conducting unlawful warrantless civil immigration arrests.
Under federal law, immigration officers conducting warrantless civil immigration arrests must have probable cause to believe that an individual is unlawfully present in the United States and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained.
However, DHS officers routinely carry out warrantless arrests without determining if the individual is an escape risk.
The brief highlights the widespread harms that unlawful immigration enforcement practices have inflicted on communities across the country, including in Washington.
The brief was filed in Escobar-Molina v. DHS, a case challenging DHS’s policy and practice of conducting unlawful warrantless civil immigration arrests in the District of Columbia.
text:
Attorney General Nick Brown joined a coalition of 22 attorneys general in filing an amicus brief Monday in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit in support of litigation challenging the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) policy and practice of conducting unlawful warrantless civil immigration arrests.

Under federal law, immigration officers conducting warrantless civil immigration arrests must have probable cause to believe that an individual is unlawfully present in the United States and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained. However, DHS officers routinely carry out warrantless arrests without determining if the individual is an escape risk. The brief highlights the widespread harms that unlawful immigration enforcement practices have inflicted on communities across the country, including in Washington.

“The Bill of Rights protects the public from unlawful search and seizure, but the administration treats our constitutional protections as optional rather than bedrock requirements,” Brown said. “Checks and balances are essential if we want a country that is both governed and policed fairly.”

Across the country, federal immigration agents have escalated their enforcement activities, disrupting communities and undermining public health, safety, education, and local economies. Washington has seen these harms firsthand, as aggressive immigration enforcement tactics have kept students out of school, disrupted agricultural work, discouraged people from seeking medical care, blocked access to courts, prevented kids from using the library, impeded shoppers from getting groceries, undermined families’ financial stability, and weakened the relationship between immigrant communities and local law enforcement. Federal agents’ use of ski masks, dark sunglasses, plainclothes, and unmarked vehicles, and refusals to identify themselves while carrying out operations have further contributed to fear and uncertainty in affected communities.

The brief was filed in Escobar-Molina v. DHS, a case challenging DHS’s policy and practice of conducting unlawful warrantless civil immigration arrests in the District of Columbia. On December 2, 2025, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia granted in part a motion for a preliminary injunction.

In filing the brief, Brown joins the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, and Virginia.

text:
What this information is about

This blog is about the expansion of the use of conditional cautions as they relate to immigration status. A recent change means people with limited leave to remain (LLR) will now be treated as “foreign national offenders” and may be given cautions which include a condition to leave the UK.

This is a further encroachment of the hostile environment and expansion of the unjust system of double punishment faced by non-British people accused of crimes.

Who is this information for?

The recent change means that anyone with LLR, insecure or no immigration status could be impacted if they come into contact with the criminal justice system.

This blog is for the whole community, particularly for those supporting or working with people in the criminal justice system. We hope people will help us spread awareness. There has been very little publicity around this change and we are concerned that people will face these measures without knowing their rights.

What is a conditional caution?

A conditional caution can be given for any minor criminal offence that carries a sentence of two years in prison or less.

When the police suspect someone of a minor criminal offence, and that person admits the crime, this can be recorded as a formal “caution” without further action being taken. This is instead of the person being charged with the crime or prosecuted.

Accepting a caution means admitting the criminal offence. You can refuse a caution, which may mean being charged and prosecuted for the offence.

Certain conditions can be attached to a caution which must be met, otherwise formal prosecution will follow. This could include things like tackling addiction issues or paying a fine.

One of those conditions, for people classed by the Home Office as “foreign national offenders”, might be to leave the UK.

What has changed?

Previously, people classed as “foreign national offenders”, who could be issued with this kind of conditional caution, were people with no immigration status. This changed with the Crime and Policing Act 2026, which meant that people with limited leave to remain – anyone with temporary immigration status or a visa in the UK – could also be classed as a “foreign national offender”.

What can you do about it?

It is very important for people to know their rights and to get immigration advice if they are in a situation where they may be given this kind of caution. Criminal solicitors may not be familiar enough with immigration law to help.

There are in reality a lot of reasons why it may not be possible for someone on a visa to be given this kind of caution. If there are barriers to removal, this caution cannot be imposed.

According to the policy these barriers to removal are if:

there is an outstanding asylum or human rights claim or related appeal and the person does not withdraw that claim or appeal

there are medical conditions impacting on the foreign national offender’s fitness to travel

the foreign national offender claims their family circumstances in the UK preclude them from accepting a caution

a valid travel document cannot be obtained within the time period for the foreign national offender to leave the UK

there are reasonable grounds to suspect the offence is connected to human trafficking

It is unclear in the policy how these will work in practice – who will know or be able to advise about whether these barriers are in place? The policy also says:

If the foreign national offender raises any issues that may prevent removal within the time period specified in the foreign national offender conditional caution, this may be a breach of the caution.

In other words, if someone later receives immigration advice and realises that they can make a claim to asylum or for another immigration status based on family life, they will be treated as having breached a caution, which could have further consequences.

What we advise

We know that in a situation where someone is threatened with prosecution for a minor offence, accepting a caution may instead feel like the better option. However, due to the possible consequences, we advise that people do not accept a “foreign national offender” conditional caution unless they are prepared to leave the UK. Instead, we advise people get immigration advice as well as criminal legal advice.

If someone has already accepted a caution of this kind, it is still important to get immigration advice. They may also want to look into challenging the caution – please see this information from Hickman Rose.

text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, sent a letter to the Government Accountability Office (GAO) urging them to investigate the Trump Administration’s decision to rapidly establish new, hidden immigration courts. In the Homeland Security Act, Congress preserved the separation of Department of Homeland Security (DHS) immigration enforcement functions from immigration courts’ adjudicatory role. Yet the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) is establishing new courts in DHS facilities where they are managed by DHS personnel.

“DOJ regulations require that members of the public, including family members and loved ones, have access to immigration courts—but my staff documented DHS officials, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) personnel, regularly prohibiting public access to immigration courtrooms at DHS facilities. Worse still, the Administration has established new court locations—where judges are appearing virtually—without providing formal notice to the public and in apparent violation of regulations and policies intended to ensure transparency and due process in immigration court proceedings,” Durbin wrote.

Immigrants are expected to appear for their immigration court hearings unless a judge has waived their appearance, or they may be ordered removed in absentia. In the letter to GAO, Durbin noted that these new courtrooms seem deliberately designed to increase the number of missed hearings to accelerate removals. For example, EOIR does not make these locations publicly available, despite EOIR policy stating a complete list of immigration courts is available on its website.

In the letter, Durbin also noted that EOIR appears to be targeting individuals who do not have legal representation. The Administration’s unprecedented decision to open courts in DHS buildings worsens these due process concerns, given that DHS is the party seeking the removal of immigrants in immigration court proceedings, serving as the prosecutor in these matters. According to recent reports, over the summer, the White House directed DHS to find space for additional courts, and DHS components such as ICE, FEMA, the Coast Guard, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services volunteered.

Durbin wrote, “My staff have observed that these new courtrooms are not just housed within DHS facilities, but DHS is controlling access to the facilities. Immigration court proceedings are open to the public with few exceptions, yet DHS personnel—not EOIR personnel—barred my staff from entering the court in the FEMA building on three separate occasions. During these attempted visits, my staff observed that the doors to the courtroom were locked, and the courtroom lacked any signage, a violation of EOIR policy. During one of the visits, a person who identified herself as a DHS contractor stated that my staff would have to contact FEMA personnel and DHS to gain access because the courtroom was located in a ‘secure’ federal building and was ‘not open to the public.’”

Durbin continued, “My staff also observed DHS agents and contractors prevent the family of unrepresented respondents from entering the courtroom. There was no evidence EOIR personnel were physically present at the court in the FEMA building, and no DHS personnel or contractors would acknowledge that EOIR, not DHS, oversaw immigration court operations. The placement of courts within DHS buildings seems to have no other purpose than to intimidate unrepresented respondents and increase the likelihood that individuals will fail to appear at hearings and be ordered removed in absentia.”

GAO previously has reported that problems with notices, changes in hearing dates, lack of understanding of court processes, and confusion regarding the differences between immigration courts and DHS can affect respondents’ ability to appear for hearings and lead to in absentia removal orders, even when respondents intended to participate in their proceedings. The new courts raise many of these issues, in addition to unprecedented concerns regarding DHS’s direct participation in running our immigration court system.

In the letter, Durbin requested GAO address a number of questions about these new, hidden immigration courts.

Durbin concluded, “It is vital to understand the threats to due process and judicial independence posed by this Administration’s restructuring of the immigration court system. Although Congress separated immigration enforcement functions from the immigration courts, DHS-managed immigration courts should end any illusion that courts are operating independently of this Administration’s mass deportation machine.”

Full text of the letter is available here.

text:
Dive Brief:

A federal judge last week dismissed the Trump administration’s 2025 lawsuit seeking to preempt New York City’s “sanctuary” provisions regarding cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.

The U.S. Department of Justice’s claims that federal immigration law preempts New York City’s administrative code and a police department operations order aligning with its “sanctuary” policies lack standing, Judge Ramón Reyes Jr. of the U.S. District Court of Eastern New York stated. “A state’s ability to control its officers and employees lies at the heart of state sovereignty,” Reyes wrote, quoting a previous ruling.

The ruling is “a victory for New Yorkers,” New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement. “We will continue to uphold our local laws and use every tool at our disposal to protect New Yorkers from [Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s] abuses.”

Dive Insight:

The Trump administration’s lawsuit sought to preempt sections of the New York City administrative code that prohibit the NYC Department of Correction from honoring civil immigration detainers or notifying federal immigration authorities of individuals’ release unless a federal judge has issued a judicial warrant and the person has been convicted of a violent crime or is flagged in a federal terrorist screening database. The code also restricts the NYPD from sharing certain custody and non-public information with federal immigration agents.

The lawsuit also sought to preempt NYPD Operations Order No. 4, which limits NYPD officers’ assistance with civil immigration enforcement.

The DOJ asserted the provisions violated the Supremacy Clause by preempting federal immigration law and discriminating against the federal government. These claims failed, Reyes wrote, because “when courts are called upon to address preemption questions, ‘the analysis always begins with the assumption that the historic police powers of the States are not to be superseded by the Federal Act unless that was the clear and manifest purpose of Congress.’”

The Tenth Amendment’s anticommandeering doctrine further prevents the federal government from compelling local governments to participate in federal immigration enforcement, Reyes wrote.

“The court made clear that the federal government has no standing to bring this case and cannot commandeer our City workers to do its bidding,” Mamdani said. “The federal government wants to use fear to divide our city. We will not let them.”

The DOJ declined to comment on ongoing litigation.

text:
Key points:

A coalition of faith groups has grounds to sue to curb immigration enforcement activities at houses of worship, a federal appeals court ruled.

The coalition of Jewish and Christian bodies includes three United Methodist conferences and a general agency.

United Methodist churches already have experienced ICE agents targeting their ministries.

A U.S. federal appeals court ruled Oct. 20 that United Methodists and other faith groups can move forward with their lawsuit to stop a Trump administration policy that allows immigration enforcement within houses of worship.

A divided three-judge panel for the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit found that the coalition of Christian and Jewish groups has grounds to sue over the enforcement change.

The faith groups have demonstrated under the new policy, “their members face a ‘credible threat’ of enforcement that will likely cause imminent, if not immediate, injury,” Judge Florence Pan wrote for the majority.

Judge Robert Wilkins joined the majority, and Judge Neomi Rao dissented.

The ruling in “Mennonite Church USA, et. al., vs. U.S. Department of Homeland Security,” revives the lawsuit after a lower court in April 2025 denied the organizations’ bid for early relief. The appellate court has reversed that denial of a preliminary injunction and sent the case back to the lower court.

At issue in the suit is the U.S. Department of Homeland Security guidelines that permit federal agents to carry out immigration raids in “sensitive locations,” such as schools, hospitals, synagogues and churches.

Homeland Security instated the new policy in January 2025, soon after President Trump’s second inauguration. The move put an end to the longstanding practice of restraint in such locations.

The faith groups’ suit, filed Feb. 11, 2025, seeks to prevent Immigration and Customs Enforcement from intruding on ministry without a judicial warrant or special circumstances. The suit contends that the new policy violates both the Religious Freedom Restoration Act and the religious freedom protections in the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution.

The United Methodist Commission on Religion and Race as well as the denomination’s New York, North Georgia and Western North Carolina conferences are among the groups bringing the legal action.

More United Methodist ministries wanted to join the case, but the constraints of the lawsuit limited the number of plaintiffs. Each United Methodist body is a separate legal entity under federal law.

United Methodist leaders, meeting at the Leadership Gathering in Calgary, Alberta, cheered the ruling while noting this is only one step in a long legal battle.

“It’s inherent in our Wesleyan DNA to fight for justice for those that are marginalized and those that are oppressed, and this is an accentuated case,” said Bishop Thomas Bickerton, who leads both the New York and New England conferences. “This was the right thing to do because there are people that are suffering great, great injustices.”

The United Methodist Church’s Social Principles, based on multiple passages on Scripture, have long affirmed “the dignity, worth, and rights of migrants, immigrants and refugees, including displaced and stateless people.” United Methodist congregations don’t check to see if people have the right documentation before welcoming them to worship.

Bickerton added that United Methodist churches in New York have a long history of receiving immigrants into their membership. After all, New York City historically has been where multiple waves of immigrant populations first came ashore in the U.S.

“They are our people, and we’re standing with them at all costs.”

A big source of contention in the case is whether the faith groups involved have shown that the new policy endangered their members and whether reinstating the previous sensitive-location policy would provide relief.

The appellate court’s ruling sided with the faith group’s arguments on both counts.

“Plaintiffs point to several specific examples of the government engaging in enforcement activity at or near their members’ houses of worship,” Pan wrote.

In fact, shortly before the appellate court held oral arguments in the case in February, ICE agents arrested a member of North Hills United Methodist Church Hispanic Mission in Los Angeles, while the church was distributing food. United Methodist Carlos Chavez, an undocumented immigrant from Mexico, was deported shortly after — leaving behind his wife and children. He was not accused of any crime.

“The trauma that the church had to go through is incredible,” said California-Pacific Conference Bishop Dottie Escobedo-Frank, whose area includes Los Angeles.

“We’ve seen it happen in several churches that people won’t come to church if ICE is going to come in,” she said. “Why would they? And so, it affects our ability to gather as worshipping communities because people are afraid to go to church.”

Last year, armed ICE agents also staged an operation in the parking lot of a Charlotte, North Carolina, United Methodist church during preschool pickup.

Western North Carolina Conference Bishop Ken Carter, whose area includes Charlotte, said the conference’s cabinet and trustees decided to join the lawsuit precisely to ensure churches could be safe from such intimidation tactics.

“Sanctuaries are set-apart places that protect human dignity and the image of God,” Carter said. He added that sanctuaries are supposed to provide places “that value people, where they can worship God and trust God.”

The 27 plaintiffs also include the Christian denominations of the Mennonite Church USA, the African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church, the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ), the Episcopal Church, the Friends General Conference (Quakers) and the Presbyterian Church (USA). The Unitarian Universalist Association is another plaintiff.

Also joining the suit are three Jewish branches — Union for Reform Judaism (the largest Jewish movement in the U.S.), Reconstructing Judaism and the United Synagogue of Conservative Judaism.

They all share a common belief that God calls the faithful to welcome the stranger.

text:
Why Should Delaware Care?

A federal agent was seen at a Delaware middle school campus Tuesday before apprehending a man in front of the school. The action followed a surge of immigration arrests nationally over the summer that highlighted the political divide between President Donald Trump and his supporters and many leaders in Delaware.

A federal immigration agent entered the campus at Stanton Middle School on Tuesday morning, then left after school security approached, according to school officials. An agent or agents then arrested a person just off the school grounds.

The incident appears to be the first time an agent with the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement entered a Delaware school campus — a “sensitive place” where state officials have sought to restrict their actions.

It also comes just weeks after the Trump administration announced increased immigration enforcement efforts ahead of the November midterm election, including other public arrests around Delaware.

A video circulating on social media shows agents placing a man into a vehicle near the school, as school buses and other vehicles drove past.

A spokesperson for the Red Clay Consolidated School District said the apparent enforcement activity took place off of school grounds after the school’s administration and security personnel approached the agent on campus.

The spokesperson said no students were taken into custody and none were removed from the school.

“We recognize that situations like this can create concern and uncertainty for our school community, and we remain committed to providing a safe, supportive, and compassionate learning environment for all students,” the spokesperson said.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not comment on the incident when reached by Spotlight Delaware. Instead, it requested the name of the detainee in question, the location the incident took place, and photos and videos from the arrest.

What happened?

Stanton Middle School parent Sade Garnica told Spotlight Delaware she received a call Tuesday morning from her sister, who said she witnessed an ICE agent detaining a father who had previously dropped off his daughter at school.

The sister had also just finished dropping off Garnica’s own daughter at the school.

Fearing ICE could return, Garnica picked up her daughter from school later that morning. She said school officials reassured her that federal agents would not enter the school. Still, she was fearful and pushed administrators to tell her the school’s protocol for suspicious cars.

“They were on school grounds,” Garnica said.

Garnica’s sister told her that the agent’s car was in the drop-off line with other parents before the arrest occurred across the street.

Images shared with Spotlight Delaware of the suspected-ICE vehicle show no visible identifiers. The license plate on the car was also tinted to obscure it from plain view.

ICE vehicles commonly have no markings, and sometimes no identifiable license plate, according to a report last year from NPR. Such unidentifiable plates sparked a dispute last spring between four states and the U.S. Department of Justice, the USA Today reported.

Garnica said Tuesday she still plans to drop her child off at school the next morning. But she remains scared, noting her husband is a Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipient — the immigration program for people brought into the country as children.

“These are just parents. They are trying to just get to work,” Garnica said. “Listen, they don’t know if it’s their turn or not. Or you know, like how do I know I’m not gonna get picked up?”

Can ICE agents go onto school grounds?

Last month, Gov. Matt Meyer signed House Bill 94 into law, which prohibits state and local law enforcement from directly participating in ICE arrests at sensitive locations such as schools, medical facilities, and places of worship unless there is a valid court order.

But because ICE agents are federal police, the new law does not restrict their actions.

Still, Meyer expressed defiance when asked about the incident Tuesday. In an emailed statement he said, “ICE, leave Delaware alone. Our schools are not hunting grounds.”

“Parents of every ethnicity and any nationality must be able to drop their kids off at school without worrying that federal agents are watching, waiting, and tearing families apart,” Meyer said in the statement.

As of Tuesday evening, seven school districts told Spotlight Delaware that there have not been federal agents on their schools’ campuses before the Stanton incident.

Nalwamba, who has lived in Colorado for more than two decades, was released after a federal judge granted his petition challenging his continued detention and ordered immigration officials to free him by Tuesday.

His release comes after 13 months in ICE custody, during which his attorney says his health deteriorated dramatically.

"I was walking. I was exercising. I was playing ping pong," Nalwamba said shortly after his release, describing his physical condition before he was detained in September 2025.

Now, he says he cannot walk without assistance. Nalwamba told CBS Colorado that staff initially brought him toward the facility's exit in a wheelchair, but would not allow him to take it the rest of the way to his transportation.

"They get me outside and say we can't go beyond this," Nalwamba explained. "And I'm asking, 'Can't the car come here?' They say, 'No.' I say, 'So how am I going to get the car?'"

Nalwamba said two other detainees stepped in and offered to carry him. He knew one of the men from his housing unit but said he did not know the other.

"Those friends offered to carry me, and, I mean, I'm so grateful to them," he said.

The circumstances of his release have drawn criticism from Colorado U.S. Sen. John Hickenlooper.

In a social media post Tuesday, Hickenlooper said members of his staff visited the detention center earlier in the day and specifically requested that GEO staff allow Nalwamba to call his caretakers before his release and provide a wheelchair to take him to his ride home.

The senator said GEO staff assured his office that both requests would be honored.

"They failed to deliver on either," Hickenlooper wrote. "No phone call. No wheelchair. No human decency."

Hickenlooper called the incident an act of cruelty and pledged to continue holding those responsible accountable.

CBS Colorado has reached out to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security seeking an explanation for the wheelchair restrictions, the circumstances surrounding Nalwamba's release and allegations concerning his medical treatment. DHS had not responded to those questions as of Tuesday evening.

Nalwamba's attorney, Joy Athanasiou, says her client entered into ICE custody in good health but has experienced serious medical problems while detained.

"When he came to the detention center a year ago, he was extremely healthy. He was very fit. He exercised regularly. He could do 15 to 20 push-ups. Now, he is wheelchair-bound. He is extremely weak," Athanasiou said.

Athanasiou said Nalwamba was diagnosed with pneumonia in January, lost more than 30 pounds and collapsed while detained. She also says he has suffered from an ongoing respiratory illness since June, and accuses ICE of failing to provide adequate testing and treatment.

Nalwamba described experiencing chest pain, coughing, dizziness and weakness in his legs.

His attorney says his supporters are working to arrange a medical appointment and hope he can begin physical therapy and rehabilitation.

In a statement provided to CBS Colorado in June, the Department of Homeland Security defended the medical care available to people in ICE custody.

"It is a longstanding practice to provide comprehensive medical care from the moment an alien enters ICE custody," a DHS spokesperson said. According to the agency, that includes access to medical appointments and 24-hour emergency care.

Nalwamba previously served as a priest at Resurrection Anglican Fellowship in Greenwood Village for approximately 15 years. He arrived in the United States from Uganda in 2002 and remained in the country after his tourist visa expired.

Nalwamba and his supporters have said he fears returning to Uganda because of persecution connected to his pro-democracy political activities.

In its June statement, DHS said Nalwamba had overstayed his visa, was granted voluntary departure in 2007 and received a final order of removal in 2010. ICE detained him on Sept. 18, 2025.

Before that arrest, Nalwamba says he had been living under an immigration order of supervision.

His attorneys challenged his prolonged detention through a federal habeas corpus petition, arguing the government could not continue holding him indefinitely.

Athanasiou says she is concerned that ICE could attempt to detain Nalwamba again.

On Monday, a judge granted the petition and ordered Nalwamba released no later than Oct. 20. Despite that ruling, his underlying immigration case remains unresolved.

"I am back to where I was when they first arrested me," Nalwamba said. "So I was asking myself, 'Why did they arrest me in the first place?'"

text:
In this closely fought midterm election campaign, the small town of Springfield, Ohio, has become a symbol of modern America. But it is a symbol that changes dramatically depending on who is describing it.

To President Donald Trump, Springfield crystallises America's problems due to years of unchecked immigration. He once echoed a false claim that Haitian immigrants were eating pets here. Today, he says his mass deportation drive means its people are "getting their town back".

But to others, Springfield represents a well-known cycle in the story of modern America. The decline of traditional industry, followed by a spike in immigration fuelled by cheap housing and low-paid labour. It is a familiar tale across the country.

This story contains some distressing details

Pierre Damas Bel, 20, arrived in Springfield to join his father and stepmother in 2024.

He fled his native Haiti, which was gripped by political instability and gang warfare. He entered the US with the government's permission under a now-defunct Biden-era programme for migrants waiting in Mexico.

Bel, according to a family friend, then received a humanitarian protection called Temporary Protected Status (TPS), which gives vetted individuals the right to live and work in the United States.

TPS usually lasts 18 months but is routinely rolled over, often for years, if the danger remains in the affected country.

Bel aspired to build a life in America, the friend said. He was an honours student, talented athlete and cadet in a high school programme training students to become officers in the US Armed Forces.

But in June, the Supreme Court upheld the Trump administration's decision to end TPS for some 350,000 Haitians in the US.

Bel was told to report to an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) field office where he was fitted with an ankle monitor which is used to track migrants facing deportation.

He wrote on Instagram that he felt "shame and humiliation" at having to wear the tag. And on 31 August, he parked his car on the side of a highway near Springfield, walked into oncoming traffic and was killed.

His family blamed his death on his feelings at having to wear the ankle monitor.

The Department for Homeland Security (DHS) did not respond to questions from the BBC about Bel's case. ICE has previously rejected "any attempt to blame ICE for the death".

"Remaining in the country illegally, while fighting removal, is a choice. Leaving with a free flight home and $2,600 is also a choice," a spokesperson told US media earlier this year when asked about the case.

In the weeks before his death, Bel attended a Springfield support centre for Haitians facing deportation.

Its co-founder, Viles Dorsainvil, told the BBC that Bel had been in the process of filing a motion asking ICE to remove the tag.

"He went twice to the ICE facilities… begging them to remove the ankle monitor," he said. "He did everything right to be here until they put the tag on him."

In total, more than a million immigrants from 13 countries have had TPS terminated by the Trump administration. The changes meant many went from being legal to unauthorised migrants overnight.

In 2024, Trump made securing the border and the mass deportation of undocumented migrants core pledges in his election campaign. Polls suggest the border policy continues to have strong support among Republicans, but the nature of his immigration enforcement campaign has seen a drop in backing this year.

Ohio has become a swing state in the coming midterm Congressional elections, and one of two Republican-held Senate seats is up for grabs. Trump has visited the state twice already in an attempt to rally turnout and counter a slide in his approval ratings.

At a rally in Youngstown, Ohio, earlier this month, Trump returned to the topic of Springfield.

"You have a little town, beautiful little town in Ohio where they dropped about 35,000 Haitians. Well, they're being taken out and they're almost going to be gone and we're giving their town back," he said to cheers.

The Trump administration first announced in June 2025 that it would be removing the TPS for Haitians, and the ensuing legal battle went all the way to the Supreme Court, which ruled in its favour in the summer.

"The T in TPS stands for TEMPORARY, yet many of these designations became de facto amnesty," James Percival, the general counsel for the Department of Homeland Security, said after the court's ruling. "This is a win for the rule of law and common sense."

In a social media post in August, the Department of Homeland Security posted a video of Haitians in chains wearing white uniforms being led onto a deportation flight. The video, accompanied by jaunty music, told Haitians whose TPS had expired to "LEAVE IMMEDIATELY".

The Trump administration has said it is conducting law enforcement operations in the town to keep Americans safe. It has also argued that Haiti is safe enough to return to.

The country is subject to the US State Department's highest Level 4 "Do Not Travel" danger warning.

GUIDE: What are the US midterms?

EXPLAINED: Why Trump's approval rating matters in the midterms

IN DEPTH: The Republicans walking a Trump tightrope

The signs of decades of economic decline are still visible in Springfield, through shuttered factories and boarded up homes.

This part of the American Midwest was hit badly by last century's de-industrialisation, when those laid off from its once prolific factories sought work on the coasts or migrated to warmer, southern states.

Within the last five years, a Haitian population estimated to be around 20,000 strong arrived in the town. Many fled the devastating earthquake in 2010. Others left Haiti in 2021 during the violence and unrest that followed President Jovenel Moise's assassination.

It meant Springfield's population increased rapidly. With their legal status under TPS, many Haitians took on low-paid jobs in factories and distribution warehouses.

Rick Johnson, who served in the Marines, has a porch adorned with flags. The Stars and Stripes flutter close to a banner for the US Navy and another for the Marine Corps.

Johnson's wife served in the Navy while he was in the Marines at Camp Pendleton in California. Outside of his service, he has lived in Springfield his whole life. He made it clear he is a strong supporter of ICE's deportation drive.

"You get where we're coming from," he said. "We love America, we love Americans - any kind of Americans, but you kind of have to be American."

Johnson moved into this neighbourhood a decade ago, but he said the loss of industry has left much of it empty. "They've torn down every house around me, I don't really have any neighbours," he said. "The only neighbours I have are Haitians right here and they don't really bother me."

They moved in around four years ago, Johnson added, "but there's a lot of them". He referenced "the driving problems".

This is a view shared by other residents in Springfield - a perception that traffic accidents increased after the Haitian community arrived.

In 2023, an 11-year-old boy, Aiden Clark, was killed when his school bus overturned in a crash with a minivan. The van driver, Herman Joseph, originally from Haiti, did not have a valid US driver's licence and was jailed.

Aiden's father, Nathan Clark, later spoke at a Springfield City Commission meeting where he denounced politicians for using his son's death as a "political tool" to fuel anti-immigrant sentiment, saying his son was accidentally killed.

Johnson's concern is about the numbers and the speed of change. "Really it's the amount of them," he told the BBC. "If you come here you [should] come here legally. The Temporary Protected Status is done… it's time to go."

At a nearby grocery store run by Paschur Castelly, who left Haiti 20 years ago, most of the shelves are empty, except for those stocking religious candles and framed pictures of Catholic saints popular with this devout community.

With additional reporting by Gringo Wotshela

text:
Where a habeas corpus petitioner has alleged that Customs and Border Patrol officers invalidly issued her an order of expedited removal and wrongfully cancelled her H-1B visa upon her attempt to reenter the United States following her trip to Lebanon, the dismissal of the petition should be affirmed because (1) Congress, in the Immigration and Naturalization Act, has barred judicial review of such orders and (2) the petitioner does not fit within the statutory exception, 8 U.S.C. §1252(e)(2)(B).

“… [The petitioner], a Lebanese citizen, alleges that Customs and Border Patrol (‘CBP’) officers invalidly issued her an order of expedited removal and wrongfully cancelled her H-1B visa upon her attempt to reenter the United States at Boston Logan Airport following her trip to Lebanon. Because Congress, in the Immigration and Naturalization Act (‘INA’), has barred judicial review of such orders, see 8 U.S.C. §1252(a)(2), (e)(1), and [the petitioner] does not fit within the statutory exception, see id. §1252(e)(2)(B), (e)(5), we lack jurisdiction to review her claims. We affirm the district court’s dismissal of [the petitioner]’s petition for habeas corpus for lack of jurisdiction. …

“This appeal turns on whether this court has been deprived of jurisdiction over [the petitioner]’s amended habeas corpus petition. …

“We hold that we lack jurisdiction over [the petitioner]’s appeal. When [the petitioner] arrived at Logan Airport she was an ‘applicant for admission’ and subject to inspection by immigration officers. … Where, as here, ‘an immigration officer determines that an alien … who is arriving in the United States … is inadmissible under … section 1182(a)(7) of this title, the officer shall order the alien removed from the United States without further hearing or review unless the alien indicates either an intention to apply for asylum … or a fear of persecution.’ 8 U.S.C. §1225(b)(1)(A)(i).

“We are barred from reviewing [the petitioner]’s challenge to her expedited removal order by §1252(a)(2)(A)(i), which precludes judicial review of ‘any individual determination or … any other cause or claim arising from or relating to the implementation or operation of an order of removal pursuant to section 1225(b)(1),’ unless it fits within one of §1252(e)(2)’s three narrow exceptions in habeas cases. [the petitioner] challenges the validity of her expedited removal order, not whether it has issued. Only the second exception, §1252(e)(2)(B), is relevant here. Nothing in the text of §1252(e)(2)(B) gives us jurisdiction over [the petitioner]’s challenge. …

“We affirm the district court’s dismissal of [the petitioner]’s petition for habeas corpus for lack of jurisdiction.”

Alawieh v. Mullin, et al. (Lawyers Weekly No. 01-229-26) (14 pages) (Lynch, J.) Appealed from a decision by Sorokin, J., in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts. Sadaf Hasan, with whom Reem Subei, Muslim Advocates, Mark Fleming and National Immigrant Justice Center were on brief, for the petitioner-appellant; Christina Luo, Cynthia D. Vreeland and Wilmer Cutler Pickering Hale and Dorr LLP on brief for American Immigration Council, American Immigration Lawyers Association, Creating Law Enforcement Accountability & Responsibility, The National Immigration Project of the National Lawyers Guild, The National Immigration Law Center and Van Der Hout LLP as amici curiae supporting the appellant; Joshua A. Clem, with whom James J. Walker, Anthony P. Nicastro, Drew C. Ensign and Brett A. Shumate were on brief, for the respondents-appellees (Docket No. 25-2238) (Oct. 13, 2026).

text:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has launched a nationwide operation targeting illegal immigrants accused of fraudulently obtaining benefits through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), resulting in multiple arrests, Fox News has learned.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) confirmed the operation to Fox News, announcing several arrests of illegal immigrants accused of fraudulently receiving SNAP benefits.

“Illegal aliens who have no right to be here in the first place are the last people who should be using SNAP benefits and other forms of welfare,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement.

“These programs are for Americans only,” he continued. “Even non-violent illegal alien crime can still have devastating consequences when they’re defrauding the American taxpayer.”

Mullin said those already apprehended and deported by federal authorities represented “just a drop in the bucket,” adding that the Trump administration would continue pursuing individuals accused of fraud.

DHS identified several illegal immigrants accused of SNAP fraud, including multiple Haitian nationals.

According to federal officials, Rubstony Junior Theodore, a Haitian national living illegally in the United States, was arrested by ICE as part of the operation.

Theodore’s criminal history includes arrests for larceny, obstruction of officers and trespassing, DHS said.

Three other Haitian nationals living illegally in the United States — Wilbert Jean Baptiste, Louis Jean and Jhensly Charles — were also arrested, according to DHS.

Elizabeth Povea Rodriguez, a Cuban national living illegally in the United States who was previously convicted of disorderly conduct and arrested on battery and domestic violence allegations, was also arrested, according to DHS.

“These arrests mark the opening salvo in a sustained, large-scale ICE operation specifically targeting illegal aliens who have fraudulently accessed SNAP benefits that American taxpayers fund exclusively for U.S. citizens in need,” DHS said.

“Every one of these individuals entered the country unlawfully, then proceeded to draw from a program designed to feed struggling American families, in some cases while carrying criminal records,” the agency continued.

Federal law generally bars immigrants living in the country illegally from receiving SNAP benefits, although certain categories of lawfully present noncitizens may qualify for the program.

DHS said the Trump administration would continue targeting alleged SNAP fraud as part of a broader crackdown on misuse of federal benefits.

SAN JOSE — U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrested a person Tuesday morning in San Jose, according to a coalition that tracks ICE activity in Santa Clara County.

RELATED: San Jose man charged in Trump DOJ voting crackdown says he’s never voted

The incident happened around 11:30 a.m. at West Hedding Street and North San Pedro Drive, near the Santa Clara County Main Jail, the Rapid Response Network said in a social media post.

RRN members arrived at the scene around 11:50 a.m. and confirmed ICE agents were no longer in the area.

Additional details about the arrest were not immediately available.

On Monday, RRN said there have been no raids or surge in ICE enforcement in the South Bay.

Tuesday’s arrest follows two others in the East Bay. On Friday, ICE agents arrested one person in Emeryville and another in Oakland, according to the Alameda County Immigration Legal Education Partnership. They both suffered injuries that required hospitalization.

The organization accused agents of using “excessive force against the people they detained.”

Check back for updates.

title: Citizenship in a Limbo - Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy
description:
Article 11 of the Constitution has played a central role in the defence of the Citizenship Amendment Act of 2019.
It was claimed that Article 11 exempts citizenship law from any form of constitutional objection, that even encompasses part III (fundamental rights) of the constitution.
Pursuant to Article 11, it is the Parliament that is empowered to write down laws concerning Indian citizenship and the Parliament has indeed altered and modified the conditions of citizenship from time to time.
Sunali and her family are now stranded in a geopolitical limbo, having been arrested by Bangladeshi authorities for illegal infiltration.
However, the concern is, that the Court is rarely called upon to legislate in these matters of citizenship or immigration but rather to ensure that the process of determination of citizenship does not traverse due process.
text:
**Tiyasha

Introduction

The Supreme Court in Louis De Raedt and later in Sarbananda Sonowal held that the power of the Government of India to expel foreigners is absolute and unlimited and there is no provision in the Constitution fettering its discretion. Although delivered in the context of a self-admitted foreign national, years later, the constitutionally grave implications of this pronouncement are palpable.

Article 11 of the Constitution has played a central role in the defence of the Citizenship Amendment Act of 2019. It was claimed that Article 11 exempts citizenship law from any form of constitutional objection, that even encompasses part III (fundamental rights) of the constitution. Article 13 of the Constitution in clear language states that any law passed by the Parliament has to adhere to the constraints of the fundamental rights and thus citizenship laws are not outside the checks of Part III.

Despite of this seemingly straightforward proposition of what is constitutionally valid and what is ultra vires, the on-ground translation of this is rather mired with the trampling of due process, manifest arbitrariness owing to bureaucratic excess and the consequent crusade of basic rights. Pursuant to Article 11, it is the Parliament that is empowered to write down laws concerning Indian citizenship and the Parliament has indeed altered and modified the conditions of citizenship from time to time. For the purposes of this piece, the focus will be on the nascent Immigrants and Foreigners Act of 2025, the Immigration and Foreigners Order of 2025 and the May 2025 Ministry of Home Affairs letter laying down the procedure for deportation of illegal Bangladeshi nationals and Rohingyas. Before I engage with the deeper questions of constitutionality of these authorities, it is pertinent to note the current state of the process of ascertainment of citizenship in India.

What proof is enough?

Today, birth certificates, Passports or Aadhaar cards do not prove Indian citizenship. The Gauhati High Court has held that even electoral photo identity cards, PAN Cards, bank documents or land tax receipts are not sufficient to prove citizenship while a trial Court in Mumbai has held that electoral identity cards do prove a person’s citizenship.

In a press release in 2019, the Government of India stated that:

“citizenship can be proved by submitting any documents related to date and place of birth. However, a decision is yet to be taken on such acceptable documents. This is likely to include voter cards, passports, Aadhaar …….. documents relating to land or home or other similar documents issued by government officials. This list is likely to include more documents…”.

The sheer uncertainty in the language accentuates the grave vulnerability that persons, suspected of being illegal migrants, are subjected to. Justice Dhulia in one of his interviews referring to his own birth stated that during those times the idea of institutionalised registration of birth was elusive. In June 2026, the MEA stated that the Indian passport is a travel document and not a proof of citizenship. Passports are issed after a rigourous verification process conducted by the state authorities. Countries like the United States and the United Kingdom generally consider a valid passport as a strong evidence of nationality as the same is issued through a state-verified process, while the state retaining the power to revoke it in cases of fraud. In these circumstances, even minor discrepancies such as spelling errors or name changes or variations from transliteration are treated as fatal flaws that can prejudice the determination of citizenship.

On 20 June, 2025, the Delhi Police raided a slum in Rohini and detained a 25-year old Sunali Khatun, a pregnant domestic worker from West Bengal’s Birbhum district. She was detained along with her husband Danish and their eight-year old son Sabir. The family possessed localised identity cards, verified voter registration lists and official land records that dated back to 1956 tracing the last five generations of the family. However, the police demanded birth certificates, that had been lost in a recent slum fire. Bypassing a mandatory Home Ministry directive to verify citizenship claims with local authorities in her home state, the Foreigners’ Regional Registration Office (FRRO) summarily expelled the family to Bangladesh within six days based on a highly contested police “confession”. Sunali and her family are now stranded in a geopolitical limbo, having been arrested by Bangladeshi authorities for illegal infiltration. While her father has filed a habeas corpus writ petition in the Calcutta High Court, the matter may not be resolved in time, as she risks giving birth in Bangladesh before a final decision is rendered. Since May 2025, the Government of Assam has illegally “pushed-back” hundreds of persons-allegedly undocumented Bangladeshi migrants and Rohingya refugees into Bangladesh.

In this backdrop, what is the process of determining Indian citizenship? – Any person despite possessing valid documents may be suspected to be an illegal migrant on vague and remote grounds. This is exactly what the Indian Foreigner’s Act of 2025 does – it empowersthe Central Government to direct the removal of any foreigner on an “adverse security report” and the police to arrest any person without warrant against whom a reasonable suspicion of illegal migration exists. In most of these cases, the individual is neither appraised of the grounds for arrest nor furnished with the reports forming the basis of the adverse action. Veteran journalist R. Rajagopal disclosed that his application for renewal of his passport had got into a bind as his name was struck off the voter’s list during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in West Bengal. The Kolkata Police had sent an adverse report to the passport authorities mentioning the deletion of his name from the voter’s list. The passport office thereafter refrained from moving forward on his application.

According to the May 2025 Ministry of Home Affairs letter laying down the procedure for deportation of illegal Bangladeshi national and Rohingyas, all State Governments or UT Administrations have been empowered to detect, identify, conduct inquiry, deport illegal immigrants or detain them in holding centres. The Immigration and Foreigners Order of 2025 provides for the detention of foreigners and illegal migrants in holding centres and camps and is conspicuously silent as to the duration for which such persons are to be detained. And as empirical evidence shows, such persons have been detained for as long as ten years. It is this wide subjectivity in the exercise of discretion that renders the act arbitrary.

In May 2025, the Ministry of Home Affairs issued a circular to various states and union territories asking the authorities to accelerate the verification process of “suspected” Bangladeshis and Rohingyas illegally residing in India. This order on a plain reading is unchecked exercise of administrative discretion –no disclosure of grounds, no opportunity of constructive hearing given to the suspect, no maximum detention limits, no provision for legal assistance.

Suspicion to Expulsion: The Due Process Deficit

There are primarily two fundamental questions that arise from this context – Firstly, on what grounds will an individual be labelled as an illegal immigrant and secondly, given the extent of indeterminacy in this area, can a determination of such a magnitude be left solely in the hands of the executive with no effective scope of judicial review?

It is the uncertainty in the answer to the first question that affirms and reinforces the answer to the second question. Reflecting upon the status quo, the Parliament is yet to come up with a clear and coherent framework to ascertain Indian citizenship and therefore, the complete vesting of such powers in the executive is a precarious proposition. The Supreme Court has

held that the absence of arbitrary power is the sine qua non to rule of law with confined and defined discretion. Arbitrariness is uncanalised and unguided discretion bestowed upon the executive. Justice P.N Bhagwati had remarked that “mala fide exercise of power and arbitrariness are different lethal radiations emanating from the same vice; in fact the latter comprehends the former.”

The Apex Court in Sarbananda Sonowal reversed the burden of proof from the Government to the alleged illegal immigrant. In the former, when the burden of proof was on the government, it was exceedingly difficult to prove the illegality of the immigrant’s claims of citizenship. However, today when the burden is reversed the question that we grapple with is how does a suspected individual even prove his citizenship to the satisfaction of the government in the first place.

The enforcement of these laws by the authorities is exactly what was shunned by the Apex Court in Rahim Ali. The Court iterated that though the burden is on the foreigner to prove that he is an Indian, a mere allegation is not enough to doubt a person’s nationality. In the absence of substantial material to corroborate such claims, the Court observed, ‘it cannot be left to the untrammelled or arbitrary discretion of the authorities to initiate proceedings, which have life altering and very serious consequences for the person, based on hearsay or bald and vague allegation(s).”

In National Human Rights Commission v. State of Arunachal Pradesh, the Court held that the Indian State is obligated to protect the life and liberty of every human being, be he a citizen or otherwise. This approach of the judiciary is in line with Article 9 and 13 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR). Article 9 of the ICCPR states that everyone has the right to liberty and security of person and no on shall be subjected to arrest and detention.

Article 13 of the ICCPR reads thus:

“An alien lawfully in the territory of a State Party to the present Covenant may be expelled therefrom only in pursuance of a decision reached in accordance with law and shall, except where compelling reasons of national security otherwise require, be allowed to submit the

reasons against his expulsion and to have his case reviewed by, and be represented for the purpose before, a competent authority……”

The Human Rights Committee has commented that this protection does not extend to illegal migrants and aliens who have stayed longer than what the law or their permits allow, however, if the legality of an alien’s entry is in dispute, any decision on this point leading to his expulsion or deportation ought to be taken in accordance with article 13. Though India has made reservation to this Article in order to apply its own laws relating to foreigners, the point is to put forth the standard accepted by the international community – expulsion after the individual’s non-citizenship is conclusively decided in accordance with law.

The Foreigner’s Tribunals is now infamous for not serving notice on the suspected individuals or giving them an effective opportunity of defending their status as citizens and passing orders without adhering to the basic procedural guarantees. In July 2026, a bench comprising of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta set aside a series of judgements delivered by the Gauhati High Court that declared 27 individuals as foreigners. In most of these cases, the judgements had been passed ex-parte – no opportunity given to the individual to respond. The Apex Court shunned the mechanical exercise followed in determining citizenship – no service of notice, no analysis of the material forming the basis of the adjudication and no evaluation of evidence adduced by the State.

Expressly Constructing the Guardrails

The Apex Court in State of AP v. McDowell & Co. held that an enactment cannot be struck down on the grounds of it being arbitrary or unreasonable and that some constitutional infirmity has to be found before invalidating an Act. This was overruled in Shayara Bano v. Union of India. In Shayara Bano and the Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India, the Court pronounced that manifest arbitrariness is something done by the legislature capriciously, irrationally and/or without adequate determining principle. It is this “determining principle” that is elusive in the realm of India’s citizenship laws. As the situation presently stands, administrative actions undertaken in the course of detecting persons suspected of being illegal migrants is bereft of a discernible legal standard.

In Re: Section 6A of the Citizenship Act, 1955, (“Re Section 6A”) the Respondents argued that citizenship, external aggression, migration and other related issues are matters of foreign policy that are to be dealt by the government and thus must be excluded from the Court’s purview. In

upholding section 6A, the Court stated that Article 11 of the Constitution confers overriding powers upon the Parliament to make laws even when they are against other provisions.

The Court has taken an overtly cautious approach in not impinging on the powers of the legislature – something that is also evident in the SIR judgement (this time, with more authority in the hands of the Election Commission of India) – and correctly so. However, the concern is, that the Court is rarely called upon to legislate in these matters of citizenship or immigration but rather to ensure that the process of determination of citizenship does not traverse due process. It is imperative for the Apex Court to explicitly read certain limits, into the implementation of these laws as ex facie the law conferring the power prescribes no guardrails. In the same case, the Court held that a constitutional bench must be constituted to monitor the implementation of immigration and citizenship legislations.

The Supreme Court in Sonowal recognised illegal immigration as a threat to national security. However, unlike other areas of national security like decisions pertaining to warfare or military operations or defense acquisitions where the Executive has an upper hand, in the domain of immigration, actions of the executive are more susceptible to judicial scrutiny. This can be attributed to national security on one hand and the intersection of diversity, basic rights granted to both citizens and non-citizens, and protection against administrative excess on the other. The State machinery cannot use security as a blanket justification for deportation and detention.

In light of this, it is not appropriate to leave the responsibility of oversight in the hands of administrative or even quasi-judicial bodies (as can be deduced from the workings of the foreigner’s tribunals). The elevated standards of independence, impartiality and procedural fairness that is required in the process of this ascertainment of citizenship, is embodied only in the judiciary. However, the problem with judicial scrutiny is that such excesses are checked on an individual basis. Given the pervasiveness of these instances, the need is for the Court to clearly lay down a set of general legal principles that the administrative authorities are obligated to adhere to in the course of ascertainment of citizenship.

In Re Section 6A, the Court stated that any law pertaining to citizenship has to be congruent to Article 14, and review for intelligible differentia and manifest arbitrariness and that the Court has the authority to review the same. Executive supremacy in this domain does not preclude judicial supervision. To borrow from Mr. Gautam Bhatia, “Citizenship – like the fundamental rights, the directive principles, the federal structure, and the rest of the Constitution – were part of a coherent web of principle, not single strands floating in the air”.

**Tiyasha is a law student at Symbiosis Law School.

title: They Fled Ethiopia's War. Now, Israel May Send Them Back. - Foreign Policy
authors: Theia Chatelle, David E. Rosenberg, Shalom Lipner, Sharon Weinberger, Cullen Hendrix, Michael Poznansky, Ian Easton, Emma Ashford, Howard W. French, Daniel S. Hamilton
description:
Of the Ethiopians in Israel who are not Jewish, some—such as Habteab—fled during the Tigray war and its aftermath.
“It’s presented as giving them another chance, but in reality, they’re just being called in to be told they have to leave,” Paul Strauss said.
“She turns to me, ‘Please help me, save my life,’ and I have nothing to give her,” Paul Strauss said.
Paul Strauss spends hours filling in resettlement forms with families who cannot afford a lawyer.
Each time Paul Strauss submits a file, she said, the U.N. representative reminds her that completing it does not guarantee placement elsewhere.
text:
JERUSALEM—For 75 days starting in 2020, Luwam Habteab slept on the floor of a prison cell, given little food and no medical care. She was detained that November by Ethiopian security forces for her reporting on the Axum massacre, in which Eritrean forces killed hundreds of civilians over a weekend—one of the deadliest episodes of the 2020-22 Tigray war.

Upon her release, Habteab found that her apartment had been sealed by federal police. Her family had warned her not to return there, telling her that security forces were waiting. A local archbishop with a connection at the Israeli Embassy interceded, after which Habteab was ushered out of the country. She landed in Tel Aviv in August 2023 and applied for asylum. (Habteab is identified by a pseudonym out of fear of reprisal.)

Habteab now lives in Jerusalem’s Old City, where she spends most of her days praying. As of August, she was one of 1,334 Ethiopians with open asylum claims before Israel’s Interior Ministry, according to figures that the ministry confirmed to Foreign Policy.

Months after Habteab arrived, in January 2024, the Israeli Interior Ministry determined that the situation in Ethiopia was stable enough to send its nationals home, revoking the group protection that had shielded asylum-seekers from deportation. That stability did not last: This July, Tigray’s regional authorities declared that the 2022 peace agreement with the federal government had collapsed, accusing Addis Ababa of preparing for war.

Last month, an alliance of rebel groups launched a full-scale offensive against federal forces, seizing airports across Tigray and pushing into neighboring Afar and Amhara states. Federal forces have since retaken Tigray’s capital, though the rebels have vowed to keep fighting; Eritrea and Ethiopia have cut diplomatic ties. Explosions have been reported in Addis Ababa, which Israeli authorities say is safe for returnees.

Habteab has watched with dread as the fighting returned to her home province. Much of Tigray is under a communications blackout, reviving fears of the total siege during the 2020-22 war that starved the region and killed as many as 600,000 people. Habteab’s family in Tigray is almost impossible to reach, she said.

With Israel’s national elections set for Oct. 27, civil society advocates warn that right-wing politicians are once again casting asylum-seekers as a threat to gain a leg up. Israeli officials refer to some migrants and refugees as “infiltrators,” a term embedded in the country’s own laws, and successive governments have described their presence as a danger to Israel’s Jewish character.

Habteab and other asylum-seekers in Israel have few places left to go as domestic politics turn against them and Western governments dismantle the asylum system that was supposed to protect them.

Israel has a long history with the notion of asylum. Founded by refugees in the wake of the Holocaust as a safe haven for the Jewish diaspora, the country was among the first signatories of the 1951 Refugee Convention. Jewish jurists were instrumental in shaping the convention’s core nonrefoulement principle, the rule that no one may be returned to a country where their life is at risk.

Yet, since the Israeli government took over processing asylum claims from the United Nations in 2009, it has granted asylum status to less than 1 percent of those seeking it, according to HIAS Israel, a Jewish humanitarian nonprofit.

Israel has also long held a place in the imagination of Ethiopian asylum-seekers as the land of the ancient Israelites, in whose story of exile and return they saw themselves. In practical terms, the country was also the closest state offering asylum that they could reach without undertaking the perilous Mediterranean crossing.

Of the Ethiopians in Israel who are not Jewish, some—such as Habteab—fled during the Tigray war and its aftermath. But most have been in Israel for a decade or more, arriving on pilgrimage visas or by crossing the Egyptian border before Israel completed its fence there in 2013. They, too, are asylum-seekers: Almost all applied for protection after arriving, having fled earlier rounds of interethnic violence and state persecution, according to the Jerusalem African Community Center (JACC), a support and advocacy organization for the city’s African asylum-seekers.

On arrival, they opened asylum claims with the Interior Ministry and were interviewed about why they had come to Israel. Under Israeli law, the ministry was meant to review each claim and decide whether to grant refugee status—a process that, for most of these asylum-seekers, didn’t happen. Now, according to advocates, many Ethiopian applicants are being summoned back after more than a decade for a second interview to determine whether they can stay in Israel.

Asked for comment, Israel’s Population and Immigration Authority said, “there is no policy of deportation regarding this group” and that cases are examined individually. The authority added that it does not determine whether a country is safe for returnees, referring questions to the Israeli Foreign Ministry. (The Foreign Ministry did not respond to a request for comment.)

Anat Ben-Dor, who runs the Refugee Rights Clinic at Tel Aviv University, said the burden of proof placed on applicants for asylum to establish a credible fear of persecution is set very high and that interviewers look for inconsistencies between what an applicant says now and what they said on arrival.

“The whole interview is actually an effort not to find the truth, but to find flaws and problems in the testimony,” Ben-Dor said. “Very few people can successfully pass such an interview, particularly when the system is so slow that people are being interviewed about events that sometimes occurred 10 years earlier.”

Asked whether the system was dysfunctional or intentionally obstructive, Michal Pomeranz, another lawyer who represents asylum-seekers, said it was both. “They clearly want to make people’s lives here miserable, and that’s something even the Supreme Court has said,” she said, referring to a 2020 ruling that struck down a law requiring asylum-seekers to deposit 20 percent of their wages into a fund that they could recover only by leaving the country.

After the follow-up interview, the Interior Ministry decides whether an asylum-seeker may stay in Israel or must leave—but the outcome is almost always the same, according to Yael Paul Strauss, who runs the psychosocial department at JACC.

By her account, 90 percent to 95 percent of those summoned are rejected and given three to four months to leave the country. “It’s presented as giving them another chance, but in reality, they’re just being called in to be told they have to leave,” Paul Strauss said.

The cost of contesting a rejection is steep, running at around $4,000 to petition a denied application and another $4,000 for an appeal, according to Paul Strauss. Few employers will hire someone with a temporary permit, regardless of their profession or level of education in Ethiopia, leaving most asylum-seekers with few ways to raise that kind of money.

Paul Strauss described a message that she had recently received from a mother of three small children who had paid to appeal her asylum rejection, lost, and had no idea where she would find the money to try again. “She turns to me, ‘Please help me, save my life,’ and I have nothing to give her,” Paul Strauss said.

When he returned to office in 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump effectively dismantled the U.S. refugee admissions program and suspended the entry of all refugees into the country, including those who had already been screened. Following legal challenges, the Trump administration resumed limited admissions under a historically low cap of 7,500 refugees for fiscal year 2026—admissions that have been allocated almost entirely to white South African Afrikaners.

In December 2025, the Trump administration also terminated the temporary protected status that Ethiopians were granted during the Tigray war. Around 900 asylum-seekers in Israel—mainly Sudanese and Eritrean, along with some Ethiopians—were in the pipeline to be resettled to the United States as of early 2025, according to Sivan Carmel, the country director of HIAS Israel, which processed the cases.

Some had already cleared their medical and security checks, had departure dates, and needed only plane tickets. “They’d left their jobs; they’d already told their landlords they’d be leaving” before their entry to the United States was denied, Carmel said.

The office of the U.N. refugee agency in Israel, which referred those cases and managed resettlement out of the country, has been hollowed out as part of the same pattern of global retrenchment against asylum—its staff reduced to three and its Tel Aviv office cut. Agency staff struggle to keep up with the thousands of open asylum claims.

This has left the work to fall to groups such as JACC, which operates on a shoestring budget. Paul Strauss spends hours filling in resettlement forms with families who cannot afford a lawyer. Each time Paul Strauss submits a file, she said, the U.N. representative reminds her that completing it does not guarantee placement elsewhere.

For those who cannot leave for another country and cannot stay in Israel, the return of war to Ethiopia has taken away their last consolation: the hope that the danger that they fled might be in the past. As armed forces push toward Ethiopia’s capital and much of Tigray remains in the dark, many of the families that Israel intends to send back can’t even get in touch with their relatives.

For those working on behalf of the asylum-seekers, the bigger picture is not lost. “I want to live in a state that I’m not embarrassed by,” Pomeranz said. “I kept thinking things couldn’t get worse. They keep getting worse.”
