title: Will the Supreme Court Finally Dismantle Bivens's House of Cards? - Lawfare
description:
On Nov. 9, the Supreme Court will hear oral arguments in Nielsen v. Watanabe, an Eighth Amendment case that could end remedies under Bivens altogether.
The Supreme Court granted certiorari on the availability of an Eighth Amendment remedy.
Nielsen is unusual in that the briefing complicates rather than sharpens the core choices for the Supreme Court.
The government relies on Teague v. Lane and Cisco, cases in which the Supreme Court reconsidered a doctrine at its source.
The Supreme Court should accept Nielsen’s invitation to overrule Bivens, saying plainly what its cases already mean, and finally fold the shaky house of cards for good.
text:
In the wake of the fatal shootings of Alex Pretti, Renee Good, and Johan Sebastián Guerrero, many Americans were dismayed to learn of what the Cato Institute calls “the legal black hole” in which federal law enforcement officers operate. Unlike their counterparts in state agencies, federal agents cannot be sued under 42 U.S.C. § 1983.

In theory, Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics (1971) permits claims against federal agents directly under the Constitution. But the steady erosion of Bivens on various doctrinal grounds has left plaintiffs—no matter how meritorious—with vanishingly small odds of ever recovering more than a vague promise of potential liability someday in some other case. Indeed, the authors personally know of only one Bivens case in the past two decades in which a jury’s verdict for the plaintiff has withstood appeal. (We reluctantly turned to artificial intelligence as a last resort. It could not even hallucinate additional examples.)

On Nov. 9, the Supreme Court will hear oral arguments in Nielsen v. Watanabe, an Eighth Amendment case that could end remedies under Bivens altogether. Eliminating even this narrow possibility for constitutional accountability has attracted significant, understandable alarm from big names ranging from the Cato Institute and the Constitutional Accountability Center to prominent law professors such as Stephen I. Vladeck, James Pfander, and Alexander Reinert.

This article’s authors, on the other hand, would welcome Bivens’s demise. And not just because, as former Department of Justice career lawyers, we spent a combined half century defending members of the federal workforce.

The problem with Bivens is that, from any ideological perspective, it is a deeply inadequate means of addressing constitutional wrongs. Ending Bivens would be less of a bang than a whimper. And it could spur Congress to take long-overdue action—just as it did after Chisholm v. Georgia (1793), after Dred Scott v. Sanford (1857), after Westfall v. Erwin (1988), after Employment Division v. Smith (1990), after FDA v. Brown & Williamson Tobacco (2000), after Toyota v. Williams (2002), and after Ledbetter v. Goodyear (2007). For the prospect of real federal constitutional accountability, a tort doctrine of essentially pyrrhic value would be a small price to pay.

Nielsen v. Watanabe: The Easy Case That Asks a Hard Question

Nielsen v. Watanabe concerns a prison nurse’s (Nielsen’s) alleged delay in referring an inmate (Watanabe) to a medical specialist for what turned out months later to be a fractured tailbone. We agree with Neilsen’s counsel, Jeffrey Lamken: Under what remains of the Bivens doctrine, “[t]his should have been an easy case” in which to conclude that no Bivens remedy was available. And we admire the skill Watanabe’s counsel, Samuel Weiss, deploys in making the best possible argument to the contrary. But the fact remains that, even taking Watanabe’s allegations as true, the claim resembles garden-variety negligence far more closely than any scenario in which the Court has ever sanctioned a constitutional claim.

The closest analog is Estelle v. Gamble (1976), a § 1983 case over an allegedly undertreated back injury in which the Supreme Court famously declared that “[m]edical malpractice does not become a constitutional violation merely because the victim is a prisoner.” In short, under any fair reading of the modern case law, Watanabe loses. The harder question is whether his case takes Bivens down with it.

Background

By all accounts, Nielsen—the staff nurse sued for $3 million—saw Watanabe, the inmate, only once, in July 2021. This was in the immediate aftermath of a gang riot at FDC Honolulu, in which Watanabe had been beaten severely with a “lock in a sock.” Watanabe alleges that Nielsen told him to “stop being a crybaby” and refused to send him to a hospital. (On this latter point, it is worth noting that under Bureau of Prisons policy, the decision to transport an inmate to an outside medical provider appears to be above Nielsen’s pay grade.)

For months, according to Watanabe, prison officials (not Nielsen) denied him medical attention beyond over-the-counter painkillers. In February 2022, Watanabe was diagnosed with a fractured coccyx and promised a visit to an outside specialist. By July 2022, Watanabe was still waiting. Apparently attempting to prompt agency action, Watanabe, then acting pro se, filed an Eighth Amendment lawsuit against Nielsen personally under Bivens.

The Current Bivens Standard

As the law stands now, a Bivens claim cannot move forward without first surviving a virtually insurmountable separation-of-powers inquiry that favors judicial abstention:

A) Does the case present “a new Bivens context”—meaning does it differ “meaningfully” from Bivens, Davis v. Passman, and Carlson v. Green?

B) If so, do any “special factors” even “arguably” suggest that Congress is better suited than the courts to “weigh the costs and benefits of allowing a damages action to proceed”?

Courts now repeatedly warn that implying remedies is “disfavored.” Modern doctrine sets an exceedingly low bar for finding a “special factor.” It is difficult to imagine a future Bivens claim that could survive a faithful application of this level of scrutiny.

Even in the unlikely event that a court applying recent precedent nonetheless implies a constitutional remedy over the objection of Justice Department-represented federal defendants, a plaintiff must next confront qualified immunity. Qualified immunity protects federal officials unless they personally violate a right so clearly established that any reasonable officer would have behaved otherwise. The future of qualified immunity is an issue for another day, but suffice it to say the doctrine has a chorus of detractors. The Supreme Court applies the doctrine so generously in law enforcement cases that Justice Sonia Sotomayor has accused her colleagues of “tell[ing] the public that palpably unreasonable conduct will go unpunished.” It is against this backdrop that Watanabe sued for alleged deliberate indifference to his medical needs.

Nielsen’s Procedural Posture

The district court dismissed the case on “special factors” grounds, citing alternative remedies under the Bureau of Prisons’s Administrative Remedy Program and the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA). The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed and denied rehearing en banc, holding that Watanabe should have been allowed to sue Nielsen under the Eighth Amendment.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari on the availability of an Eighth Amendment remedy. Importantly, this is the only question before the Court. No court has explored in discovery, let alone determined, what actually happened between Nielson and Watanabe, whether (or how) the Bureau of Prisons denied Watanabe medical care, or whether any aspect of his treatment was “cruel and unusual.”

Petitioner and respondent have now filed their merits briefs. Three amici support Nielsen: the United States, a coalition of 19 states, and an attorney and self-described whistleblower. A bevy of amicus briefs support Watanabe.

The Hard Question: How Much of Bivens to Raze?

As it stands, as a practical matter, the Supreme Court has affirmatively recognized an implied constitutional tort remedy against individual federal law enforcement officers in only two contexts: Bivens itself (a Fourth Amendment claim for a warrantless search inside a home), and Carlson (an Eighth Amendment deliberate indifference claim by a federal prisoner). A third case, Davis recognized a remedy for a Fifth Amendment claim by a congressional staffer who alleged she was fired because of her gender, but subsequent federal statutory developments made that context obsolete. In response to the exploding use of the Bivens remedy, particularly in the post-9/11 era, the Supreme Court spent basically the next half century explaining when and why a constitutional tort remedy does not exist.

Nielsen is unusual in that the briefing complicates rather than sharpens the core choices for the Supreme Court. Watanabe, of course, advocates for Carlson’s preservation (and, by implication, Bivens). Nielsen invites the Court to use the case as an opportunity to confront and overrule Bivens, for reasons we essentially agree with: the Supreme Court’s repudiation of its core reasoning, the doctrine’s unworkability in practice, the false hope Bivens gives litigants, and the cover it gives Congress for failing to act. No surprises there.

More curious is the government’s proposal: Do not overrule anything just yet. Merely “clarify that Carlson is now moribund” and leave the question of the future of Bivens for a later Fourth Amendment case (maybe). The government’s suggestion would sweep all federal prisoner claims off the table while leaving Bivens itself nominally alive. The government offers no explanation for its preference for such an artificially narrow ruling. And the government’s willingness to read prisoner cases out of existence entirely while leaving Bivens’s corpse on the table is as doctrinally backward as it is unsettling.

Our Hot Take: Bivens Is a Teardown

We do not know why the government would prefer that the Court address Carlson but not Bivens, when the cases’ legal and theoretical underpinnings are virtually indistinguishable. Even those amici who argue that Watanabe ought to be allowed to sue a prison medical provider under the Eighth Amendment for an alleged delay in medical care generally acknowledge, at least implicitly, that Carlson and Bivens rise—or theoretically fall—together. That is a point with which we agree, and it exposes why the government’s position misses the mark. For the most part, the amici set aside the past 50 years of Supreme Court precedent in favor of a paradigm that treats common law constitutional damages actions as the historical status quo. The few amici who do squarely confront that intervening half century, such as Vladeck, candidly acknowledge they do so to explain why the Court’s later approach to shrinking Bivens got it wrong.

Neither Watanabe nor his supporting amici grapple in any significant way with the practical realities of litigating implied remedies in the constitutional-tort arena—the realities actual judges confront in actual cases. Congress needs to step in. The plethora of scholarly theories that have developed in an attempt to discern which federal or state common-law claims may (or may not) continue to coexist alongside modern federal statutes like the Westfall Act (making a claim against the United States the exclusive remedy for certain common-law torts) and the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (permitting lawsuits for government activity that substantially burdens religious exercise) bear this out. If the rules governing those remedies need recalibration—or more importantly, setting in the first instance—and 50 years of litigation make clear that they do, Congress—not a series of ad hoc judicial adjustments—is the institution in which the solution properly lies.

Perhaps surprisingly, many of the government’s other arguments give us pause. For just one example, its discussion of modern “special factors” analysis is oversimplified: The brief all but ignores the central difference between Nielsen and Carlson, what Nielsen’s counsel describes as “the immediacy of the inmate’s medical emergency and death.” This matters because in a life-threatening emergency—such as Carlson—potential administrative and equitable relief cannot address the constitutional violation. The government buries the point under a digression on state survivorship law and the costs of off-site medical care.

The government also repeatedly invokes the political branches’ “special province” in running prisons. The deferential standard articulated in Turner v. Safley, with respect to day-to-day prison administration, is simply not on par with military, national security, or border security concerns—each with explicit textual roots in the Constitution that carry significant separation-of-powers weight when raised appropriately—that the government invokes here. And then there are the arguments (mostly from the government) that, in our view, warrant special attention because they attempt to cabin Carlson yet belie the fundamental instability of the Bivens doctrine itself. We address those here:

Continuing to Indulge the Fiction of a “Moribund” Remedy Serves No One

Even as it concedes that Bivens litigation involving prisons is dead, the government asks the Supreme Court to “clarify that Carlson is now moribund” rather than overrule it. As the Court observes in Edwards v. Vannoy (2021), “continuing to indulge” a fiction that offers litigants no real chance of success “misleads litigants and judges” and “needlessly expends the scarce resources of” courts and counsel.

The government does not dispute this point. Instead, it quotes the same line, inexplicably replacing Edwards’s “litigants” with “prisoners.” The government does not explain how zombie case law such as Carlson and Bivens would somehow cause less harm if labeled “moribund.” Nor does the brief explain why Carlson is any more worthy of the designation than the equally dead letter of Bivens. This case is like Edwards. The Court should finally “acknowledg[e] reality and stat[e] the obvious.” The government offers no reason—compelling or otherwise—to ignore that reality.

Along the same lines, the practice of hollowing out precedent without overruling it is jurisprudentially muddy. The Court recently did something similar in Cisco Systems, Inc. v.Doe, leaving Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain technically on the books while draining it of any practical force. Certainly, the Court can overrule precedent even in far more consequential matters. But this is not housekeeping. A precedent left on the books can still govern issues the Court has not silently erased, while lower courts and litigants must guess what remains. If the Court means to write a case out of existence, it should have the institutional courage to say so. Judicial evasion not only is antidoctrinal, but it also invites legislative evasion.

Justices Neil Gorsuch and Clarence Thomas have already said that “the time has come to consider discarding the Bivens doctrine altogether.” Chief Justice John Roberts and Justices Samuel Alito, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett joined Cisco’s rejection of judge-made rights of action, a logically indistinguishable scenario. If anything, Cisco had stronger statutory support: There is an Alien TortStatute at least, with far greater specificity than the general federal question statute.

Nielsen offers Justices Elena Kagan, Ketanji Brown Jackson, and Sotomayor an opportunity grounded in constitutional accountability—not indifference—to agree with the other six: Overruling Bivens, rather than resurrecting it, is doctrinally sound and likely the only way to force serious consideration of a statutory remedy.

There Is No Principled Reason to Save the Bivens Question for Another Day

Bivens cases are extraordinarily expensive to litigate for everyone involved, including taxpayers. To name just a few of its unique burdens: lost employee productivity lost, agency resources diverted to meet discovery demands, qualified candidates deterred from federal service, and official judgment unduly compromised for fear of liability.

So we are mystified by the government’s insistence that the Supreme Court kick the Bivens question down the road to be addressed “in the context of a Fourth Amendment case that more closely resembles Bivens itself.” This, too, comes with no explanation. Surely the government would raise whatever benefit exists to postpone the inevitable. And if Bivens had enabled meaningful recovery for more than just the one plaintiff we know of in the past two decades, that would have been worth mentioning. The government’s silence on this point is deafening.

A third omission is also telling: The reference to “a Fourth Amendment case that more closely resembles Bivens itself” without acknowledging the petition for certiorari it filed in Herzon v. Arias this July. Herzon involves “a Fourth Amendment excessive-force claim arising out of the execution of an arrest warrant.” The government’s petition did not ask the Supreme Court to reconsider Bivens. Stranger still, the government’s Herzon brief alternatively asks the Supreme Court to hold Herzon for Nielsen—because Nielsen might recast the new-context inquiry—all without acknowledging the possible overruling of Bivens. The elephant remains squarely in the room.

Watanabe’s counsel correctly points out Carlson’s “unusually weighty” presence when it comes to prison litigation, and the danger of “redefining Carlson as a null set.” But far from being reasons to retain it, this is strong evidence for putting the entire judicial misadventure of implied constitutional tort “remedies” to rest. That is especially so when even Watanabe acknowledges that “Carlson would likely be decided differently today.”

Understandably, given his stake in Carlson’s survival, Watanabe and his amici stitch together a patchwork of unrelated federal statutes (for example, the Westfall Act and the Prison Litigation Reform Act) urging that Congress has somehow affirmatively endorsed Carlson’s “viability, scope, and substance.” Watanabe maintains Congress, not the Court, should overrule Carlson. But Congress has never tried to craft a damages remedy for the constitutional torts of federal actors—whether against federal inmates or anyone else—and no amount of creativity can fill that legislative vacuum.

True, as several amici point out, Congress has legislated around Bivens. But whatever might be gleaned from individual legislators or passing references in legislative history is a far cry from adopting a statutory remedy into law. Despite some amici’s protestations,Congress has not in fact “done the hard work.” To suggest otherwise places the cart miles ahead of the horse.

Equally as certain, adopting the government’s proposed half measure of a decision would leave judges with the Sisyphean task of applying precedents the Supreme Court refuses to either honor or overrule. It would also preserve the fiction that a federal damages remedy exists, allowing Congress to continue treating constitutional accountability as someone else’s problem. The Court should not wait for some mythic Fourth Amendment case identical to Bivens (which, remember, involved officers of the Federal Narcotics Bureau, a long-shuttered agency with no modern-day analog). By the government’s and indeed the Supreme Court’s own logic, one will never exist.

Every Argument for Declaring Carlson “Moribund” Counsels in Favor of Eliminating Bivens

The government gives renewed weight to the FTCA as an alternative remedy, even though Carlson rejected that argument. The government’s reasoning is summarized in four bulleted arguments, three of which apply equally outside the prison and Eighth Amendment contexts.

The government relies on Teague v. Lane and Cisco, cases in which the Supreme Court reconsidered a doctrine at its source. Cisco is particularly telling: It described the class of cases in which courts may create private rights of action without invading the political branches’ prerogatives as “in truth a null set.”

The government argues that current doctrine, faithfully applied, would “finish off Carlson entirely,” that later decisions rejected Carlson’s rationales, and that the decision was “egregiously wrong.” Every proposition applies at least as forcefully to Bivens, the source of the doctrine.

The government calls Carlson unworkable and invokes stare decisis values of evenhandedness, predictability, and consistency. Yet federal judges—not merely a litigant or amicus—have repeatedly identified Bivens itself as the source of the unworkability. And the government’s concluding principle supplies the answer: When the judiciary usurps authority assigned to Congress, it has an independent duty to correct the encroachment.

And perhaps our favorite of the government’s arguments, “Carlson also had harmful ‘jurisprudential and real-world effects.’”

Retiring the fiction of individual liability invites reform far more meaningful than briefly reviving Watanabe’s one Eighth Amendment claim. History suggests this must come from congressional oversight, public pressure, political consequences, official-capacity suits for declaratory and injunctive relief, and direct judgments against the United States.

A New Deck: Laying a Solid Foundation for Federal Constitutional Accountability

We, the authors, are eternal optimists. Reversing Bivens could bring us a gigantic step closer to sound federal statutory reform. A common sense, political and legislative consensus is achievable as early as the 2028 election cycle by finding common ground across a wide range of equity holders, from civil rights plaintiffs to federal law enforcement and carceral employees and their agencies, to federal courts, to the public at large.

When the horrors of Abu Ghraib—another failed Bivens context—surfaced, Congress intervened swiftly to prohibit waterboarding and limit interrogation practices. Congress has acted at other times when tort systems proved ill-suited to redress injuries that fairness and public opinion demanded be addressed. Consider the Vaccine Injury Compensation Act, the RadiationExposure Compensation Act, and the September 11th Victim Compensation Fund. These measures—including several recent amendments and extensions—illustrate that with enough motivation, Congress can design targeted tort and quasi-tort remedies that balance victim interests, public accountability, and institutional stability while insulating putative defendants who carry out vital federal functions.

We are in no position to speculate as to whether or why the Trump administration may prefer that Congress not address the fundamental quagmire that is Bivens. But leaving Bivens impotent on the books will lead to exactly that. Drawing on the practical lessons learned from litigating a broad range of Bivens claims, we encourage Congress to step up by crafting a statutory regime that serves victims, federal employees, courts, and the public. Our suggestions:

Create a statutory damages remedy for (a) Fourth Amendment misconduct by hands-on federal law enforcement officers and (b) Eighth Amendment violations when the nature of the injury makes administrative, declaratory, or injunctive relief impossible (such as in Carlson but not in Neilsen).

Pave the way for entity liability by waiving sovereign immunity to permit claims under these two theories based on unconstitutional federal conduct.

Pay judgments from agency funds.

Borrow from the FTCA provisions that make the United States the exclusive party responsible for acts and omissions committed within the scope of federal employment, except in a narrowly defined class of willful or wanton misconduct that could support punitive damages.

Foreclose individual-capacity liability for Cabinet officials and other senior policymakers whose reach extends nationwide (the claims best suited to resolution via alternative means, the most likely to discourage competent individuals from serving in federal office, and which involve so many plaintiffs that no individual could ever satisfy judgments).

Replace qualified immunity with clear statutory standards and procedures that give victims, federal employees, and courts more predictable outcomes.

The Supreme Court should accept Nielsen’s invitation to overrule Bivens, saying plainly what its cases already mean, and finally fold the shaky house of cards for good. Only then will Congress have to confront what federal constitutional accountability should actually look like.

text:
There is outrage in the Bronx following the arrest of a beloved immigrant in the community by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Aleksander Nilaj, founder of the Open Hand food bank in the Bronx, was detained last Monday while attending an immigration court hearing. He was taken to the Delaney Hall Detention Center in New Jersey.

Community members reacted to his sudden arrest.

“Since he’s been here, he’s been a blessing to the community," Bronx resident Alex told News 4. "So I don’t feel he should go back for something like that.”

Nilaj began this work about 20 years ago after immigrating to New York from Albania.

Congressman Ritchie Torres confirmed to News 4 that he has been fighting for his release.

“It’s an injustice against his family and the community that loves him,” Torres added. “The federal government should focus on the most violent and dangerous criminals, not on public servants like Alex.”

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security shared the following statement:

“On October 13, 2026, ICE detained Aleksander Nilaj, an undocumented immigrant from Albania. He legally entered the United States temporarily on October 1, 2006, and after his authorized stay expired, he remained in the country illegally, violating our laws. He received due process, and on July 22, 2008, an immigration judge ordered his removal.”

The food bank, located on Lydig Avenue, will not distribute food until Nilaj is released.

Several members of the community, especially the elderly, have relied on the meals provided by Open Hand.

“There are many elderly people here who need the food that comes with the fruit and vegetables,” said a local resident. “There are many people here who are in great need.”

Congressman Torres told News 4 that Nilaj has no criminal record or charges against him and that his lawyer would demand his release by filing an appeal.

text:
Following the arrest of a man swarmed by armed tactical officers and plainclothes agents in San Francisco, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement confirmed Tuesday that its officers carried out the operation.

Federal officials said agents from the ICE San Francisco field office arrested 51-year-old Milton Ramos-Rodriguez, a citizen of El Salvador, on Monday morning in the city's SoMa neighborhood.

According to ICE, Ramos-Rodriguez was previously deported from the U.S. and has a prior conviction in California for voluntary manslaughter.

Federal authorities did not provide details regarding the conviction or specify when he was originally deported. ICE officials also alleged Ramos-Rodriguez has ties to the Sureños gang, but did not elaborate on how that connection was established.

"ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) remains committed to protecting public safety by locating and arresting criminal aliens who pose threats to our communities," said ERO San Francisco acting Field Office Director Julio S. Hernandez in a statement. "This enforcement action reflects the dedicated work of our officers and law enforcement partners to uphold the law and prioritize the safety and security of the public."

Bystander footage captures arrest

The operation took place Monday morning outside 360 6th Street. Video clips shared by an anonymous witness show Ramos-Rodriguez, dressed in a suit, backed against a metal grate and wall as officers move in.

"I'm not doing anything," Ramos-Rodriguez can be heard saying as at least four men struggle to detain him.

In one clip, a plainclothes agent wearing a red flannel shirt and a badge around his neck brandishes a firearm. Three other agents wearing tactical gear have their faces covered.

"I'm a U.S. citizen. You're not supposed to touch me," Ramos-Rodriguez says in the video, repeatedly asking to see the officers' badges and telling them, "Don't touch me."

Ramos-Rodriguez was eventually handcuffed and led away by agents. He remains in ICE custody.

Advocates, city officials respond

The San Francisco Rapid Response Network said it is aware of the video footage and is in contact with the San Francisco Public Defender's Office regarding the immigration case.

On Tuesday, city officials announced an emergency rally for immigrant services on the steps of City Hall.

At that rally, Ramos-Rodriquez's lawyer with the SF Public Defender's Office, Francisco Ugarte, said he is working to determine his client's immigration background and verify the allegations that his client is a criminal.

"That's what they always do," Ugarte said. They call everyone criminals. They call everyone felons. It's the language of criminalization that's very powerful that tends to win popular support. But we're catching up to that. So, I don't think we can trust anything that they say."

Ugarte said he's working to mount a defense in this case and others. "We're just going to fight back very, very hard. We are united on the political, the organizers, the ground, the lawyers. We're acting better than we've ever acted. We're responding immediately to arrests. We're getting people out of jail."

On the day of the arrest, the public defender's office issued a scathing statement.

"It is outrageous for a plainclothes ICE agent to pull a gun on someone walking down the streets of our city," the public defender's office said. "Our Immigration Defense Unit is mobilizing to ensure that the man has legal representation. We are part of a robust network of Bay Area immigrant rights advocates who will not tolerate violence by ICE agents in our communities."

Immigration legal services budget

The detention brought broad condemnation from other San Francisco city leaders who said they will not stand by and allow immigration officials to snatch people off the streets without due process. Supervisor Jackie Fielder announced that she is introducing an emergency budget supplemental to direct funds to immigration legal services.

"We cannot wait for things to get worse in San Francisco," said District 9 Supervisor Jackie Fielder, who represents the Mission District, which has a large Latino population and cultural district. "That is why today I'm introducing a piece of legislation to enhance funding for local immigration services and the Rapid Response Network.

Board President Rafael Mandelman promised to fast track the plan.

"This, I am confident, will be very unanimous. We will waive the 30-day rule. The mayor will sign it and we will get the money flowing as soon as we possibly can.

The immigration case

At this point, we don't have a court date for when Ramos-Rodriguez's case will go before an immigration judge. City leaders said this is an example of why they have to act now.

text:
Mexico is once again expressing concern for the safety of its citizens in the United States after a recent death in a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement processing center.

Mexico’s foreign ministry said in a statement the man who died after being held at the facility in Laredo, Texas, on Saturday is the 18th Mexican national to die in immigration custody or enforcement operations since the start of the second Trump administration.

“The situation demands an effective response from U.S. authorities to guarantee the life, safety and human rights of migrants,” the ministry said.

ICE says 56-year-old Emiliano Andrade was found unresponsive at the Rio Grande Processing Center and his cause of death remains unknown pending an autopsy.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum also called for human rights protections for her citizens living in the United States at her daily press conference Monday.

“They are always going to have an ally in Mexico,” Sheinbaum said of Mexican migrants in the United States.

Sheinbaum said Mexico has been in touch with Andrade’s family, who says he may not have been receiving sufficient medical care while detained. ICE said in a statement Andrade had a medical history that included diabetes, hypertension and anxiety, and that he received proper medical care while detained.

The agency says Andrade was a lawful permanent resident of the United States and was detained by U.S. Customs and Border Protection in June while crossing the border. ICE claims Andrade failed to disclose a 2004 arrest during immigration proceedings, leading to fraudulent legal status in the United States.

Mexico has for months complained about the treatment of Mexican citizens in ICE detention centers, as the number of deaths in ICE custody grows. That includes the deaths of two Mexican nationals in Arizona since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term.

Mexico’s foreign ministry says it filed a complaint with the Webb County district attorney requesting a thorough investigation into Andrade’s death. That follows several other similar complaints Mexico says it has filed with prosecutors’ offices in other parts of the United States where Mexican nationals have died in ICE custody.

UPDATE: The Borough of Red Bank has issued a statement describing the incident as a pursuit of a suspect by ICE agents that resulted in a crash injuring an agent and the target of the operation. Borough officials are also asking county and state officials to investigate the incident. See update below.

Federal immigration agents arrested at least two people after what appeared to be a traffic accident involving one of their cars in Red Bank Friday morning.

Multiple videos posted to social media show immigration agents arresting at least two men as numerous law enforcement officers converged in unmarked cars on Catherine Street just east of Shrewsbury Avenue near Juanito’s grocery.

The contents of the videos was confirmed by redbankgreen interviews with eyewitnesses.

The videos also show a green pickup truck facing westbound on Catherine Street nose-to-nose with an eastbound facing grey sedan and what appears to be steam or smoke rising from one of the cars.

An ambulance arrives on the scene, but it is unclear from the videos if anyone received treatment.

Multiple cars and trucks, including at least two with covered license plates were parked on the scene as a mix of masked and unmasked agents detain two people and appear to be investigating vehicles on the scene.

Red Bank Police officers arrive on the scene as the area is taped off with crime scene tape.

An email to U.S. Customs and Immigration Enforcement’s media office seeking information went unreturned.

Several hours after this post was published, the Borough of Red Bank issued the following press release. redbankgreen is publishing it in its entirety.

“RED BANK, NJ – The Borough of Red Bank is providing the following information regarding an incident involving U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents that occurred earlier this morning in the vicinity of the Red Bank Train Station.

Based on information currently available, ICE agents attempted to conduct a traffic stop of a vehicle near the Red Bank Train Station. The vehicle did not stop, and the subsequent pursuit continued several blocks to Catherine Street, where the vehicle was involved in a collision with a vehicle operated by an ICE agent.

The Red Bank Police Department was not notified of any planned ICE enforcement activity within the Borough and had no prior knowledge of or involvement in the federal operation. Red Bank officers became involved only after the collision occurred, when they were called to the scene to conduct a motor vehicle accident investigation.

Both the driver of the pursued vehicle and an ICE agent sustained minor injuries as a result of the collision. Both vehicles were rendered inoperable and subsequently towed from the scene.

The Borough wishes to reiterate that the Red Bank Police Department did not participate in the federal enforcement operation or the attempted traffic stop. The Department’s involvement was limited to responding to and investigating the resulting motor vehicle accident.

The Borough urges the appropriate county and state agencies to conduct a further review of the circumstances surrounding this incident to ensure a thorough and independent examination of the actions taken. Additionally, the Borough encourages anyone who witnessed the incident or has information regarding potential misconduct by federal agents to report their observations through the New Jersey Office of the Attorney General’s reporting portal at https://www.njoag.gov/portal/.

The Borough remains committed to public safety, transparency, accountability, and ensuring that residents have accurate information regarding incidents occurring within our community.

All additional media inquiries regarding the federal enforcement operation should be directed to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).”

text:
Rick Carroll is changing his vote this year. The 71-year-old Roxbury, New Jersey resident said he’s voted ”straight line Republican all the way” for most of his life, including two consecutive ballots for his current member of congress, Republican Rep. Tom Kean, Jr.

Roxbury Township has been good to Kean, delivering him his highest 2024 vote count in all of Morris County, the most populated of the six counties in New Jersey’s 7th Congressional district.

That was before the Trump administration purchased a warehouse in Roxbury earlier this year with plans to transform it into a 1,500-bed ICE detention facility, one of the largest in the country. The move has been met with bi-partisan opposition from locals who say the warehouse is unfit to hold human beings. Roxbury’s all Republican township council condemned the plan, which is on hold pending a lawsuit.

But Kean was largely absent from the fight, and it’s left many longtime Roxbury Republicans like Carroll and his wife Paula rethinking their votes, questioning whether Kean is willing to stand up to the president on issues that matter to them.

“ I just think he does what Trump says, so he won't go against him,” Paula Carroll said.

The ICE-owned warehouse is a three minute drive from their house they’ve lived in for 36 years. They support strong borders, but Rick Carroll said “throwing” undocumented immigrants into a converted warehouse is “not the way to go about it.” He’s also worried the facility will “destroy my property value.” Both plan to break from their party and make an exception in this year’s midterm elections.

“I'm leaning just for that one Democrat,” Rick Carroll said.

Political experts say those kinds of one-off defections could pose a danger for Kean, who is locked in a tight race this year with his Democratic challenger Rebecca Bennett and did ultimately voice some opposition to the detention facility last month.

”If he's losing a lot of support [in Roxbury], that's going to matter,” said Dan Cassino, government and politics professor at Fairleigh Dickinson University. “When you have a close race like this, we're in street fight mode. They're going street by street, block by block. You need to be competitive there, especially when it's a town where you'd expect to do very well.”

Kean’s campaign did not respond to questions about the loss of some Republican support in Roxbury over the warehouse and how Kean plans to respond to residents’ concerns over the facility.

Not just ICE – Kean “disappeared”

News that the White House planned to use the 470,000-square foot warehouse off Route 46 in Roxbury as part of its rapid expansion of ICE’s detention capacity, first reported by the Washington Post in January, landed like a meteor in what is otherwise a sleepy suburban community roughly 43 miles west of New York City.

Locals and activists packed town council meetings demanding answers from local officials. The fully Republican township council said the White House had provided no information about its plans. Councilmembers immediately passed a unanimous resolution opposing the project, arguing the warehouse lacked the sewer capacity and other infrastructure needed for such a large detention center.

Anger in the town and surrounding area only grew in February when the Trump administration paid Goldman Sachs and a partner nearly $130 million dollars for the property.

Local officials said they asked Kean for help in fighting the Trump administration. In a statement a day after the sale of the warehouse was reported, Roxbury’s Republican Mayor Shawn Potillo released a statement saying the township committee raised concerns with “every level of government.”

“Despite repeated outreach, our federal representative, Congressman Tom Kean Jr., did not engage to the level we had hoped to provide the advocacy our residents deserved,” Potillo said.

Kean responded to the criticism with claims that he had engaged high-level staffers at the Department of Homeland Security. At the time, he did not say whether he opposed the facility or not.

It wasn’t clear at the time, but it was the beginning of what would be a long absence for Kean from public life. On March 5, Kean cast his last vote in Washington before mysteriously vanishing from Congress for over 100 days and offering little explanation about where he had gone. When he reemerged at the end of June. Kean revealed that he’d been hospitalized for severe depression.

On the campaign trail, Bennett has commended Kean for getting the treatment he needed. But for some Roxbury residents, the lack of clarity around his absence, and his failure to intervene in ICE’s warehouse purchase, has soured their opinion of a Republican with a long history in New Jersey. His father is a former governor of the Garden State. Before Congress, Kean served in the state Legislature for two decades.

“He just disappeared,“ Rick Carroll said. “He should've put it out there in some fashion for us to understand why he's been MIA for four, five months, during this critical time really.”

Brian Kiernan, who has lived in Roxbury for 37 years, said he’s voted Democrat since the first Obama administration but was a Republican prior to that, including time spent campaigning for Richard Nixon as a Young Republican.

This year, Kiernan has been knocking on doors in Roxbury, canvassing for Bennett. He said Kean’s lack of involvement in the ICE facility has shifted some people’s opinions in the heavily Republican town.

“There’s dissatisfaction with respect to what our congressman has not done, where he could have done things to protect our local interest,” he said.

But both Kean, and Trump’s plans for the warehouse, continue to find support in Roxbury and the surrounding area.

Vanessa Gleason lives about two miles from the warehouse. She is in favor of ICE using the facility to detain people, and unhappy that Kean eventually opposed Trump’s plan. Nonetheless, she said she’s still “all for” Kean in order to keep Democrats out of power.

”I don't think I can support the Democrats, any day of the week,” she said.

Steve Langland, a Republican from Mount Olive, which borders Roxbury, lives about 5 miles from the warehouse. He said he’s also voting for Kean because someone from the “alternative party” would be worse.

”It's just getting too lunatic. And the higher [the Democrats] numbers, the worse it's going to get,” he said.

Debate comment means little

It wasn’t until the candidates’ one and only debate last month that Kean was finally forced to take a position on the ICE facility in Roxbury. He was asked if he understood Roxbury residents’ frustration over not knowing where he stood on the issue.

Kean responded by saying he is against the Trump administration’s plans for the warehouse, one of the few times during the campaign he’s come out against one of Trump’s policies.

“ My focus is to make sure we don't have an ICE facility in Roxbury,” he said.

Bennett, tongue-in-cheek, thanked him for his answer.

“ This is the first time we have heard Congressman Tom Kean Jr. actually be explicit about his position on the detention facility in Roxbury,” Bennett said.

But some local residents remained just as frustrated by Kean’s debate response.

Megan Dray, another longtime Roxbury resident, is a Democrat who said she was raised Republican and only recently changed her party affiliation. She said she believes Kean only denounced the facility at the debate because it’s “what he thinks people wanted to hear.”

Dray said she’s frustrated with both parties’ inability to come together and find a solution for immigration reform, but she’ll still be supporting Bennett.

“ I am voting for Rebecca because she is not Tom Kean. And I wish I could say something stronger or better than that,” she said.

text:
A 56-year-old father of three who died in Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention over the weekend was a lawful permanent resident, The Texas Tribune reported Monday.

Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias was found unconscious in his bed Saturday morning at the Rio Grande Processing Center. ICE had detained Andrade-Covarrubias on June 26, as he was returning to Texas from Mexico through the port of entry in Laredo. The agency claimed that he’d failed to disclose a prior arrest when applying for his green card in 2004.

Andrade-Covarrubias’s daughter, Estefani Andrade, told the Tribune that her father had disclosed his criminal record during his application process and was still approved. Andrade-Covarrubias was scheduled to appear at an immigration court hearing on November 2.

As of Monday, his cause of death was still unknown.

Andrade told the Tribune that her father had a heart condition, diabetes, high blood pressure, and experienced a lasting toll from being hospitalized with Covid-19 in 2021. She claimed that staff at the processing center had refused to give him his medication, and that when her father began reporting symptoms, such as a persistent cough, difficulty breathing, and tightness across the chest, medical personnel “would just ignore him.”

In a statement, ICE claimed that Andrade-Covarrubias received proper medical care.

A Bloomberg Law investigation concluded that 37 people died in ICE custody between October 2025 and September 2026, marking the fiscal year 2026 as the deadliest in the agency’s recorded history.

Under the Trump administration, ICE has subjected tens of thousands of people—including U.S. citizens, lawful immigrants, and immigrants with no criminal convictions—to overcrowded rooms, unsanitary conditions, and insufficient food and water. Immigrants have been denied adequate medical care and legal counsel, and were even locked in cages.

CNN is threatening to file another lawsuit against the Trump administration for continuing to deny it access to the Air Force One press pool.

“These efforts to retaliate and discriminate against CNN based on the content of its news coverage are mistaken, counterproductive, and unlawful,” Ted Boutrous, the network’s outside counsel, wrote in a letter to the Justice Department on Tuesday. He added that CNN “will be forced to pursue additional judicial relief” if Trump does not stop.

CNN, MS NOW, and Politico all moved to sue Trump last month when he dramatically banned the trio of networks from the White House because he didn’t like the way they were covering him. While most access has been temporarily returned as the lawsuits continue in court, the administration has still decided to keep CNN off the presidential jet.

“Those spaces belong not to any particular president or administration but to all Americans, and CNN and other members of the press serve as surrogates for the public when covering the White House,” Boutrous continued. “If these actions persist … CNN will have no choice but to return to the court to defend its rights, and it is prepared to fight as long as is necessary to secure them.”

The White House maintains that its decision to shut out CNN is justified.

“No person and no journalist have a constitutional right to access to the President’s Oval Office, Air Force One, or other sensitive and private facilities,” it wrote in a statement. “When publications lie, fabricate, and ignore the truth, proximity matters less and they can write their fiction from outside of these secure facilities.”

Secretary of State Marco Rubio doesn’t see anything wrong with how Donald Trump is interacting with America’s foreign adversaries.

The secretary defended Trump’s intended meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, telling reporters Tuesday morning that the U.S. president’s detractors need to “grow up.”

“People need to grow up when it comes to foreign policy a little bit. I don’t think it’s unusual for the three most powerful, nuclear-armed nations on earth—for their leaders to communicate with one another,” Rubio said. “I think it makes all the sense in the world.”

Rubio argued that Trump “does not consider talking to someone to be a concession.”

“For example, how are you going to reach a peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine if you don’t talk to Russia and Ukraine? You have to talk to them, right?” Rubio continued. “That’s the bottom line of diplomacy and negotiation.”

“Frankly, I think if there’s an opportunity … to have a conversation about things like arms control, that would be a very positive thing for the world,” he said. “I think the world is a safer place when the leaders of the world are at least communicating with each other.”

Trump mused Monday that he would be open to an unprecedented three-way meeting with Xi and Putin regarding nuclear weapons and disarmament.

“We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearization,” Trump told reporters outside the White House. “If President Xi wants to have it, I’d have it. I’m sure we’d talk about other things like trade too.”

But the optics of Trump’s latest encounters with China and Russia have leaned more toward kowtowing than communicating. Last year, Trump had the U.S. military literally roll out a red carpet for Putin during his first visit to the U.S. in more than a decade. Trump did the same for Xi last month, when service members were filmed on their hands and knees picking and brushing imperfections out of the carpet fibers.

Why was President Donald Trump waving at empty space?

A video of the president departing for Kansas Monday afternoon showed him wandering off across the White House’s newly renovated helicopter pad, waving, saluting, and bowing as if he were interacting with a crowd of onlookers. When the camera panned out, however, it was clear that there was no one in the vicinity.

From another angle, Trump can be seen dragging his right leg and patting it as he approaches Marine One. He suddenly stops walking and starts waving to no one. Meanwhile, his aides approached from an entirely different direction.

Users on X speculated that the president might’ve been hallucinating or waving at his reflection—both troubling possibilities.

Brian Krassenstein, a political podcaster and social media influencer critical of Trump, responded to the strange moment. “I now have absolutely no doubt that Donald Trump has major mental decline,” he wrote on X. “Just think for one minute if Joe Biden had waved into the abyss like Trump just did here. Imagine what Fox News would be saying.”

This isn’t the first time Trump has appeared to wander off confusedly. In October last year, Trump seemed to forget where he was going as he walked through a room filled with dignitaries and a military band during a visit to Japan, at one point even leaving Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi behind.

This strange behavior is just the latest example of Trump’s apparent cognitive decline. Since returning to office, the president has often appeared to lose track of his thoughts, his whereabouts, and even his grasp on the English language.

Harris County, Texas—Texas’s most populous county, which Kamala Harris won in 2024 with 52 percent of the vote—broke its early voting record on Monday, eclipsing the previous mark by a whopping 41,000 votes.

More than 104,600 people in Harris County voted in person on Monday, the first day of early voting in Texas, according to the county’s elections department. That breaks the previous record set in 2018, when 63,188 votes were cast and Democrats went on to recapture the House.

While Monday’s turnout isn’t necessarily indicative of a Democratic advantage, the broken record indicates that Texans have been strongly compelled to participate electorally by any number of factors, which could include affordability, ICE raids, and President Trump’s war on Iran.

“The coffee that I buy two years ago was $12 for a big can, and now it’s $25 for the same thing, it’s ridiculous,” one voter told KPRC-TV’s Sandy Torres.

“[The] cost of living is way too high, war in Iran, our support to Ukraine,” said another.

“Thirty years of one party dominating the state; it’s time to get the other guy’s chance,” said one more.

This comes ahead of one of the most contested Senate races in the country between Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico—a contest that could turn the state blue for the first time in over three decades.

This positive development also comes less than a week after voting rights groups sued the Texas Department of Public Safety over a “glitch” that caused 600,000 Texans to have their voting registration delayed.

Refugees fleeing persecution have their claims processed outside the United States before entering the country under the bipartisan Refugee Act, passed by Congress in 1980. After one year, they become eligible to apply for lawful permanent residency, at which point they are no longer considered refugees.

The new policy targets refugees who have not yet obtained permanent residency or had their refugee status reviewed. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services processes applications to adjust refugees’ status to that of lawful permanent residents, and the policy comes as the agency faces significant backlogs. Between the second quarter of fiscal 2025 and the same period in fiscal year 2026, the number of pending I-485 applications, used to apply for permanent residency, rose 190%, according to a September analysis by the American Immigration Council.

The Department of Homeland Security has identified 186,000 cases involving “unadjusted” refugees who entered the United States between fiscal years 2015 and 2025. Data from the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program shows that about 30,000 refugees arrived in New York during that period.

Information from the Refugee Services program within the state Office of Temporary and Disability Assistance, which oversees services for refugees, shows that the majority of refugees in recent years were resettled in upstate New York.

Community-based organizations such as Albany’s Refugee and Immigrant Support Services of Emmaus help support those new arrivals. A representative of the organization told the Times Union that the effects of delays in granting permanent residency are already being felt locally. “It’s always important to get those in as quickly as possible,” said the representative, who requested anonymity because of concerns about retribution. “There are all these refugees nationwide who still haven’t received their green cards. In Albany, we have submitted the applications for all of them, but it’s a real vulnerability.”

Processing an application for permanent residency and terminating refugee status are two distinct legal procedures under U.S. immigration law. Refugee status can be terminated if the federal government determines that an individual was never legally a refugee at the time of admission.

title: Attorney General Rayfield Backs Challenge to Unlawful Warrantless Immigration Arrests
description:
Attorney General Dan Rayfield filed a brief in federal court this week supporting a lawsuit that challenges the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) practice of making warrantless civil immigration arrests that break federal law.
“The law sets a basic standard – if you’re going to arrest someone without a warrant, you need a real reason to do so,” said Attorney General Rayfield.

text:
Attorney General Dan Rayfield filed a brief in federal court this week supporting a lawsuit that challenges the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) practice of making warrantless civil immigration arrests that break federal law. The filing comes as neighbors, coworkers, and parents have been disappearing from communities across Oregon and the country, swept up in arrests made without a warrant and without the basic check the law requires: whether the person is actually a flight risk.

“The law sets a basic standard – if you’re going to arrest someone without a warrant, you need a real reason to do so,” said Attorney General Rayfield. “DHS is ignoring that standard, and Oregonians are paying the price. We’ve seen kids stay home from school, farm workers afraid to show up for work, and families skipping medical appointments because they don’t know who might be waiting for them. Our communities are less healthy and less safe because of DHS’ actions.”

Under federal law, immigration officers can only make a warrantless civil arrest if they have probable cause to believe a person is in the country unlawfully and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained. DHS officers have routinely skipped that second requirement. The brief lays out the real damage these practices are doing in communities across the country, including in Oregon.

Over the past year, federal immigration agents have ramped up enforcement nationwide, and the ripple effects have reached public health, public safety, schools, and local economies. Aggressive tactics have kept students out of classrooms, disrupted agricultural work, discouraged people from seeking medical care, strained family finances, and eroded the trust between immigrant communities and local police. And when agents show up in ski masks, dark sunglasses, plain clothes, and unmarked cars, and won’t say who they are, it only deepens the fear and confusion neighbors are feeling.

The brief was filed in Escobar-Molina v. DHS, a case challenging DHS’s policy and practice of warrantless civil immigration arrests in the District of Columbia. On December 2, 2025, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia partially granted a motion for a preliminary injunction.

Attorney General Rayfield filed the brief alongside the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, and Washington.

text:
A man in ICE custody found dead Saturday in his bed at a for-profit immigration detention center in Laredo, Texas, was a lawful permanent resident of the U.S., the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement about the death.

Customs and Border Protection arrested 56-year-old Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias at a border crossing in June after suspecting he obtained legal status in the U.S. “through fraudulent means” by failing to disclose an arrest for theft in 2004, the DHS statement said.

The man’s daughter disputes that, telling The Texas Tribune that the arrest was known to immigration authorities who approved her father's request for a green card. He lived in the Dallas area for decades where he worked as a house painter, she said.

DHS did not offer any evidence of Andrade-Covarrubias ever being convicted of a crime, despite calling him a “criminal alien” in the news release about his death.

ICE INC | ICE waived rule requiring detainees receive medical checkups within two weeks

ICE held Andrade-Covarrubias at the Rio Grande Processing Center in Laredo, Texas, where he remained until security staff found him unresponsive on Saturday. A cause of death has not been identified yet, DHS said. His family claims he could not get the medical attention he needed for pre-existing conditions including high blood pressure and diabetes.

Rep. Henry Cuellar, D-Texas, has requested ICE quickly respond to a list of questions about the latest ICE detainee to die in the agency’s care.

"Was he asking for help? Was he asking for medicine?” Cuellar said in an interview with Scripps News. “I want to see the specifics, starting off with, was he a legal resident? Because if he was a legal resident he should have never been in there.”

Andrade-Covarrubias is the 60th ICE detainee to die since the start of President Trump's second term, according to a count by Relevant Research, a group that collects and tracks detainee deaths. Eighteen of those deaths were people born in Mexico.

The Mexican government is requesting the U.S. provide a full investigation into what led to Andrade-Covarrubias' sudden death.

"We are also going to file a complaint in the United States because there must be protection of human rights," Mexico President Claudia Sheinbaum told reporters Monday.

The for-profit GEO Group corporation owns the detention center and houses detainees under government contract. The company deferred questions to ICE.

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Judge orders pause on collection of sky-high civil immigration fines

DHS, which responds to questions for ICE, says the Andrade-Covarrubias received proper medical care. Similar claims by DHS about detainees receiving adequate medical care before their deaths have later been contracted by ICE’s own comprehensive mortality reviews.

A January 2025 compliance inspection report by ICE’s Office of Detention Oversight faulted the Rio Grande Processing Center for not always conducting health assessments for new immigrant detainees within two weeks as required by national detention standards.

The report listed the facility’s rating as “good.”

title: 'Their Power Rests on Fear. Ours Rests on Each Other.' - Institute for Policy Studies
description:
The power of the few rests on fear.
The power of the many rests on each other.
And they carry the same certainty Orlando carried.
Every time he tries to shame Minnesota, Minnesota answers the same way.
Their power rests on fear.
text:
This speech was delivered by Emilia Gonzalez Avalos, Executive Director of Unidos MN, while accepting IPS’s 2026 Domestic Letelier-Moffitt Human Rights Award on behalf of her organization. The speech, and the rest of the ceremony, can be viewed in full here.

Gracias. Thank you to the Institute for Policy Studies, to the Letelier and Moffitt families, and to everyone who has carried this award for 50 years. To our compañeros y compañeras at La Liga: it is an honor to stand beside you tonight.

Fifty years ago, on a September morning in this city, a bomb went off at Sheridan Circle. It took Orlando Letelier and Ronni Karpen Moffitt from their families and from their community.

In Minnesota, we know that grief. Last year our Speaker Emerita Melissa Hortman and her husband Mark were assassinated in their home in an act of political violence. Political violence carries one message, in Santiago, in Washington, in Brooklyn Park. Sit down. Stay quiet. Stay home. We answered the same way this room has answered for 50 years: we stood up, we found each other, and we kept organizing.

Eleven days before Orlando died, the Pinochet dictatorship stripped him of his citizenship. He answered from a stage in New York: I was born a Chilean, I am a Chilean, and I will die a Chilean.

I have carried that sentence all year. Because every tyrant learns the same lesson. The first thing they come for is our belonging. They send their armies to your front door. They follow you to school drop off. They park outside your church and photograph our communities. They want us to wake up in our own neighborhoods and feel like a stranger.

Orlando gave the answer for all of us. Belonging is ours. No matter who is in power, we — the people — declare it ourselves, we defend it together. And we defend it ruthlessly.

This year a new class of tyrants sent masked agents into the streets of the Twin Cities. And here is what they were counting on. The oldest lie in this country. The lie that says immigrants, refugees, and people of color are different. That their pain belongs to them alone. That if you keep your head down, this will pass over your house.

That lie had already done its work. Last session, undocumented adults in Minnesota were stripped out of healthcare. Across the country, immigration became radioactive for Democrats. The polls, the experts, and all their processed data said immigration was a losing issue anywhere and some leaders chose to hide.

But Minnesotans didn’t hide.

I want to be careful here, because I do not want to romanticize what happened. People were terrified. People are still grieving. The cost was real and it is not over.

But something happened in those weeks that I have been trying to find words for, and the only word I keep coming back to is recognition. People recognized each other. Affluent grandmothers in Edina recognized themselves as immigrant mothers in St. Paul. Lutheran pastors recognized the face of Christ in undocumented teenagers. Union members recognized that the boot on their neighbor’s neck was the same boot that would come for them. Small business owners recognized that the Constitution was either for everyone or it was for no one, and they chose everyone.

We put signs in our windows. We opened our homes for children, elders, and pets left behind. We said no to men with badges and guns, and we said it together, and we said it out loud.

Every raid awakened a neighbor. Every neighbor became a defender. They sent an army to tear Minnesota apart. Instead, they introduced Minnesota to itself.

Social movements have shown the world, and Minnesota confirms it. The power of the few rests on fear. The power of the many rests on each other.

Chile teaches one more thing, and this room knows it. The coup that brought Pinochet had help from this capital (DC). You see, migration is the return address of war and authoritarianism. People arrive at the door of the country whose policies moved them. The families in Unidos’s membership carry 50 years of this country’s foreign policy in their bodies. And they carry the same certainty Orlando carried. Immigrants and refugees belong here. And all of us belong to each other.

My faith teaches me that the divine thing in every human being is the power to decide. Authoritarianism is the theft of that power. Democracy is that same sacred power, practiced together, in public, on purpose.

And Minnesota taught us how a frightened person comes to use it. The capacity to look away and the capacity to stand live in the same person, on the same morning. What decides between them is what that person practiced, and who that person already knew.

Courage is an outcome of preparation and relationships.

So the path forward is plain, and it belongs to everyone in this room.

Know your neighbor before the crisis comes. The relationship you build on a quiet Tuesday is the one that answers the door on the hard Thursday. Prepare. Practice democracy on the mornings when nothing is at stake, so your hands know the way on the morning when everything is.

And build power that lasts. Mutual aid keeps us alive. Organized power keeps us free. Organized people and organized money, owned by the communities who need it most, sending leaders from our own kitchens into the halls where the decisions get made.

The few believed a bomb on Embassy Row would end a movement. Fifty years later, that anti-authoritarian movement is rebuilding its strength in every corner of the U.S. and Latin America.

So tonight, we choose. We can have a quiet that forgets, or a democracy that remembers.

We choose the democracy that remembers. We say the names. And we keep organizing.

And just today, the President of the United States went online to insult my state again. I will tell you what I told my neighbors this afternoon. Let him post. We will organize. He has a phone. We have each other. Every time he tries to shame Minnesota, Minnesota answers the same way. We show up for each other, and we show up at the polls.

Orlando said it for himself. Let us say it for each other. We were born free. We are free. And together, we will stay free.

Their power rests on fear. Ours rests on each other. Ours is sacred. And ours endures.

Thank you.

ICE at elections. The organization Human Rights Watch (HRW) asked the United States Government on Tuesday to keep Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents away from polling stations during the November 3 midterm elections, due to fears that their presence could "intimidate" voters.

The NGO warned that the presence of immigration agents at polling stations can "generate fear, especially among immigrant communities".

They ask the Trump Administration to guarantee that immigration operations "do not interfere"

ICE at elections: ICE has detained 368,135 people

The warnings come ahead of the midterm elections, in which the entire House of Representatives and a third of the Senate will be renewed, in a context of intense political debate over the Trump Administration's immigration policy.

HRW argues that any action that can be perceived as "intimidatory" threatens to "hinder electoral participation".

So far in the 2026 fiscal year, which began on October 1, 2025, and ends on September 30, 2026, ICE had detained 368,135 people, according to data analyzed by the Deportation Data Project, from the University of California, Berkeley, and Los Angeles.

text:
WASHINGTON (OSV News) – The Trump administration on Oct. 18 extended protections from deportation to people from Ukraine and Sudan, allowing them to continue living legally in the United States for now.

Temporary Protected Status grants the U.S. government the power to shield eligible migrants from deportation if they are from countries experiencing dangerous conditions such as war, disaster, or other unrest. The Trump administration has sought to end TPS for several countries, notably Haiti, which is racked by extreme levels of gang violence, but it also recently granted an extension to migrants from El Salvador.

In a written statement provided to OSV News, a spokesperson for DHS confirmed the extension without sharing a rationale. The spokesperson stated an announcement on each country's TPS “will be made at the appropriate time,” and until such announcements are made, nationals of those countries “present in the U.S. under TPS retain protection.”

David Spicer, director of policy and engagement for migration at the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, told OSV News Oct. 19 the conference “is closely monitoring the situation facing people relying on TPS without clarity on the future of their designations.”

“These include hundreds of thousands of Salvadorans, Ukrainians, and Sudanese who are lawfully present in the United States, but face the reality of suddenly having their protection and work authorization revoked,” Spicer said. “The conference continues to urge the administration to abide by the requirements of the TPS statute, to carefully consider conditions in countries of origin and the threats to human life that could come with forcibly repatriating people, and to provide meaningful notice about the future of these designations so that families, employers, and communities can plan accordingly.”

Ashley Feasley, the legal expert in residence at the Immigration Law and Policy Initiative at The Catholic University of America Columbus School of Law, told OSV News that while the DHS statement “is a welcome reprieve to TPS holders from Ukraine and Sudan,” it “does little to clarify the growing confusion and uncertainty they face with regards to their lives here in the U.S.”

“In addition to enduring growing conflict and war in their home countries, these individuals must continue to navigate an unpredictable day-to-day existence here in the U.S. given so much recent uncertainty over TPS generally,” Feasley said.

“Congress created TPS and codified it into law and the Executive is required to implement that process accordingly,” she continued. “For both Ukraine and Sudan, it is clear that both countries face ‘ongoing armed conflict,’ as is described in the statute designating TPS. It is absolutely not safe for these individuals to return to their home country.”

Earlier this year, the U.S. Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to end TPS designation for Haitian and Syrian nationals. Catholic leaders have also urged protection for people from those countries who would be subject to dangerous conditions in their countries of origin.

The Trump administration terminated TPS for Haiti after that ruling, and has since carried out mass deportations of Haitians back to Haiti, which is among the immigration policies the U.S. bishops have criticized, calling it incompatible with their God-given right to life, human dignity, and unity of the family.

(Kate Scanlon is a national reporter for OSV News covering Washington.)

text:
A Chinese player on the Mississippi Valley State men's basketball team, detained by ICE three weeks ago, was released on $12,000 bail Tuesday afternoon but still faces a hearing that could lead to his deportation.

Qingfang Pang, 21, who came to the United States from China three years ago, was arrested Sept. 29 as he tried to board a flight from Jackson, Mississippi, to New York, shortly after Mississippi Valley officials informed him his student visa had expired.

Speaking through a family adviser, Pang thanked his family, teammates, Coach Mike Davis and the school's assistant coaches who, he said, "believed in me and never stopped supporting me."

Pang's attorney, Marcus Session, told ESPN that the 6-foot-9 forward was the victim of a "procedural mistake" and was unaware he had not filed the proper paperwork to renew his visa. As of Tuesday afternoon, Pang was still awaiting his release from the Richmond (Louisiana) Correctional Center, Session said.

"He's a strong kid, but even a strong kid would have his emotions and faith tested," Session said.

Davis told ESPN that he's eager to get Pang back on campus, where he says the medical staff will make sure he's at full strength before letting him return to basketball.

"It's been hard. When one of your guys is going through something like this, the whole team feels it," Davis said. "For me personally, it reminded me that what we do is bigger than basketball."

Pang's arrest was the second such incident since September. Aminata Seck, a Kentucky State University women's basketball player from Senegal, was released on bail Oct. 7 after spending two months in ICE custody.

Session said that officials "coerced" Pang into signing a voluntary departure document when he was initially detained but that, with his limited English, Pang didn't understand what he was signing. Session said that document was rescinded and that Pang clearly wants to remain in Mississippi.

A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, said in a statement: "He legally entered the U.S. on November 17, 2023 on a temporary basis not to exceed September 5, 2024, but illegally overstayed. All of his claims will be heard by an immigration judge, and he will receive due process. This administration will not ignore the rule of law."

The DHS statement also noted that the department is offering $3,000 and a free flight to any "illegal alien" who chooses to self-deport. "We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream. If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return," the statement said.

Pang, who played high school basketball in New York City, attended Monroe University and transferred as a junior this season to Mississippi Valley, where the school discovered his F-1 student visa had expired. Session said that school officials told Pang he had to leave campus and that he was headed to his guardian's home in New York when he was detained.

An immigration judge in Jena, Louisiana, approved the request for bail Monday. Pang is expected to appear at a hearing Oct. 27, hoping a judge allows him to stay in the United States.

Nichole Francis Reynolds, a Washington-area attorney and Davis' cousin who has advised Pang and his family, said he is aware of the stakes at next week's hearing. While he was detained, she and other representatives helped file the paperwork he would need to stay, and she said the family hopes that paperwork and the support he's had from Mississippi's two senators, Roger Wicker and Cindy Hyde-Smith, will be enough to convince a judge he should remain in the United States.

"We are hopeful, and we respectfully ask for privacy for him and his family as the process continues," Reynolds said.
