text:
A federal appeals court ruled today that a group of twenty-seven Christian and Jewish religious denominations and associations, including the Unitarian Universalist Association (UUA), have standing to sue the Trump administration over its policy of immigration enforcement at houses of worship.

In response to the ruling, the UUA issued a statement: “The Unitarian Universalist Association welcomes the decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, which means that the Mennonite Church USA v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security suit can move forward. We were pleased to join a multifaith coalition last year in becoming a plaintiff in this case. Since then, we have seen how this administration has violated the rights of people of faith in various ways, including no longer protecting our sacred places.

“As the threats to our sanctuaries—including documented instances of surveillance of UU congregations—and religious practices intensify,” it continued, “we will continue our practice of faithful dissent against such oppression, and we look forward to being a part of the next step of the legal process.”

In its 2–1 decision in Mennonite Church USA et al. v. United States Department of Homeland Security et al., the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals overturned a lower federal court ruling made in April 2025. That ruling held that the plaintiffs did not demonstrate imminent harm from a DHS “Rescission Memo” that allows immigration enforcement near places of worship. Issued on the first day of President Donald Trump’s second term, the memo revoked a Biden administration “sensitive locations” policy that restricted immigration enforcement in such places as houses of worship, schools, and hospitals.

Today’s decision means the case can move ahead.

The lawsuit, filed on February 11, 2025, asserts that subjecting places of worship to ICE enforcement actions without a judicial warrant substantially burdens their right to exercise their religious beliefs in violation of the First Amendment and the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA). Such action interferes with the religious activities of the plaintiffs and their ability to fulfill their religious mandate to welcome and serve immigrants, the plaintiffs assert.

In addition to the UUA, other plaintiffs include the Mennonite Church USA, the African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church, the Episcopal Church, the Union for Reform Judaism, the Latino Christian National Network, and the Central Atlantic Conference United Church of Christ.

text:
NORTH BERGEN, New Jersey (WABC) -- A North Bergen high school senior says he was stopped and questioned by masked ICE agents while on his way to school Monday morning, prompting criticism from community members and local officials.

George Castillo, 18, said he was waiting for a friend at JFK Boulevard and 85th Street at about 7:30 a.m. Monday when the encounter occurred.

"I was just confused," Castillo said.

Asked by Eyewitness News what the first question was, Castillo responded: "if I was American again and they asked about my age."

Gloria Estrada, who recorded video of the encounter, said she was concerned by what she witnessed.

"I see that they are speaking to my neighbor, who is a high school student, and that didn't seem right to me," she said. "I just thought it's not right what they're doing because I was just a high school student who was probably waiting for their friend or just wanting to sit down really quickly, and they stereotyped him for being looking Hispanic."

Assemblymember Gabriel Rodriguez criticized the incident and said New Jersey law requires law enforcement officers, including federal officers, to reveal their facial identities while performing official duties.

"At first glance, it's heartbreaking," Rodriguez said.

He said his office is increasing efforts to educate residents about their rights.

"They want people to feel fear," Rodriguez said. "They're several or institutions and organizations that have been promoting new rights campaigns, putting out paraphernalia, putting stuff up on websites and social media. Our job now is unfortunately, to extend that information, that education now. So, where parents are having these conversations not only amongst each other and their community partners, but with their children."

Castillo said he has a message for others in the community.

"I say the people shouldn't be afraid of these people. They are just people that are just trying to scare you," he said.

In a statement to Eyewitness News, ICE disputed the allegations.

The agency said allegations that ICE questioned minors or targeted schools are false. ICE said agents were conducting a targeted operation Monday during which they arrested nine undocumented immigrants with criminal histories and that, during the operation, they spoke with an adult, not a child.

The incident has sparked outrage in North Bergen as questions continue about the encounter and the actions of federal agents.

name: Human Rights
title: Unsafe and Unwelcome - United Church of Christ
description:
The laws and the accompanying signs were explicit in identifying that Blacks and other minorities were unsafe and unwelcome.
Yet the spirit of Jim Crow lives on across the United States, resurrected with other names, ensuring that the law is still weaponized and deciding through discriminatory practices who is safe and unsafe, who is welcome and unwelcome.
Immigrants are unsafe and unwelcome along with millions of others who do not fit criteria laid by individuals who claimed the right to decide who is in and who is out.
A closer and further reading identifies the challenge to the latest group targeted en masse for expulsion from the United States.
The signs are out, and the message continues to be clear: immigrants are unsafe and unwelcome.
text:
Issues of safety and welcome have long been a topic of conversation in the United States. The days of racial segregation provided overt and legal signs that warned of potential dangers. Separate waiting rooms, water fountains and schools for Whites and Blacks were clear in their discriminatory practices, and was also the case for housing, access to hospitals and other community services like parks. The laws and the accompanying signs were explicit in identifying that Blacks and other minorities were unsafe and unwelcome.

Jim Crow laws were enacted in the 1870s and ensured that racial segregation was enforced, White supremacy was maintained, and African descendant people were relegated to being second class. “Separate but equal” was the rule of the day in a country where equity and equality were not an option extended to all. These were state and local laws present in the south, laws which came on the heels of the emancipation of enslaved people. Slavery may have been over, but the law was used to keep freed Blacks “in their place” with reduced access to better living conditions for their lives and better options for their economic success.

Jim Crow laws were struck down with the passage of a series of federal legislations in the 1950s and 1960s and court cases during the years of the Civil Rights movement.

These days, the “Whites Only,” signs and other physical signs of racial discrimination are gone from the windows of the stores, over the bathroom doors and are missing from public spaces. The signs live on as historical relics in museums and landfills. Yet the spirit of Jim Crow lives on across the United States, resurrected with other names, ensuring that the law is still weaponized and deciding through discriminatory practices who is safe and unsafe, who is welcome and unwelcome. Jim Crow abides with us, resurrected for another generation.

White Christian nationalism is the shroud of the new Jim Crow with the accompanying war on immigrants, intention to change birth right citizenship, reduction to scholarships for Black students, attacks on diversity, equity and inclusion programs, rolling back the civil and human rights of millions.

State and local laws are no longer the problem when enforcement of discriminatory practices are coming with the stoke of the pen through Executive Orders signed by the current President of the United States. The signs in the windows are back, but the truth is they never went away. Now they are being dusted off and returned, metaphorically, to the restaurant windows and movie theaters of our lives. There is nothing invisible about the signage of this moment. Immigrants are unsafe and unwelcome along with millions of others who do not fit criteria laid by individuals who claimed the right to decide who is in and who is out.

The pen is being wielded as a weapon as rule by executive order moves the inaction of law without public debate.

The President signed Executive Order 14406, Restoring Integrity of America’s Financial System on May 19, 2026. Another innocuous title for an executive order with implications that cannot be grasped from the title. The purpose of this one is however, clearly stated very early. Executive Order 14406 states: “My Administration will not tolerate national security and public safety risks caused by illicit cross-border financial activity, nor will it permit risks to our financial system posed by the extension of credit or financial services to the inadmissible and removable alien population.”

The order appears to be concerned with drug trafficking, money laundering and other activities related to the war on drugs, or more specifically, Mexico based cartels. A closer and further reading identifies the challenge to the latest group targeted en masse for expulsion from the United States. “Banks and other financial institutions should also be attentive to the credit risks posed by the extension of mortgage and auto loans, credit cards, and other consumer credit to the inadmissible and removable alien population.”

“Federal law does not give government agencies the power to stop people from opening bank accounts or applying for credit based on their immigration status. But the Trump administration has been aggressive in using any power it has to make immigrants feel unsafe and unwelcome in the United States.”

The Executive Order attempts to limit the access immigrants will have to affordable banking services – that is immigrants documented or undocumented. Like Jim Crow laws of old, the limitations being placed on access to banking services is critical for investment in financial well-being and economic viability for immigrants. Buying homes. Money in a safe place. Earning interest. Investing funds. Business loans. All these aspects of life are threatened by the order which is a veiled approach to addressing the challenges being place on banks by illegal activity which targeting the financial viability of immigrants in these United States.

The signs are out, and the message continues to be clear: immigrants are unsafe and unwelcome. White Christian nationalism is the new Jim Crow.

title: Lawyers Accuse Trump of Building a “Deportation Assembly Line” for Children | Truthout
authors: Anton Woronczuk, Mike Ludwig, Sharon Zhang, Chris Walker, Colleen DeGuzman, Alex Nguyen, Ariana Figueroa, Gwynne Hogan, Eileen Grench, Julia Conley
description:
The Trump administration has stripped protections from unaccompanied migrant children and undocumented minors to fast-track deportations, a new lawsuit challenging the administration argues.
“It’s a very coordinated attack on children.” Today, all unaccompanied minors apprehended by federal immigration police must be handed over to the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR).
Baltimore said many children arrive at the border unaccompanied but are trying to reunite with family in the U.S.
They are living with families, but because of an ICE detention on the street or criminal arrest where they are sent to ICE or ORR, they become ‘unaccompanied children,’” Baltimore said.
Additionally, ORR is supposed to provide children with legal services, and traditionally did so by paying nonprofit legal aid providers.
text:
The Trump administration has stripped protections from unaccompanied migrant children and undocumented minors to fast-track deportations, a new lawsuit challenging the administration argues. The administration’s policies have created harrowing scenes in courts across the country, where an increasing number of kids appear before judges without a lawyer or the legal support necessary to navigate a complex legal system that will determine their future.

One legal organization that is part of the suit described representing a child with a documented heart condition who applied for asylum based on her experiences of sexual abuse in her home country. She was forced into a hours-long virtual asylum interview one day after being hospitalized for a cardiac event. She requested to end the interview because she was experiencing pain in her chest, visibly crying and clutching her heart. The asylum officer insisted she continue; only after hours of subjecting this child to severe distress did the officer agree to reschedule.

In the lawsuit, filed in a federal court in Maryland on October 15, a coalition of immigration advocates and legal aid providers say the administration has ignored federal law to create a “deportation assembly line” for unaccompanied children and undocumented minors.

The number of unaccompanied minors removed from the U.S. has more than tripled compared to President Trump’s first term, according to ProPublica. Children who have parents or sponsors in the U.S. have been separated from them and denied due process within Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) byzantine system of detention centers and jails, the lawsuit argues.

In some cases, children who crossed the border to seek asylum and, in many cases, to be reunited with family in the United States, could potentially be deported back to the dangerous conditions they attempted to flee, according to Cristel Martinez, an immigration attorney in Chicago.

“It’s basically sending the kids back to countries where their life is in danger, and may end up getting killed,” Martizen told reporters on October 15.

Martinez is herself an immigrant, and her law office has represented more than 400 unaccompanied minors in immigration court. That job has become increasingly difficult under a series of policy changes made by the Trump administration to fast-track deportations and cut off federal funding for nonprofits that provide legal support established by Congress for unaccompanied children. Attorneys previously had months to gather documents, perform psychological evaluations, and prepare a case. Now judges are setting asylum hearings and issuing removal orders at a speed never seen before.

Mickey Donovan-Kaloust, a director of children’s representation at the Immigrant Defenders Law Center, a plaintiff in the lawsuit, said she has worked with undocumented children for 15 years but has never witnessed the “chaos, cruelty, and disregard for due process that I’m seeing today.”

“The government is stopping at nothing to fast-track the deportations of these children,” Donovan-Kaloust told reporters on Friday. “Instead of promptly releasing children to their family members as the law requires, the government has been trapping children in government custody for months on end.”

Minimum standards for caring for unaccompanied migrant children were not established until the Flores Settlement of 1997, a consent decree resulting from years of litigation filed by human rights groups. Then, until the early 2000s, children who arrived at a U.S. border without a parent or guardian were often detained indefinitely in a prison system designed for adults and could not meet basic childhood needs such as education.

Pushing for a bill to reform these practices in 2008, Sen. Dianne Feinstein described witnessing a 15-year-old girl appear “shackled and in prison clothing” at an asylum hearing ostensibly about her seeking safety in the U.S.

“As she told her story to an immigration judge, she could not wipe away her tears because her hands were chained to her waist,” Feinstein said at the time.

A series of legal challenges in the 1980s and 1990s began to set new standards for unaccompanied children, culminating in provisions included in the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (HSA), and later in the William Wilberforce Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008 (TVPRA). Congress proposed these laws to help children fleeing violence and exploitation find safety in the U.S., the plaintiffs say.

“Together, the HSA, the TVPRA, and their implementing regulations try to account for the vulnerability of a child navigating a foreign immigration system alone — without a parent, without a lawyer, and frequently without English fluency,” the new lawsuit reads.

The laws established child-appropriate procedures for unaccompanied children, such as “affirmative” asylum interviews with specially trained officers, so that kids are not forced to recount the most traumatizing moments of their lives before an immigration judge.

However, the Trump administration is now violating these laws by denying migrant children due process rights and fast-tracking their removal from the country, according to the lawsuit.

“They are making it impossible for children to get competent representation, and they are accessible to the government [for maximizing deportations] because they are in their custody,” Beth Baltimore, interim managing director of legal services at The Door, a youth center in New York City, told Truthout. “It’s a very coordinated attack on children.”

Today, all unaccompanied minors apprehended by federal immigration police must be handed over to the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR). ORR is not an enforcement agency and operates shelters where parents and potential sponsors can be screened to become caregivers for the children.

However, advocates for immigrants rights say the Trump administration is now rushing these same children — and others taken during chaotic ICE raids and separated from parents — through the legal proceedings in ways that deny them due process and put them in danger. ORR and other agencies under the Department of Homeland Security tasked with protecting their rights are instead dismantling them, according to the lawsuit.

“I’ve been in immigration court observing as well for the past few weeks, have seen firsthand kids getting removed, even when attorneys from the organization that is supposed to be helping them are present and not speaking up for the kids,” Martinez said.

The lawsuit specifically challenges two new policies that attorneys say have eroded due process, including requiring children to apply for asylum within weeks of entry and providing as little as one day’s notice before an asylum interview, which establishes whether they qualify as a refugee fleeing danger. The administration abruptly changed the asylum interview format and instructed judges to complete their detained child docket by January 2027 regardless of circumstance. This has left attorneys little time to prepare cases as children are mandated to appear in court multiple times a week.

Baltimore said many children arrive at the border unaccompanied but are trying to reunite with family in the U.S. The fear created by Trump’s violent mass deportation scheme has made this impossible for many families.

“Some of them, they are not unaccompanied. They are living with families, but because of an ICE detention on the street or criminal arrest where they are sent to ICE or ORR, they become ‘unaccompanied children,’” Baltimore said. “They are being placed into ORR custody and then there are these huge barriers for release, but they are already living with families and it was fine; there are no allegations of abuse or neglect with those parents.”

As Democrats in Congress have pointed out, federal law also requires special protections for suspected child victims of human trafficking, but the administration appears to be circumventing these rules to increase deportations.

Additionally, ORR is supposed to provide children with legal services, and traditionally did so by paying nonprofit legal aid providers. However, after a dispute with a nonprofit in which the Trump administration demanded sensitive personal information about defendants, the federal government let the contracts lapse on July 31, potentially leaving an estimated 26,000 children and teens without paid legal representation. Advocacy groups are digging into reserve funding to pay attorneys and are also challenging this in federal court.

Speaking to reporters on Friday, Donovan-Kaloust described another recent case.

“Last week, a 5-year-old child who had been abandoned by his family was ordered deported in a docket where [our organization] was present,” she said. “A five-year-old. That should stop this country in its tracks.”

text:
WASHINGTON - A predawn raid on Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar’s home by federal agents stemmed from an expanding investigation into her US immigration paperwork, three people familiar with the case said this week.

The investigation appears to center on whether the Somali-born Omar, who has represented a Minnesota district since 2019, or her relatives gave false information upon entering the US as refugees in the mid-1990s or during the process of becoming American citizens.

The sealed warrant for Monday's search listed conspiracy, false statements on immigration paperwork and immigration fraud as potential crimes being investigated, one of the people familiar with the matter said. Like the other people, they spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation.

One of the people familiar with the probe told Reuters that one potential aim could be to strip Omar of her US citizenship and deport her, ideas that both President Donald Trump and his Homeland Security chief have floated.

The targeting of a left-wing member of Congress whom Trump has long attacked in personal and bigoted terms has renewed concerns that his administration is using federal law enforcement to punish his political opponents, especially three weeks before an election when Omar is running to retain her seat.

Omar has denied wrongdoing, characterizing the raid as an act of “political intimidation.”

The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees the immigration enforcement agency, referred questions to the Justice Department. A DOJ spokesperson declined to comment on the Omar investigation.

But in a statement, the spokesperson said that US citizenship "must be obtained lawfully and honestly" and the Trump administration would investigate any case where the facts support denaturalization, the legal process of revoking citizenship that was acquired after birth.

A spokesperson for Omar had no immediate comment.

A rare step

Former immigration officials said denaturalization investigations have historically been rare, and it is extremely unusual for them to involve search warrants, as the government should already have the relevant immigration records.

"Most of the denaturalization cases that we engaged in related either to very serious international human rights violations, or very serious crimes, such as Nazi war criminals,” said Kerry Doyle, a former deputy general counsel in the Department of Homeland Security during the Biden administration.

Agents with Homeland Security Investigations, a branch of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, seized Omar's personal cell phone during the search, according to two of the sources. Federal prosecutors also issued more than a dozen subpoenas, including to at least one of Omar’s relatives, the two people said.

One of the people said a sister of Omar spoke voluntarily with federal agents.

It was unclear what evidence prosecutors presented to the federal magistrate judge who approved the raid.

A coalition of 14 news organizations, including Reuters, asked a federal judge on Thursday to unseal records related to the search.

Protections for Congress

The DOJ has traditionally refrained from investigative acts against political figures that are likely to become public within 60 days of an election, particularly if the evidence can be collected after votes are cast.

Omar's status as a sitting member of Congress made the timing all the more unusual, and the probe potentially more fraught.

Courts have ruled that federal authorities cannot review material related to the legislative acts of a member of Congress, which is protected under the US Constitution.

Before approving the search, US Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh ordered screening procedures to prevent such a review, according to three people familiar with the matter.

Under the terms of the warrant, prosecutors were supposed to inform Omar's lawyers about the protocol for protecting legislative records, but that has not happened, one of the people said.

Denaturalization

Omar was 12 when her family arrived in the United States in 1995 after fleeing civil war in Somalia and spending years at a refugee camp in Kenya. She became a naturalized citizen in 2000.

Omar's background has been central to her political rise -- and a consistent target of her right-wing critics.

Trump has repeatedly attacked her heritage, her Muslim faith and the Somali community in Minnesota.

Asked by the New York Times in January if he thought Omar should lose her US citizenship, Trump replied: "Oh, absolutely."

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told a conservative podcaster last month there may have been "some illegal activity for them (Omar's family) to come to the United States to begin with" and suggested deportation as a possibility.

A naturalized US citizen can lose citizenship if a judge finds it was obtained illegally or through the concealment or willful misrepresentation of material facts.

The DOJ has filed at least 164 denaturalization cases in Trump's second term. Between 1990 and 2017, just 11 denaturalization cases were opened on average each year, according to the Immigrant Legal Resource Center.

___

Reporting by Andrew Goudsward and Kristina Cooke.

text:
By ZACH LAIRD, InDepthNH.org

A coalition of advocacy groups has gained support from people from 80% of the municipalities in New Hampshire for a petition to have 29 police agencies in the state exit a program run by Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE), where they perform immigration officer functions under the direction of ICE.

According to Larry Brown, the total number of signatures gathered from 187 cities and towns won’t be publicized to keep it from becoming a political tool. Brown said other groups involved in the coalition are organizations such as the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) New Hampshire, the American Friends Service Committee and other state-wide organizations.

“In late Spring and early Summer people were so upset about what ICE is doing nationally — and certainly in New Hampshire — that a number of groups in the state in New Hampshire, religious groups and human rights groups, decided that we needed to let the Governor (Kelly Ayotte) know we’re not happy for being the pariah state — the only state where the Governor has invited ICE agents into our communities,” Brown said.

After multiple attempts, Ayotte did not respond for comment.

After the deadline to sign it ended on Sept. 30, the coalition sent it to Gov. Ayotte’s office, and asked for a meeting with her to discuss “why New Hampshire is different from all the other states, and the fact that we don’t want ICE in our communities abducting people, children, and even citizens.”

Brown said Ayotte’s office responded by saying she’s too busy to meet with them for the next two months.

Brown continued that people in New Hampshire are usually pretty focused on their own freedom and independence, and to have ICE agents come around “abducting people who are neighbors, like hardworking immigrants, was not something that we wanted.”

The letter to Ayotte reads: “Federal officials say ICE is targeting dangerous criminals. The record does not support that claim. ICE’s own data reveal that most of the people being surveilled, detained, and deported have no serious criminal history. Many are following the legal immigration procedures, waiting for their applications to be decided. Others have overstayed a visa, which is not a crime. Most immigrants work in our towns, pay taxes, send their children to school, and contribute to New Hampshire’s economy and civic life.”

It added: “No one wants dangerous criminals in our neighborhoods, whether they are citizens or immigrants, and local law enforcement officers already address this. But New Hampshire residents do not need heavily armed federal agents operating with little transparency and no accountability in our communities. We oppose 287(g) agreements that turn our local police into ICE accomplices.”

The full list of police departments participating in ICE-related activity is as follows: Auburn; Belknap County Sheriff’s Office; Brentwood; Candia; Carroll; Chester; Chichester; Colebrook; Danville; Epping; Gorham; Hillsboro; Hillsborough County Sheriff’s Office; Kingston; Middleton; Milton; New Boston; New Durham; New Hampshire State Police Department; Newington; Ossipee; Pittsburg; Pittsfield; Rindge; Rockingham County Sheriff’s Office; South Hampton; Troy; Weare; and Whitefield.

All of them are signed on for the Task Force Model, which “enhances public safety and national security by allowing designated immigration officers to enforce limited immigration authority while performing routine police duties or as an active participant in an ICE-led task force, per ICE’s website.

As part of the Memorandums of Understanding (MOU) between ICE and the various departments, law enforcement personnel must complete training on “relevant administrative, legal, and operational issues tailored to the immigration enforcement functions to be performed as provided by ICE instructors, and thereafter pass examinations equivalent to those given to ICE officers.”

It also gives local law enforcement the power and authority “to interrogate any alien or person believed to be an alien as to his right to be or remain in the United States,” and to “process for immigration violations those individuals who have been arrested for State or Federal criminal offenses.”

As well, the MOU also gives them the authority to “arrest without a warrant any alien entering or attempting to unlawfully enter the United States in the officer’s presence or view, or any alien in the United States, if the officer has reason to believe the alien to be arrested is in the United States in violation of law and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained.”

Back in March, the Town of Carroll received a wire transfer for $122,515 from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security as a part of the police department’s involvement in ICE’s 287(g) program.

In a follow-up interview, Police Lt. Ian MacMillan said the funds have since been used to purchase vehicles for the department, update technology services and improve security equipment in cells. The funding was earmarked by the government for vehicles and equipment police departments use, rather than just for being part of the program.

MacMillan reiterated the way the program works related to salary is that ICE reimburses the department for time spent assisting immigration efforts, though it’s separate from the $122,515 funding. He said the only way he expects future money from ICE is more work is done in conjunction with the program.

Alix Olson — who retired in New Hampshire after working 30 years in law enforcement in a different state — started to get involved with anti-ICE activity and outreach efforts during the first Trump Administration.

“The main reason I got involved with the statewide petition and anti-ICE work in general is because I feel like local police, of which I was a part in a different state, don’t really have the need to work with ICE. They already — and my department did, too — work with federal agencies like the DEA (Drug Enforcement Administration), FBI (Federal Bureau of Investigations), Postal Inspectors; it’s pretty standard stuff.

“But we as local police have never been trained to work as federal agents. We’ve always kept our own autonomy as far as local policing goes, and it’s clear to me that ICE has no regard whatsoever for the value of any human lives. It doesn’t really value its partnership with local police, except for the fact that they can make it comfortable for them to accept a whole bunch of money (and) equipment ‘if they’ll just come on and work with us to beat up on immigrants,’” Olson said.

Olson continued that local police take an oath to serve and protect, tell the truth and follow the constitution of the state and the country, but she doesn’t see ICE doing any of that. She said ICE is a force that works with absolute impunity and immunity “thanks to the crook in the White House, and they are a reflection of how horrible he is.”

She cited data from the Deportation Data Project that states between 2025 and 2026 in New Hampshire, approximately 1.9% of all detainees and deportations by ICE had criminal backgrounds. She said the myth that ICE is out there rounding up hardened criminals is just that; a myth.

text:
Vice President JD Vance is used to being confronted by questions from the press. Over the weekend, he faced questions from a Catholic sister.

Sr. Nancy Sylvester, of the Sisters, Servants of the Immaculate Heart of Mary of Monroe, Michigan, was among attendees at a televised town hall event Oct. 17 in Detroit featuring the vice president and was able to ask him a question about immigration.

"We are sisters who minister at the southern border in the United States, as well as here around Detroit, and they are constantly seeing families who are affected by our immigration policies," Sylvester told Vance in the video from CBS News. "They see the trauma of children who are separated from their parents, sometimes on a moment's notice — they go to school and they come back and [the parents are] not there."

She went on, citing the "fear and violence" of Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers.

"How would you justify to people of faith, especially those of us who try to follow the Gospel, how the behavior of the ICE men and women can constantly be justified in terms of the kind of values we want to live by?" asked Sylvester, who is a senior contributor for Global Sisters Report. "And also, what policies would you advocate to try to promote more compassionate and respective behavior toward our immigrant sisters and brothers?"

Sr. Nancy Sylvester confronts Vice President JD Vance in this video. (YouTube/CBS News)

Vance, who is Catholic, began his answer by saying he appreciates her "and hopefully I'll be in your prayers as you'll certainly be in mine." He said the federal government is "trying to strike a balance" between the need for law enforcement and acting humanely.

Despite the host's efforts, Vance did not address specific instances of alleged violent incidents by ICE officers, such as shooting American citizens, but allowed that mistakes have been made.

"Most of them are amazing people who are patriots and they want to do a good job protecting their country. Sometimes you have some people who make mistakes, sometimes you have some people who really screw up, and obviously we have a responsibility to prosecute, investigate when people do screw up," Vance said.

Incidents where ICE officers have been ordered to receive more training or discipline may not be advertised, Vance said, but that doesn't mean it's not happening.

"We believe people have to be judged in a court of law and through a normal investigatory process," he said. "We don't jump in and try to accuse people just again because of what we've seen in a news media article."

Advertisement

Vance seemed to imply that the government has had to be aggressive because of the Biden administration's policies, saying, "What we saw over the last five years, before we came in, I mean is, we have to talk about the fact that drug cartels were sex trafficking thousands and thousands of children, thousands of thousands of girls who were sold into sex slavery. Of course, the fentanyl trade which killed a lot of people in Michigan."

"Despite what some people say in the press, I promise you that we wake up every day and we try to balance law enforcement with humane law enforcement," he said. "And of course, when you're dealing with hundreds of thousands of law enforcement officials, you're never going to get everything perfect, but I think the men and women of ICE, by and large, have done a good job and where there are people who've screwed up, of course they should suffer consequences."

Sylvester is founder and director of the Institute for Communal Contemplation and Dialogue, has served in leadership of her own religious community and in the presidency of the Leadership Conference of Women Religious, and is a columnist for GSR. Previously, she was national coordinator of Network, the Catholic social justice lobby.

Police dascham footage captured the dramatic moment a Tesla plowed into a California Highway Patrol (CHP) vehicle on Tuesday, October 13, leaving two officers seriously injured. The CHP said in a statement two officers were at the scene of a crash when their patrol vehicle was struck from the rear. Both officers sustained injuries from the crash and were transported to the hospital. The driver stated he was asleep while the vehicle was in driver assist mode, authorities said. text:
Hidden within President Donald Trump’s midterms campaign sales pitch is what amounts to a legislative agenda for his final two years in office, priorities that almost certainly would be met with opposition if Democrats win the majority of one or both chambers of Congress.

Trump spent the months leading up to the election cycle’s homestretch pushing Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D. to bring the “SAVE America Act” to the floor. Trump has vowed to pass that package of GOP-crafted elections changes at a number of campaign stops, but while delivering his midterm pitch — his self-described “weave” speaking style — he also has promised loyal crowds that a Republican-run House and Senate would send him several other big-ticket items.

The legislative to-do list often has been relegated to the end of his midterm rallies, several of which have approached two hours in length. That was the case Friday at a rally in Dalton, Ga., where polls suggest Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff is in the driver’s seat against GOP Rep. Mike Collins.

“So, in conclusion, if you elect a Republican House and Republican Senate on November 3rd, you get $5,000,” he said of his proposed payments to all U.S. adult citizens after speaking for more than 90 minutes at a late-afternoon airport hangar rally he admitted was “hot as hell.”

“If we lose, you get absolutely nothing because the Democrat policies cannot get you there. They can’t even if they wanted to, never,” he added. “So, if you lose, you get nothing.”

Despite some GOP lawmakers having bristled at those so-called “Trump dividends” since he first mentioned them at a midterms convention last month in Dallas, he has told rally crowds that a Republican-run Congress would allocate $1 trillion for the payouts quickly following the Nov. 3 elections.

And while any tax-related legislation typically is a heavy lift for Congress, Trump has been promising rallygoers that keeping both chambers under Republican control would mean the slew of tax cuts in the party’s 2025 “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” would be here to stay.

“We will make all Trump tax cuts permanent, including no tax on tips, no tax on overtime, no tax on Social Security for our great seniors,” he said Friday to applause.

Also on his tax to-do list is the estate tax, which he long has called “unfair.”

“We gotta make them permanent because they (Democrats) could change them. They wanna change them,” he said Saturday in Highland Heights, Ky.

Meantime, the “SAVE” bill, which would seek to block individuals in the U.S. illegally from voting by mandating proof of citizenship, is not the lone immigration bill Trump has put on his final years agenda.

He has plugged his envisioned “No Invasion of Our Country Act” multiple times on the stump. He first proposed such a measure at the Dallas convention, saying it would codify into law his second administration’s aggressive anti-immigration measures. Trump told the north Kentucky crowd that the bill, which has not been crafted, would be aimed at “prohibiting any future president from ever opening our borders to illegal immigrants again.”

Rounding out the list are several pieces of legislation long promised by Trump that have never quite taken shape. He uses each rally to vow to present and sign — after more than a decade as a professional politician — a sweeping health care overhaul bill. There’s his pledge to permanently end “no-cash bail” and codify into law his executive orders aimed at blocking men from playing in women’s sports and a measure to ensure there is “no transgender mutilation of your children.”

Senate week

Trump was scheduled to spend this week focused on competitive Senate races, with a Monday night rally in Kansas and others planned in North Carolina (Tuesday), South Carolina (Wednesday), Iowa (Thursday), Georgia (Saturday) and Michigan (Sunday). He also is due in Florida on Friday afternoon to campaign for Rep. Byron Donalds, the GOP nominee for governor, against Democrat David Jolly, a former GOP House member.

And his various political fundraising groups reportedly were preparing to dump millions into close races. But one GOP strategist, Texas-based Matt Mackowiak, said that potential cash infusion would have been more helpful months ago.

“It’s far too late for that,” he wrote on X. “Needed to start Labor Day at latest.”

What’s more, Trump spends ample time at his rallies talking about his pet projects around Washington, D.C., typically to tepid applause. He also dismisses voters’ concerns about the cost of living, calling the term “affordability” a Democratic-created sham.

House Democratic Conference Chairman Pete Aguilar, during a Sept. 15 Capitol press conference before the chamber departed for a midterms recess, said Trump’s and Republicans’ “only real accomplishment” over the last year-and-a-half was “giving billionaires a tax break and cutting health care and food assistance for American families.”

“Since Trump and Republicans came into office, people across the country have been forced to make financial trade offs. Wages haven’t kept pace with inflation,” he told reporters. “Democrats are offering real solutions. We’ll extend the [Affordable Care Act] tax credits. We’ll reverse Trump’s Medicaid cuts and undo his costly tariffs. We’ll hold this administration accountable for its corruption.

“And that’s just the beginning. Democrats are on a path to take back the majority,” the Californian said of the House. “And when we do, unlike Republicans, we’ll fulfill our promise of bringing down costs.”

title: Trump ramps up third-country US deportations - Genocide Watch
description:
United States immigration authorities have dramatically stepped up detentions and deportations since January 2025, when Donald Trump became president.
Third-country deportations, as the practice is known, have been criticised by the US as well as global rights groups like Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, as well as the UN.
Third-country deportations are not new, but rights groups say they were extremely rare before the Trump administration, and have never been used by the US at the scale they are now.
A closer look at the third-country deportations Rights groups have tried to tally forcible third-country deportations, and according to the nonprofits Refugees International and Human Rights First, more than 25,000 people have been subject to forcible third-country deportations so far, based on media reports and information from attorneys.
The Department of Homeland Security’s own data includes more than 16,000 cases of third-country deportations since Trump came into office in January 2025 and August 2026, the latest month for which data is available.
text:
By Alia Chughtai and Umar Farooq

October 15, 2026

Official data shows tens of thousands of migrants and asylum seekers have been sent to countries they have no ties to.

United States immigration authorities have dramatically stepped up detentions and deportations since January 2025, when Donald Trump became president.

Trump campaigned on a pledge to implement the “largest deportation operation in American history”. Officers with the Department of Homeland Security, the agency tasked with the crackdown, now make thousands of arrests a day across the country.

That includes people who are seeking asylum in the US, who are supposed to be given a chance to explain dangers they might face in their home country. And US law and international treaties, like the United Nations Convention Against Torture, prohibit authorities from deporting someone to any country in which they will be persecuted or tortured.

Many of those being detained in the US immigration crackdown say they are at risk of being hurt or killed if they return to their native countries, so the Trump administration has looked for alternative places to deport them, including places someone might have no cultural or legal ties to.

Third-country deportations, as the practice is known, have been criticised by the US as well as global rights groups like Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, as well as the UN.

Critics of the practice say some of the countries taking in the deportees have a record of human rights abuses themselves, or are so dangerous that the US government tells its own citizens not to travel there. They also say there is little to ensure these third countries will give deportees a fair hearing on their cases for asylum, and in the end might send them back to their native countries to face persecution there.

Third-country deportations are not new, but rights groups say they were extremely rare before the Trump administration, and have never been used by the US at the scale they are now. Those being sent to other countries, rights groups say, would not have been deported without their consent. Some US courts have said the practice is illegal, but the US Supreme Court has allowed it to continue, including in a ruling in September.

Experts at the UN have said the practice was leading to a “cascade of human rights violations” across the globe, threatening to undo norms around how refugees and asylum seekers are treated.

A closer look at the third-country deportations

Rights groups have tried to tally forcible third-country deportations, and according to the nonprofits Refugees International and Human Rights First, more than 25,000 people have been subject to forcible third-country deportations so far, based on media reports and information from attorneys.

The Department of Homeland Security’s own data includes more than 16,000 cases of third-country deportations since Trump came into office in January 2025 and August 2026, the latest month for which data is available. The data, provided to the Deportation Data Project based at the University of California, Berkeley and the University of California, Los Angeles and analysed by Al Jazeera, is likely an undercount.

Deportations to these countries need the approval of authorities there, so the Trump administration has sought to make agreements, or reach informal understandings on how to send deportees to a growing list of countries.

Some countries have agreed to keep deportees in prisons, like El Salvador and Eswatini.

Others have agreed to hold deportees temporarily, with some signing Asylum Cooperative Agreements with

the US, or “Safe Third Country Agreements”, which allow deportees to pursue asylum claims in a third country that has agreed to host them.

According to rights groups Refugees International and Human Rights First, many of those deported have no idea where they are being sent, and end up finding themselves in countries where they do not speak the language and have little cultural understanding. Some don’t even have any documents like passports or identification cards, making it difficult to live there.

The list of countries people are being deported to has grown as the US offers financial aid, or business or visa concessions, in exchange for countries taking in third-country nationals the Trump administration wants to remove.

Liberia has agreed to take up to 1,200 deportees, for instance. The Trump administration at one point said it would extend the validity of certain visas for Liberians from 12 to 36 months, and has committed $124m for the country’s health services.

In Cameroon, which agreed to take third-country nationals from the US in December 2025, the Trump administration has pledged to give $30m for the UN’s refugee work there, and $400m over the coming years for the country’s health services.

text:
[Episcopal News Service] A federal appeals court panel has ruled in favor of The Episcopal Church and 26 ecumenical and interfaith partners in a lawsuit contesting the Trump administration’s removal of “sensitive locations” protections for houses of worship in immigration enforcement.

The three-judge panel of the Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit ruled, 2-1, that a lower court judge erred in finding that the faith-based plaintiffs lacked standing to file their lawsuit. The plaintiffs have argued that the Trump administration’s intensified immigration enforcement actions have driven some worshippers to stay home.

The lower court judge ruled in April 2025 that The Episcopal Church and other plaintiffs had not sufficiently demonstrated an imminent threat. The Court of Appeals reversed that decision, sending the case back to the U.S. District Court to rule on the merits of the plaintiff’s arguments.

“Plaintiffs’ members likely face imminent harm from increased enforcement at their houses of worship,” the Court of Appeals opinion says. “That harm is traceable to the new enforcement policy.”

Presiding Bishop Sean Rowe and House of Deputies President Julia Ayala Harris issued a joint statement Oct. 20 after the appellate court ruling was handed down.

“As faith leaders who have borne witness to the harm of ICE enforcement on our congregations — and the impact of immigration in one of our families — we give thanks to God for today’s milestone in our multifaith effort to protect religious freedom,” the presiding officers said. “In The Episcopal Church, we cannot truly be ourselves when some cannot freely worship with us. Civic engagement is an important way Christians can demonstrate love for our neighbors, and with this litigation, we are challenging unjust policies that fall short of respecting the dignity of all people.”

The interfaith group of religious denominations and organizations sued the Department of Homeland Security in February 2025 after the Trump administration rescinded a policy that had protected houses of worship, schools and hospitals.

Since then, the Trump administration has escalated its campaign of immigrant detentions and deportations to include aggressive enforcement operations in targeted cities across the country. The deployment of Immigrations and Custom Enforcement officers, as well as Customs and Border Protection agents, has rattled communities, sparked protests and sometimes resulted in violent and deadly confrontations with both immigrants and U.S. citizens.

There have not been widespread reports of raids inside houses of worship, though in cities with a large federal presence, some churches have been joining efforts to assist immigrant families who are afraid to leave their homes to go to work or school or even to get groceries. One Episcopal church in Minnesota also was on a list of houses of worshiped where Homeland Security was reported to have spied on activists holding meetings there.

The Episcopal Church is one of 12 denominations that have signed onto the federal lawsuit, which also includes the Disciples of Christ, Mennonite, Methodist, Presbyterian and AME Zion churches. Other plaintiffs include regional denominational bodies and other religious associations.

The plaintiffs, represented by the nonpartisan Georgetown University Law Center, have argued the Trump administration is violating religious freedom protections in the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution and the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993.

text:
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday warned that Europe will collapse unless it addresses immigration, pointing to the recent protests in France.

"It’s about immigration,” Trump told reporters at the Oval Office when asked by reporters if education could stop the unrest.

“They have to straighten out their act; otherwise, there won’t be a Europe left," he added.

“If you look at what’s going on in France, I’ve been doing this stuff for a long time ... I have never seen anything like that. That wasn’t a little bit of a riot. That wasn’t a little bit of a protest. That was a full-on revolution, and it continues,” he said.

“When you look at France, and it happened in Italy too, smaller scale, but it’s right there. It’s simmering,” Trump said. “You’re going to have to remove those people that are insurrectionists. You’re gonna have to get them out of the country.”

“If you don’t get them out, you’re not going to have a France,” he added.

Asked whether he would endorse Marine Le Pen, a leading figure in France’s far-right National Rally party, in next year’s French presidential election, Trump said: “I don’t know her. I haven’t met her, but I thought she was badly treated.”

“It would look like a weaponization to me when they did what they did,” he said, referring to Le Pen’s March 2025 conviction over embezzling European Parliament funds.

This July, an appeals court cleared her to run in the French presidential election, set for next spring.

France has been gripped by protests since Sept. 18, when high school students began demonstrations and blockades that also spread in lesser form to Belgium, Albania, Greece, and Italy. The movement has since grown into nationwide protests over rising living costs, fuel prices, and education funding.

Around 550,000 people took to the streets on Saturday, as the protests turned violent and government buildings were set on fire, according to French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez. One police officer and one protester were killed, and Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said 1,200 people were arrested.

description:
The 75-year-old retiree believes U.S. President Donald Trump is doing “a pretty good job,” especially compared with the “disaster” of his predecessor, Democrat Joe Biden.
The rising cost of living is complicating the efforts of Mike Lawler — a relatively popular politician — to hang on to his seat for another two years.
“Do you pledge your allegiance to Donald Trump?” Lawler was asked during a debate.
Lawler’s difficulties are also affecting other centrist Republicans who fear being dragged down by Trump’s shadow.
But all it takes is crossing a street to reach the 17th District, represented by Republican Mike Lawler.
text:
Dan Hanover has planted a sign in the front yard of his home in Tarrytown as if trying to ward off a curse. It bears just three words, “Mike Lawler for Congress,” but that is more than enough for everyone here to understand what it means: the retiree is determined to do whatever he can to help the Republican who represents this charming village north of New York City keep his seat in the House of Representatives after the November 3 election.

Above all, he fears that Democrats will end up controlling everything in a state where they already hold the governorship under Kathy Hochul, the mayoralties of the major cities and 19 of the state’s 26 seats in the House. “This is looking more and more like a one-party state. Someone has to offer an alternative. And that’s the Republicans,” Hanover says from his kitchen.

The 75-year-old retiree believes U.S. President Donald Trump is doing “a pretty good job,” especially compared with the “disaster” of his predecessor, Democrat Joe Biden.

The problem for Republicans is that Hanover’s positive view of Trump is not widely shared among his neighbors. In this part of the Hudson Valley, complaints about the high cost of living are constant, and many residents blame the Republican administration that came to power riding a wave of frustration over inflation during the Biden years.

The rising cost of living is complicating the efforts of Mike Lawler — a relatively popular politician — to hang on to his seat for another two years. Polls suggest a dead heat with his Democratic challenger, Army veteran Cait Conley.

Mike Lawler, like other Republicans desperate to create some distance from the top of the ticket, is running a campaign defined more by what separates him from Donald Trump than by what binds him to his supposed political ally.

His district is a good barometer of the national mood. It was one of only three congressional districts in the entire country that, in 2024, elected a Republican to Congress while simultaneously voting for Democrat Kamala Harris for president.

“Do you pledge your allegiance to Donald Trump?” Lawler was asked during a debate.

“I pledge my allegiance to my constituents, which I always have. It’s why I’ve been rated among the most bipartisan and effective members of Congress. I’ve been praised by presidents of both parties, including Joe Biden and Donald Trump [...] My best friend in Congress is a Democrat,” he replied.

“I’ve clashed with the president on numerous issues,” Lawler said on another occasion, after Democratic candidate Cait Conley blamed him for the economic difficulties facing local families because of his support in Congress for Trump-backed measures. According to an analysis by Congressional Quarterly, the Republican voted in favor of legislation proposed by the president 94% of the time.

On Monday, Lawler did break with Trump over the war in Ukraine. In an interview with CNN, after footage emerged of the U.S. president blaming Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy for the failure to reach a peace deal, the congressman responded: “Vladimir Putin, and Vladimir Putin alone, is responsible for this war.”

Perhaps because of what is at stake — it could help determine which party controls the House of Representatives — it has become one of the most expensive races in the country, with the two parties spending more than $40 million between them.

Each side is targeting the other’s vulnerabilities. Democratic ads highlight the ties between Donald Trump and Mike Lawler, while Republicans have closely scrutinized Democratic candidate Cait Conley’s links to artificial intelligence companies and have sought to associate her with the alleged antisemitism of Zohran Mamdani, the mayor of New York City.

Lawler’s difficulties are also affecting other centrist Republicans who fear being dragged down by Trump’s shadow. Among them is Senator Susan Collins, who is fighting to hold on to her seat in Maine by distancing herself from the Republican administration on issues such as the war with Iran, the sweeping tax package known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which increased healthcare costs for many families, and tariffs on Canada.

“The president did not have a good plan,” Collins acknowledged during a debate last Tuesday.

A town split in two

Tarrytown has an unusual characteristic: it is split in two. One side of the town of 12,000 residents belongs to New York’s 16th congressional district, represented in Washington by a Democrat. But all it takes is crossing a street to reach the 17th District, represented by Republican Mike Lawler. Two ideologies sit side by side in this world of perfect lawns filled with professionals who spend their weekends mowing the grass.

Lawler says he has broken with Trump on issues such as lifting caps on tax deductions, extending temporary protections for Haitian migrants and expanding tax credits for health insurance. Taxes, immigration and healthcare are, in fact, among the issues that most concern residents of the Hudson Valley.

Faced with criticism over the excesses of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), local Republicans highlight crimes committed by immigrants in their campaign ads to underscore the need for tighter border controls.

“During Biden’s presidency, illegal entry got out of hand. Now, with Trump, there may have been some excesses, but the problem has been solved. Illegal immigrants have no place in this country,” says Hanover, the resident with the Republican campaign sign in his yard.

New York’s 17th District is particularly revealing because it shows how voting patterns shift depending on the makeup of local communities. Many residents moved here from New York City to escape increasingly unaffordable housing costs. As these generally more progressive families settled in the area, the district gradually became more Democratic.

The district’s diversity is evident from one town to the next. Home to about 780,000 people, it includes one of the largest Jewish populations in the United States as well as sizeable Haitian and Hispanic communities. Wealthy enclaves such as Chappaqua, home to Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, coexist alongside working-class communities.

People here are not fond of extremes. Lawler is a traditional Republican who steers clear of Trump-style bombast, while his opponent, Conley, is a centrist Democrat who highlights her military service, her support for Israel and her call to reform, rather than abolish, ICE — positions far removed from those of New York progressives such as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Mamdani.

Peter Bartolacci is another Republican who lives in this landscape of family homes and manicured lawns. He is far from enthusiastic about the Trump administration’s performance, but says it was still the better option given the alternative.

“The Democrats haven’t presented a good candidate since Obama, whom I wasn’t a big fan of either. That’s when identity politics began, which hasn’t brought us anything good,” he says in his living room.

He is certain he will vote Republican on November 3. When asked if he likes what Trump is doing in Washington, Bartolacci answers with a line often used by former New York City mayor Ed Koch: “If you agree with me on nine out of 12 issues, vote for me. If you agree with me on 12 out of 12 issues, see a psychiatrist.”

text:
WASHINGTON – With polls showing Democrats on the verge of winning a majority in the House and perhaps the Senate, congressional leaders from both parties are starting to map out their agenda after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

Democrats are promising to focus on affordability and holding President Donald Trump and his administration accountable for alleged corruption and abuse of power, while Republicans are vowing to continue pursuing Trump priorities like border security and domestic fossil fuel production during his final two years in office.

But even if Democrats win back both chambers, they will quickly run into a pair of barriers – the Senate filibuster and Trump’s veto pen – that will make it hard for them to enact many of their plans.

Neither party has released a detailed agenda for the next two years, but their leaders have given hints about what Americans should expect.

House Democrats plan to focus on driving down the high cost of living, lowering the price of groceries, gas and housing, and fighting to make healthcare affordable for every American, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York said in an interview with USA TODAY earlier this month.

"We are explicitly promising to fight for an affordable America, and we will have a responsibility to do everything in our power to make that happen," said Jeffries, who is almost certain to become House speaker if Democrats win a majority.

House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, has suggested voters could expect more of the same from the GOP if it defies the odds and hangs onto its slim majority after November.

"What we would do in the next two years is exactly what we have been doing already, and that is putting the conditions in place for a strong America again," Johnson said during a recent interview on CNBC, pointing to the party’s push for border security, energy dominance and pro-growth policies.

In the Senate, Democrats face tougher odds in the November midterms because they need to flip at least four seats, including at least three in states carried by Trump in 2024. But polls suggest their campaign to win back the majority is within reach, thanks to leads in North Carolina, Alaska, Ohio, and even surprising places such as Texas and Kansas.

Democratic Senate Leader Chuck Schumer of New York told reporters recently that, over the next two years, Democrats would focus on affordability and keeping Trump and his administration in check.

"We’re going to do everything we can to lower costs," Schumer said. "You’ve seen some of the things Trump has done that has raised costs. We’re going to do everything we can to clamp down on this horrible corruption and to end the chaos."

It won’t be easy.

Democrats will face Senate filibuster, Trump veto

Trump, a Republican, has two more years in office, meaning Democratic victories in the House and Senate would usher in a new era of divided government. Trump has said he would use his veto power to block many Democratic priorities and keep them from becoming law.

Democrats would be powerless to stop him. Overriding a veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers (290 votes in the House if all members are voting, 67 in the Senate). Even if there’s a blue wave in the midterms, Democrats are unlikely to come close to those numbers.

Just getting legislation through the Senate would be a challenge. Republicans could stall or even kill Democratic bills with a filibuster, a parliamentary maneuver allowing any member to delay or prevent a vote on a bill. Sixty votes are needed to overcome a filibuster, meaning Democrats would need help from a few Republicans to move forward – an unlikely prospect given the hyperpartisan climate in Washington.

Given those obstacles, "I don’t think Democrats are going to accomplish much legislatively," said Ron Bonjean, a political strategist with close ties to Republicans on Capitol Hill.

Democrats have pledged to end the eight-month-old war in Iran. But there's not a lot they can do to ensure it happens.

They could try to limit or cut off funding for the conflict by inserting provisions into must-pass bills, such as the Defense Department's budget, that would bar federal funds from being used in operations in Iran. Trump would probably veto such legislation, setting up a confrontation with Congress that could lead to another government shutdown – something that carries political risks for both parties.

Another option would be for Democrats to try to force a vote on the War Powers Resolution, which would restrict Trump’s ability to launch or expand military operations without congressional approval. House Democrats and a handful of Republicans have joined forces to pass the resolution three times since June. The Senate even passed the House-approved measure in June, but the Trump administration ignored it amid questions whether it carries the force of law.

Democratic strategist Josh Schwerin said that since Trump probably won’t allow most of their agenda to become law, Democrats should spend the next two years "blocking him from doing more harm and showing voters that Democrats have real answers to the country’s biggest problems."

What can Democrats do?

One way Democrats could rein in Trump is by blocking his appointees, which require Senate approval, and by launching investigations into Trump, his cabinet and his other allies.

Democrats have accused Trump and his allies of enriching themselves while in office, and Jeffries has vowed repeatedly to "hold the crooks accountable."

In the House, those accountability efforts would be led by Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, and Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee.

Raskin has already tangled with the Trump administration over tariffs, presidential pardons, and other issues. Garcia has pushed for the release of the files on convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and has accused Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Department of Homeland Security of misconduct and abuses against U.S. citizens.

Corporate donors to Trump's ballroom and participants in business deals brokered by Trump family members are expected to be among the first targets of investigations if Democrats take control of the House or Senate in the midterm elections, multiple Capitol Hill staffers, lawmakers and attorneys recently told Reuters.

Control of either chamber would give Democrats subpoena power and funding to bolster their investigative staff, enabling them to launch probes as early as February and potentially triggering lengthy legal battles that would place the Trump family business empire in the spotlight.

The investigations could dominate the second half of Trump's term after two years of dealmaking in which the Trump family expanded into crypto, drones, artificial intelligence and prediction markets, while the president's personal wealth grew by an estimated $2.2 billion.

Trump, who was impeached twice but acquitted by the Senate during his first term, could face other impeachment attempts if Democrats win the majority in either chamber. Top Democratic leaders have tried to tamp down such speculation, saying impeachment is not a priority for them. Jeffries told reporters in September that Democrats had not made any decisions about whether to pursue impeachment if they win the majority, but he refused to rule it out.

Democrats also could push to impeach members of Trump's cabinet, such as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has faced criticism over the war in Iran and his decision to fire or sideline dozens of senior military officials, or Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has come under fire over his opposition to vaccines and for pushing out top health officials at agencies such as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

'You make deals'

Will anything get done in the next two years?

Maybe. One area with bipartisan potential, Schwerin said, is artificial intelligence safety paired with guardrails against data centers – "more transparency, tech companies paying for grid and infrastructure upgrades, and tough clean air and water standards."

Establishing AI rules of the road has been a priority for years for the current Senate majority leader, Republican John Thune of South Dakota. Thune has worked for months with his Republican and Democratic colleagues to find common ground on the issue.

Trump has suggested he could work with Democrats on some issues.

"You know they’re going to want some stuff, and we’ll get – you make deals," Trump told Fox News’ Laura Ingraham in an interview Sept. 10.

Contributing: Reuters

Michael Collins writes about the intersection of politics and culture. A veteran reporter, he has covered the White House and Congress. Follow him on X: @mcollinsNEWS

“The results are in: Trump and his GOP allies in Congress cut critical nutrition assistance that helps millions of Latinos and working people across the country meet their basic needs—all to deliver historic tax giveaways to billionaires and business elites,” said Jodie Rubenstein, executive director of Americans for Tax Fairness.

In June, Collins—who has described herself as pro-choice—said she did "not regret" her vote to confirm Kavanaugh, falsely claiming that Roe was overturned by a 6-3 margin and was therefore doomed regardless of her vote. In fact, the precedent was overturned by a 5-4 margin, meaning Kavanaugh's vote proved decisive.

Now in a dead heat race with Democratic nominee Troy Jackson, who has repeatedly hammered her on abortion rights, Collins has continued to defend her confirmation vote. She's also kept fudging the truth.

“I’m very disappointed in his vote to overturn Roe v. Wade,” Collins said of Kavanaugh during an interview published Monday by Maine ABC affiliate WMTW. “There was no way for me to anticipate that.”

Collins had, in fact, been warned that Kavanaugh might overturn Roe v. Wade. In her October 5, 2018, speech supporting his confirmation, she explicitly acknowledged “the concern that Judge Kavanaugh would seek to overturn Roe v. Wade” and noted that President Donald Trump had pledged to nominate judges who would do so.

Reproductive freedom advocates cautioned her that Kavanaugh was not being truthful when he said he considered Roe to be settled precedent, citing his history of ruling against abortion access and praising former Chief Justice William Rehnquist’s dissent in Roe.

But Collins dismissed these advocates' warnings, arguing that Republican-appointed Justices Sandra Day O’Connor, David Souter, and Anthony Kennedy had voted to reaffirm Roe despite opposition to some of their nominations from abortion rights groups. “Suffice it to say, prominent advocacy organizations have been wrong,” Collins said.

In this case, they were not. Lisa Margulies, spokesperson for Planned Parenthood Votes in Maine, said it was dishonest of Collins to plead innocence.

"It’s just a flat-out lie that Susan Collins had ‘no way’ of knowing Brett Kavanaugh would overturn our federal right to abortion," she said. "Mainers drove down to DC and begged her not to confirm him. They knew he was a direct threat to abortion, and so did Susan Collins."

"This is just another flimsy attempt to avoid responsibility for her actions," Margulies said. "Enough is enough. Mainers deserve better than a senator who will throw their rights under the bus and then refuse to acknowledge the harm done."
