title: ICE Appears to Be Ramping Up Enforcement in San Diego
description:
On Friday, a map where people can report ICE sightings had 28 sightings flagged across San Diego County.
The ICE San Diego Field Office made nearly 2,000 arrests in July.
Aryan Dixit, executive director of the organization and a UC San Diego student, said that local colleges and universities have failed to protect their students from ICE.
After the incident, the college installed signs on the campus that say immigration enforcement is prohibited on the school’s campus.
Activist raided: I wrote for Daylight San Diego that ICE agents raided the home and car of a local activist who has documented immigration enforcement operations.
text:
Many media outlets have reported that Immigration and Customs Enforcement has ramped up its efforts in San Diego as part of Operation Safe California in the 45-day window prior to the November election.

At first, I wondered if the headlines were an attempt by ICE to scare people and to drum up support from President Donald Trump’s base going into the midterms. The fear of a potential ICE raid in immigrant communities can be as paralyzing and life-altering as the devastation following an actual raid.

I and some of my peers have worried about journalists spreading this message before we knew whether arrests were actually increasing and the effects that could have on people’s lives and well-being if it turned out to be a ruse. But, we will likely have to wait months to have clear data confirming whether and how much ICE arrests increased because data about these arrests are not immediately available.

The Deportation Data Project gathers and releases federal data related to ICE activity. Its most recent information on ICE activity is from July.

Meanwhile, activists who document ICE activity around the county are starting to sound the alarm about increased enforcement now.

TikTok influencer Arturo Gonzalez told KPBS last week that what’s happening now is the biggest increase he has seen since he started documenting ICE at the beginning of the Trump administration.

The American Friends Service Committee issued an advisory to community members on Thursday that they should be prepared to exercise their rights, including the right to remain silent, amid ramped up ICE raids. The organization offers Know Your Rights information on its website and workshops throughout the community.

“Immigration agents are clearly racially profiling people off the street, targeting working class communities, and causing trauma and harm to families affected by their violent operations,” said Pedro Rios, director of the American Friends Service Committee’s US-Mexico Border Program.

On Friday, a map where people can report ICE sightings had 28 sightings flagged across San Diego County. A month ago on Friday, Sept. 18, the county had three flags throughout the entire day.

On Friday, July 17, the county also had three flags throughout the entire day. According to the Deportation Data Project, that was the month with the most ICE arrests locally, statewide and nationwide in the data available.

ICE did not respond to a request for comment.

Though 45 days before the November election would fall in mid-September, ICE seems to have ramped up its efforts in San Diego and across California since well before that.

ICE arrests nationally have increased steadily since May, rising to nearly 50,000 — the highest monthly total under the current administration — in July, according to the Deportation Data Project.

The arrest trend in California follows a similar trajectory, with more than 4,000 arrested in the state in July after steadily increasing since February.

Almost half of those arrests occurred in the San Diego area, according to the data. The ICE San Diego Field Office made nearly 2,000 arrests in July.

Community members are pushing back against the raids.

On Wednesday, City Heights Defense Committee hosted a demonstration at the corner of University and Fairmount avenues to protest ICE sightings and arrests near local schools, including Hoover High School, John Marshall Elementary School and Ibarra Elementary School.

The Students’ Civil Liberties Union hosted a rally Thursday at City College, where ICE detained a student driving near campus and chased another through campus last month.

Aryan Dixit, executive director of the organization and a UC San Diego student, said that local colleges and universities have failed to protect their students from ICE.

“We’re here to talk about how Immigration and Customs Enforcement has been taking people from our families, has been taking people from our lives, our friends, our relatives, and kidnapping them to God knows where,” Dixit said.

Zavahna Chavarín, a student leader at City College with MeCHA and Students for Justice in Palestine, said campus officers should have escorted ICE officers off of campus instead of directing traffic during last months’arrest.

Jack Beresford, San Diego Community College District vice chancellor of marketing, communications and public affairs, said that Chancellor Gregory Smith said during a Board of Trustees meeting on Thursday that he’s open to meeting with any students or employees who want to discuss the issue, including how campus police should respond.

“We fully understand how upsetting this incident was and are doing everything in our legal power to protect our students and employees,” Beresford said via email. “This includes offering additional training and education so individuals know their rights, it includes updating our ICE response protocols, advocating for federal legislation that would keep ICE off campus, and adding signs at the entrances of our campuses.”

He added that the school provided legal support to the student detained by ICE.

Chavarín called for the school administration to place campus officers on leave during an investigation into the matter, set up a perimeter around campus that ICE cannot legally cross and organize community self defense training.

After the incident, the college installed signs on the campus that say immigration enforcement is prohibited on the school’s campus.

“$75,000 signs will not suffice,” Chavarín said.

The family of the detained student is raising funds for his case on GoFundMe. A judge ordered his release from custody on Friday.

Thank you for reading. I’m open for tips, suggestions and feedback on Instagram @katemorrisseyjournalist and on Bluesky @bgirledukate.

In Other News

El Niño: Alexandra Mendoza reported for The San Diego Union-Tribune that the promise of a wet winter caused by El Niño is prompting an extra layer of urgency in conversations over fixes to the Tijuana River sewage issue.

Activist raided: I wrote for Daylight San Diego that ICE agents raided the home and car of a local activist who has documented immigration enforcement operations.

Kidnapping migrants: A judge sentenced a San Diego man to 12 years in prison for his role in a scheme that involved kidnapping migrants trying to cross the U.S.-Mexico border and requiring their families to pay ransom, City News Service reported via Times of San Diego.

Disappeared: Tijuana topped a recent list of Mexican cities with the highest number of disappeared people, Juan Miguel Hernández reported for El Sol De Tijuana.

Construction vests: Guillermo Méndez reported for NBC 7 that ICE officials are wearing construction safety vests to blend in while doing enforcement operations, including at a construction site in North Park.

Bittersweet homecoming: A Navy sailor who was aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln during its record long deployment returned home to face her father’s recent deportation, CNN reported.

text:
Just before 6:00 a.m. on Monday morning, a group of about 50 protesters gathered outside the main entrance to Highland Hospital in Oakland to call attention to a patient in the custody of Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

" We wanna let the world know that Oakland will not quietly let the feds kidnap our community," one person told KALW on the condition of anonymity.

Many would not share their names out of fear of retaliation from ICE, which has detained protesters in the days following actions like this one. According to Alameda County Immigration Legal Education Partnership — the county’s rapid response network — the patient was taken to Highland after being injured during their arrest on Friday.

Earlier this month, the Washington Examiner reported that ICE is actively increasing enforcement across California. And according to a UC Berkeley deportation data project, ICE arrests in the Bay Area increased by about 70% during the first seven months of this year, compared to the same period last year.

At Highland, community members started gathering over the weekend, leading to the action Monday morning.

"I am very aware of the limited power that any of us have individually to stop armed men with government support, government resources," said one anonymous community member. "Why is resistance important? Resistance is all we have."

Around 7:30 AM, a group of protesters blocked an SUV from exiting the garage. It had been flagged as an ICE vehicle by community reporting networks.

At least six sheriff's deputies arrived to respond to protesters and made a dispersal order, threatening to arrest anyone who was obstructing access to the parking garage. As of publication, no arrests have been made.

Many voiced concern about sheriff’s deputies — and the hospital — cooperating with ICE, which is a violation of the county’s policies.

In January, Alameda County supervisors unanimously approved “ICE-Free Zones,” barring immigration enforcement on county-owned property including parking lots, and the private areas of buildings that are owned or controlled by the county.

Highland is a public hospital, owned by the county and operated by Alameda Health System. As such, it is subject to the ICE-Free Zones policy.

The hospital’s website says that it’s committed to protecting patient privacy, and does not voluntarily disclose information to immigration officials. However, the hospital’s policy on patients who are admitted in ICE custody is unclear.

In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security said that it is standard procedure for officers to accompany detainees to the hospital for monitoring when they need medical care.

Alameda Health System did not respond to KALW’s request for comment.

As the sun rose on Monday, Highland’s hospital staff arrived for work. Some walked by without comment, while others honked in support.

text:
Elected officials on the local, state, and federal level are denouncing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after agents questioned North Bergen children going to school this morning.

By John Heinis/Hudson County View

A short video posted on Instagram this morning by advocacy group Estamous Unidos NJ showing ICE agents approaching at least one male student sitting outside a cafe before school around 7 a.m. this morning.

“Leave him alone, he’s a minor! Leave him alone!” the woman filming the video shouted at an ICE agent.

The agent responded “get out of here, get that dog out of here too: you’re gonna have a real bad day.”

The woman filming continued to shout to leave the boy alone, with the agent replying “get out of here, you’re 12 years old,” urging her to leave, noting he could arrest her for obstruction.

U.S. Rep. Rob Menendez (D-8), a staunch opponent of ICE who spoke out against a Downtown Jersey City arrest on Saturday outside a Mexican restaurant, called the incident in North Bergen “completely unacceptable.”

“ICE was stopping and questioning students on their way to school this morning in North Bergen. This is completely unacceptable and should be condemned by every elected official,” he wrote on X.

“ICE has no business targeting our schools or stopping and questioning our children. Full stop. If your child was stopped or you need Know Your Rights guidance, please contact our office immediately at (201) 309-0301 or through the ‘Request Assistance’ form at http://menendez.house.gov.”

North Bergen Mayor Nick Sacco and the board of commissioners also came out against the conduct of ICE, noting that the North Bergen Board of Education is investigating the incident and legal action – such as denying access to school buildings without a warrant – will be taken.

“The ongoing presence of masked ICE agents in our community is continuing to cause widespread fear and outrage among North Bergen residents. While our local government has extremely limited authority regarding federal law enforcement actions, we want residents to know that we share their concerns and are monitoring the situation closely,” the five commissioners, which includes Sacco, said in a statement.

” … We join immigration advocates and residents in calling on ICE to cease its operations in Hudson County and stop terrorizing our communities. We will remain vigilant to ensure that North Bergen is a safe place for everyone.”

Sacco, who is not seeking re-election in May, joined Parks and Public Property Commissioner Hugo Cabrera – who has endorsed to succeed him – to speak out against ICE detaining her mother and two sons in June.

In July, the board of commissioners also decried the possibility that the FBI would no longer be in charge of probing ICE assault cases.

Finally, Assemblyman Larry Wainstein (D-33) noted he felt the matter was personal since he is the son of immigrant that calls North Bergen home.

“Today in North Bergen, children were stopped and questioned by ICE on their way to school. That is unacceptable. No child in North Bergen should have to fear walking to class, and no parent should have to worry about whether their son or daughter will make it home safely. When federal agents target students in our community, they create fear where there should be safety,” he noted in his own statement.

“As the son of immigrants who came here from South America and built a life in this community, and as a parent myself, this hits especially close to home. North Bergen is a working-class town built by immigrant families. Our children deserve the opportunity to go to school, learn, and grow without being treated as suspects because of where they live or what they look like.”

title: Arizona election officials prepare for possibility of ICE at the polls in 2026 - Votebeat
description:
But even the possibility of such a deployment — or immigration enforcement activity near, but not at, voting sites — could discourage people from voting.
As a result, election officials and voting rights groups across Arizona are preparing for such scenarios, even though they may not materialize.
There was at least one sighting of ICE agents near a voting site on the day of the state primary.
A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson declined to explain what ICE agents were doing in the area, citing “operational security” and officer safety concerns.
The agency also provided a short list of individuals arrested in Arizona by ICE agents, complete with mugshots.
text:
Votebeat is a nonprofit news organization reporting on voting access and election administration across the U.S. Sign up for Votebeat Arizona’s free newsletter here.

On a recent weeknight, standing at the head of a small room in a nondescript office building, Karime Rodriguez projected a map of metro Phoenix onto the wall.

The green dots, she explained, represented voting sites. The red ones were reports of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity that her organization, Living United for Change in Arizona, or LUCHA, had vetted and verified over the last year and a half.

In some areas, the green and red dots overlapped. That was the inspiration for LUCHA’s event — a training for those interested in keeping an eye out for federal agents at voting locations in November.

It’s a possibility that has loomed large in Arizona since earlier this year, when some of the state’s farthest-right lawmakers proposed now-dead legislation that would have forced counties into agreements with federal agents to monitor voting sites during this year’s elections.

And, in May, when asked whether he would deploy ICE or the National Guard to voting sites, President Donald Trump said he would do “anything necessary” to ensure “honest elections.”

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security told Votebeat that ICE does not plan to patrol polling places. But they left open the possibility that agents could respond to threats or serve warrants nearby.

Experts and election officials broadly say that deploying armed federal agents or military troops to the polls is clearly barred by federal law and would likely be abruptly slapped down in court. Arizona law also prohibits a wide range of behavior that could intimidate voters, and experts say armed agents at the polls would likely violate those statutes.

But even the possibility of such a deployment — or immigration enforcement activity near, but not at, voting sites — could discourage people from voting. As a result, election officials and voting rights groups across Arizona are preparing for such scenarios, even though they may not materialize.

That includes LUCHA. Though only a handful of people attended its recent training, the organization says it has trained hundreds of poll observers — more than ever before — to respond if they see ICE or other federal law enforcement at the polls, primarily by documenting the incident and reporting it to community groups. Rodriguez described the efforts as preparing to meet “a serious moment.”

“The threat is just so great,” said Alejandra Gomez, the group’s executive director, adding that “anything, unfortunately, is possible to stop people from being able to vote.”

Voting rights groups are readying to respond to feds at the polls

Some have questioned what Trump and his allies would gain by sending ICE to the polls and suggested that the idea is merely an intimidation tactic.

Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes, a Democrat, said he believes the threats aim to “diminish voters’ motivation to vote.” Ben Ginsberg, a longtime GOP election lawyer, agreed, adding that ICE or troops at voting sites is “a really unlikely scenario.”

“You drop the rumors and the innuendo and that does, they hope, have a suppressive effect on who goes out to the polls,” Ginsberg said. “I think it is a whole lot tougher, just as a practical matter, to actually put people at the polls … not only the legal problem with it, but I really do think there’d be a huge political backlash, and it would potentially taint the elections.”

Voting rights organizations say even intimidation is a huge problem. They’re scrambling to respond through observer programs, lawsuits, and more.

One such group, Mi Familia en Acción of Phoenix, joined eight others last month in filing a preliminary complaint in federal court that aims to block officers from the polls.

Others are laying the groundwork for a swift legal response. The ACLU of Arizona sent a letter to each of the state’s counties outlining applicable federal and state laws that prohibit the presence of troops or armed federal agents at the polls.

“Because it has never been categorically ruled out, and because the administration has floated the idea repeatedly, counties should not treat this as a remote or hypothetical concern,” the letter read. “Preparation and clear policy now will prevent a crisis later.”

Katelynn Contreras, a policy strategist at the ACLU of Arizona and one of the authors of the memo, said it aimed to ensure counties, particularly those with few resources, had a clear outline of voter intimidation statutes and weren’t “caught on the back foot” if federal agents showed up.

“Some of the smaller counties perhaps don’t have the capacity or have the legal know-how of how all of these inner workings with federal statutes, state statute, and the various voting rights constitutional amendments interplay,” she told Votebeat. “So we wanted to provide that resource to them.”

Meanwhile, LUCHA and its partner groups are tracking immigration enforcement already occurring in heavily Latino communities across the state. Rodriguez told those assembled for observer training that the organization has repeatedly seen immigration enforcement activities near schools, churches, and other places that serve as community institutions — and, during election season, as neighborhood polling sites.

There was at least one sighting of ICE agents near a voting site on the day of the state primary. The agents were spotted near 67th Avenue and Indian School Road in Maryvale, a heavily Latino and largely residential neighborhood in Phoenix.

About a half-mile down the street — past a grocery store, a pediatric dentist, an elementary school, a YMCA, and a Boys & Girls Club — voters cast ballots at the Cartwright School District Annex. Rodriguez said the reports indicated that agents were “circling” neighborhoods near the voting site.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson declined to explain what ICE agents were doing in the area, citing “operational security” and officer safety concerns.

“Every day, DHS enforces the laws of the nation across the country, including in Arizona,” the spokesperson said. The agency also provided a short list of individuals arrested in Arizona by ICE agents, complete with mugshots.

It’s unclear if ICE’s presence deterred anyone from voting that day. But Rodriguez said her group has used the incident as an example of what observers could see in November.

“It was a reminder that this work is not theoretical, it is a response to what is actually happening on the ground,” she said.

Officials are skeptical they’ll see interference, but are bracing regardless

Most of Arizona’s election officials have been preparing for an array of potential federal interference scenarios since before the state primary.

Those include ICE or the National Guard appearing at the polls, federal civil rights monitors — a routine part of elections since the 1960s — interfering with voting, or federal agents showing up at counties’ election centers with warrants.

At the state level, Fontes said he wouldn’t “speculate” about how his office would respond to federal interference scenarios, and he doubted one would arise in November. But he acknowledged that he and Democratic Attorney General Kris Mayes planned to be “well enough prepared to be able to present the appropriate information to courts, if it becomes necessary.”

“Obviously, we’re going to have, and we’ve already had, and we will continue to have, conversations about those possibilities,” he said.

Officials have been weighing how to respond at the county level, too — particularly in Arizona’s larger jurisdictions. Pima County Attorney Laura Conover, a Democrat, told reporters earlier this year that her office was “going to protect our community.” Her remarks suggested that she had already drafted litigation to handle federal agents, rogue federal monitors, or armed vigilante groups at the polls in the county, the second-most populous in the state and home to bright-blue Tucson.

“It doesn’t matter what uniform you’re wearing or what agency you claim, you cannot violate state law,” she said on July 10, weeks before the state primary, which appeared to run uneventfully in Pima County. “We expect anyone who visits us from a national level to do any kind of observing, which the law does allow, we expect them to follow the law. That will be the expectation. Should they not, then we are prepared to go straight into court with that information.”

Pima County Recorder Gabriella Cázares-Kelly confirmed at a conference last month that local prosecutors “already have all the paperwork ready.” She said she was not expecting to see federal agents at the polls, but if they appeared, a staffer would “literally run to a judge who will issue a restraining order.”

“We have had the meetings,” Cázares-Kelly, a Democrat, said. “We have a plan in place.”

In neighboring Pinal County, a tabletop exercise last month simulated what might happen if a federal officer showed up at the deep-red county’s election headquarters in Florence, a small town roughly halfway between Phoenix and Tucson.

One elections staffer noted that the county had a new, formal policy for such situations. Under its provisions, he would immediately contact county attorneys and await their guidance. One attorney noted that even if the agent had a warrant, they’d still want to see it and ensure its legitimacy.

Recorder Dana Lewis, a Republican, told Votebeat that the new guideline was put into place following the FBI’s search of an elections office in Fulton County, Georgia, earlier this year.

“Most people are good, godfearing, law-abiding citizens — they wouldn’t know what to do if a federal agent showed up and said, ‘Hi, I’m here to speak with the recorder,’” she said. “So we had to establish that.”

Lewis added that she didn’t expect to see federal law enforcement at her voting sites on Election Day. After all, she said, “there’s nothing here that could possibly be of concern.”

“But it’s one of those things,” she said. “I never know what’s going to happen.”

text:
(Washington, DC) – The United States government should order federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers not to operate in the vicinity of polling places, early voting locations, or drop boxes during the midterm electoral period, Human Rights Watch said today. The presence of these federal agents could deter people from voting.

“ICE officers’ abuses have already seriously affected US citizens who have been stopped, beaten, detained, deported, and even killed,” said Philippe Bolopion, executive director at Human Rights Watch. “Voters should not have to fear being caught in an ICE dragnet when they head to the polls.”

In-person early voting is already taking place in the majority of states. In a nationwide September poll, 40 percent of respondents said they expect some kind of ICE presence at polls, with even higher percentages among non-white respondents expecting to see ICE agents in places people vote.

Federal law generally prohibits federal officials from sending “troops or armed men” to voting sites. Several state laws prohibit any armed officers, including police, from engaging in acts that could interfere with the elections or intimidate voters by their presence near polling places. Some states bar law enforcement officers, including police, from being in close proximity to polling places at all unless they are responding to a specific incident.

Despite these robust prohibitions, neither President Donald Trump nor the heads of the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation have been willing to rule out the possibility that federal agents, including ICE, may be at places where people vote.

In March, then-Deputy Attorney General and now-Attorney General Todd Blanche said, “Why is there an objection to sending ICE to polling stations? ... Illegals can’t vote. It doesn’t make any sense.” In February, Karoline Leavitt, who was White House press secretary at the time, said she could not “guarantee” that ICE agents won’t be around a polling location in November.

In early September, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there were no plans to station ICE agents at polling places but left the door open for them to be there if “serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down” or if “there is a threat to that polling place.”

Three lawsuits are pending in federal courts to prevent ICE from operating at the polls, with an additional court case seeking to require the government to disclose its plans regarding ICE agents at polling places. In Washington, DC, the Board of Elections in October asked the National Guard to limit their presence near drop box locations for the midterm election following complaints that troops had been spotted near a drop box in Foggy Bottom.

The Trump administration has long touted the idea that large numbers of noncitizens unlawfully cast ballots in US elections but has not produced any evidence suggesting that the problem exists at a scale that would have affected the result of any election, anywhere in the country. Multiple research studies, including from the Fair Elections Center, Bipartisan Policy Center, Brennan Center, and the Cato Institute, have found no evidence of mass voting by noncitizens and concluded that the problem is insignificant in electoral outcomes.

ProPublica found that federal immigration officers have detained at least 500 US citizens since the start of Trump’s second term, including 36 incidents in which detained US citizens were prevented from contacting their family or lawyers for 24 hours or more. The same study also found that agents who questioned their claims of citizenship detained more than 100 US citizens, nearly all of them people of color.

In Minnesota, Human Rights Watch found that ICE’s Operation Metro Surge abuses terrified many people, causing them to stay home and miss work, school, and even essential health care appointments. US citizens of color whom Human Rights Watch interviewed at the time said they were so fearful of racial profiling that they began carrying their passports everywhere.

Human Rights Watch analysis also suggests that in 2025, ICE used race and ethnicity in Los Angeles as a crude proxy for identifying a person’s nationality, and detained people on that basis. Perceptions of the risks associated with an encounter with ICE may well be higher among non-white communities.

The notoriety of those incidents and of ICE’s widespread abuses over the last two years risks dissuading some people from voting if they feel they are likely to encounter ICE agents near polling places, Human Rights Watch said.

“ICE agents should be publicly ordered to stay away from the polls and anywhere ballots are being cast,” Bolopion said.

Incumbent Democrat Gabe Vasquez and Republican challenger Greg Cunningham debated for New Mexico's 2nd Congressional District.

The candidates clashed over tax policy, with Vasquez defending his vote against a bill he said favored billionaires.

On immigration, both candidates agreed the system is broken but differed on the role of Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Vasquez called for an end to the military conflict in Iran, while Cunningham expressed support for the war effort.

Candidates for the 2nd Congressional District faced each other for the only time ahead of the Nov. 3 General Election in a televised debate.

Democrat incumbent Gabe Vasquez and Republican challenger Greg Cunningham appeared together in Albuquerque for a debate hosted in the KRQE studio.

The 2nd Congressional District remains an important seat to both major political parties. The seat has flipped parties three times in the past eight years. Vasquez defeated Yvette Herrell in 2022 and was re-elected with another victory over Herrell in 2024. Republican U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson made a stop in Las Cruces to stump for Herrell in 2024 and did the same for Cunningham, making an appearance in Albuquerque on Aug. 26 and at a private fundraiser in Las Cruces in October.

Cunningham cited multiple votes made by Vasquez pertaining to his record while in Congress during the debate.

"When Gabe Vasquez had a chance to cut taxes for people like me, a police officer who depended on overtime to get by to make ends meet, for tipped workers in our service industry here in New Mexico and our social security residents," Cunningham said. "That is a fixed income. That would be my focus."

Vasquez said many of the issues Cunningham raised were provisions tied to the Donald Trump Administration's Big Beautiful Bill Act legislation, which Vasquez voted against.

"When you put that bill inside a bill that takes health care away from 90,000 New Mexicans, 10,000 kids and tax cuts for billionaires, no, that is not an honest vote. It's not an honest way to do business," Vasquez said.

Regarding immigration, Vasquez touted his New American Immigration Plan, which includes bills to improve technology at points of entry. Vasquez also called the illegal immigration enforcement system "broken" amid increasing Immigration and Customs Enforcement actions across the country under Trump.

"The process is so broken and immigration has been used as a political football from both parties for way too long," Vasquez said. "It is way past time to do it and my New American Immigration Plan addresses many of those issues."

Cunningham, a former Albuquerque police officer and Marine veteran, described ICE as a law enforcement agency and accused Vasquez as calling to abolish ICE, which Vasquez said was false.

"The path to citizenship has to be streamlined," Cunningham said. "We have to make sure that the people that are in America, that are looking for opportunity and doing things the right way, have a real path to citizenship."

The two candidates also differed in their view of the ongoing military conflict in Iran.

"We have got to end this reckless war with Iran," Vasquez said during a question on affordability. "It's an understanding that times are tough right now.

"The promise of the President was not to have endless wars. That was one of the promises he made to voters. He broke that promise and because he broke that promise today we are seeing gas prices spike to $4.30 on average. We must end the war of Iran and bring our troops home who are bravely serving."

Cunningham expressed his support for the war in Iran.

"Nobody wants war and nobody wants this war over any faster than the men and women who are serving because I did that," Cunningham said.

"I am against a terrorist regime having a nuclear weapon. And them being able to control gas prices for the rest of the world."

text:
Video shows the moment a Long Beach man was allegedly injured during an arrest following an apparent Immigration and Customs Enforcement operation over the weekend.

The man has been identified by his family and Rep. Robert Garcia, who represents California's 42nd congressional district, as Ricardo Gonzalez, a U.S. citizen.

The video, which has now gone viral, shows masked federal agents dressed in uniforms bearing the words "Police ICE" restraining Gonzalez. While on the ground, he can be heard yelling that his arm was broken.

It is unclear what led up to the arrest.

In a statement to CBS LA, a spokesperson for ICE said agents were conducting a targeted enforcement operation to "arrest an at-large criminal illegal alien." The spokesperson added that during the operation, anti-ICE agitators attempted to impede, damaging government vehicles "despite officers giving lawful commands."

"Officers followed their training and used the minimum amount of force," the statement said. "ICE did NOT hit an individual on a bike. An individual was arrested after he smashed the mirror of a government vehicle."

ICE officials said the person was transferred to the custody of local police. The department is investigating potential charges for the damage to a government vehicle.

In an online post, Gonzalez's daughter said her father was struck by an ICE vehicle and "tased twice, pinned to the ground, and taken to the hospital for serious injuries."

Garcia posted on X alleging ICE agents "brutally attacked and broke the arm of a North Long Beach resident and U.S. citizen."

"The videos are horrific and should concern not just our community but the country," Garcia wrote. "Long Beach stands with our community and our immigrant families. ICE is not welcome in Long Beach."

During a news conference on Monday, Garcia called the incident "incredibly disturbing" and added that there should be an investigation into what took place.

"The immigration actions, the terror that happened in North Long Beach over the weekend, is not welcome in our city or our community," Garcia said.

When asked by reporters about the incident on Monday, First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said he didn't believe it was a criminal operation and added that DHS was conducting its immigration enforcement.

"There may be charges coming out of that," Essayli said. "I'm not sure; it has not been presented to my office yet."

In a statement, the Long Beach Police Department said it responded to an incident on Saturday after ICE "requested emergency assistance" due to "vehicle vandalism taking place and a subject in need of medical aid."

"Upon arrival, officers observed a large group disturbance involving the ICE agents," the department said. "One officer located a handcuffed male adult, being detained by ICE, who was bleeding."

The department added that officers were "not involved in any immigration enforcement and LBPD personnel did not make any arrests."

title: Proposed trafficking credibility rules risk punishing victims for being victims - Free Movement
description:
The government intends to alter the way in which the credibility of possible victims of trafficking is assessed.
The government itself acknowledges that genuine trafficking victims may delay in coming forward, give partial accounts and have trouble with their memories.
The proposed provision states that the competent authority ‘must take account, as damaging the person’s credibility, of’ those particular matters.
The system for protecting trafficking victims relies on professionals spotting possible victims; adults have no option of referring themselves to the NRM.
Why does this version differ from what you stated in your asylum interview?
text:
The government intends to alter the way in which the credibility of possible victims of trafficking is assessed. According to clause 36 of the Immigration and Asylum Bill, matters such as having made a late disclosure, or material inaccuracies, inconsistencies or failing to provide information, should be regarded as damaging to credibility unless there are ‘good reasons’ for them having arisen.

For those of us who work with survivors of trafficking, there is a basic issue with this proposal. Many of the behaviours which decision makers would be asked to treat as damaging credibility are in fact behaviours that the Home Office’s own guidance acknowledges can occur in genuine trafficking cases.

The Modern Slavery Statutory Guidance notes that possible victims may not recognise themselves as having been trafficked or enslaved and may tell their stories with ‘errors and/or omissions’. The guidance also clearly acknowledges the connection between trauma and delayed disclosure. It identifies the impact of trauma, including post-traumatic stress disorder, as one possible reason for the delay. It also explains that a delay in disclosing facts should not automatically be treated as manipulative or as showing that the facts are untrue.

Significantly, it recognises that ‘Disclosures often come slowly and in a piecemeal way, sometimes over years.’ The same guidance acknowledges the memory difficulties linked to trauma, such as trouble remembering facts and ‘gaps’ or confusion regarding events. This is important because the reasonable grounds decision represents only the first stage of the National Referral Mechanism. The guidance acknowledges that an account with gaps or inconsistencies may still meet the reasonable grounds threshold and recognises that a possible victim might be unable to give a detailed account.

Therefore, there is a contradiction with the government’s approach. The government itself acknowledges that genuine trafficking victims may delay in coming forward, give partial accounts and have trouble with their memories. Yet some of these same features would now be incorporated into a legal framework in which they are treated as damaging to credibility.

Impact of clause 36

Clause 36 would insert a new section 60A into the Nationality and Borders Act 2022. The proposed provision states that the competent authority ‘must take account, as damaging the person’s credibility, of’ those particular matters. This involves any delay in filing a claim stating that one is a victim of slavery or human trafficking, any delay in supplying the relevant information, and any material inaccuracy, inconsistency or omission in the information given. It would also include any material inconsistency between the details given in a trafficking claim and those provided in an asylum or human rights claim or in civil or criminal proceedings.

The Bill includes an important safeguard in that these matters should not be regarded as damaging to credibility if the competent authority considers that there are good reasons for them. That does not eliminate the concern, though. Instead of evaluating delays or inconsistencies in a neutral way according to all the circumstances, the decision-maker would need to regard them as damaging to credibility unless it could be satisfied that there was a good reason.

No definition of ‘good reasons’

The difficulty is that clause 36 does not define a good reason. Instead, the competent authority must have regard to guidance issued by the Home Secretary. Existing Home Office guidance recognises trauma, PTSD, fear, memory difficulties and other barriers to disclosure, but the Bill does not expressly say that any of them will satisfy the new statutory test.

It might even be difficult to determine the reason for an inconsistency or a delay in the disclosure. How can a person with PTSD show that trauma was the reason for a particular omission they made during an interview several months earlier? What would happen if they had not at that time obtained the relevant medical evidence?

Then there is the shame experienced due to sexual exploitation, the continued fear of traffickers, fear of the authorities, difficulties with interpretation or simply not realising that what had taken place constituted trafficking.

Victims are not immigration lawyers

Another problem with demanding early disclosure is that victims may not realise that what has happened to them amounts to trafficking, enslavement or domestic servitude. A client might say that their passport was taken from them, that their movements were controlled, that they were forced to work or that they were threatened. They know what they went through, but they may not understand its legal importance.

Many of my clients have only a limited knowledge of English and a few have had little formal education. It is not reasonable to expect them to understand the legal definition of trafficking or exploitation or to be able to tell the difference between trafficking and smuggling or to know what the National Referral Mechanism is. Often it is only after a lawyer or other qualified professional has taken a thorough history that signs of trafficking appear and a referral is considered. It would not be suspicious for a more detailed account to come to light after seeking legal advice; in fact, that is one of the reasons for getting such advice.

Is an asylum interview really a safe opportunity to disclose?

It is especially worrying when the changes to the Modern Slavery Statutory Guidance are taken into account. Since 11 May 2026, those making decisions have been told to take into account past opportunities to disclose exploitation. The recommendations state:

An asylum interview should normally be regarded as a safe and relevant environment for disclosure of exploitation, unless specific concerns are identified at the time that would undermine its suitability.

Where someone has had the opportunity to come forward but has not done so, such circumstances may be considered when evaluating their credibility. In certain cases, the guidance allows decision makers to reach a negative decision on credibility grounds. However, a different document from the Home Office greatly complicates that assumption.

The Home Office’s own Asylum Interviews guidance acknowledges that:

in some circumstances and particularly in relation to highly sensitive information, disclosure may not happen during the interview, despite the interviewer’s best efforts.

It also recognises that claimants might find it more comfortable to give sensitive information to immigration advisers, clinicians or support workers. An asylum interview is not a specialist assessment of trafficking. The claimant might think that the purpose of the interview is to explain why they are unable to go back to their home country. They could be communicating through an interpreter, or may feel that they are unable to talk about the sexual exploitation or criminal activities which they were forced to carry out. The fact that an interview is described as a safe environment does not mean that the person taking part in it actually feels safe enough to disclose information.

Identification is not solely the victim’s responsibility

In some cases the victim has already disclosed the facts, but no one realised how important they were. A claimant may have told an asylum interviewer that they had been controlled, had had their documents taken from them, had been threatened and had been forced to work. Who is at fault if the interviewer does not recognise those signs and no referral is made?

A lawyer several months later could take a detailed history, notice the signs of trafficking and recommend a referral into the National Referral Mechanism. Home Office guidance urges its staff to be alert to the signs of modern slavery and specifically notes that victims might not be able to identify themselves. If the state failed to recognise a possible victim and then relied on the delay or later development of that person’s account to damage their credibility, an institutional failure of identification would become an evidential problem for the victim.

The system for protecting trafficking victims relies on professionals spotting possible victims; adults have no option of referring themselves to the NRM. The fact that there are designated first responders shows that vulnerable people may need someone else to realise what has happened to them.

The European Court of Human Rights has likewise stressed the positive obligations of the state in this respect. In V.C.L. and A.N. v United Kingdom (Applications nos. 77587/12 and 74603/12), the court held that, once the relevant credible suspicion arises, the individual should be ‘assessed promptly by individuals trained and qualified to deal with victims of trafficking’.

Clause 36 could shift responsibility in the opposite direction. Rather than inquiring whether the officials in question had identified the signs of trafficking when they should have, the emphasis might turn to asking: Why didn’t you tell us before? Why did you omit this? Why does this version differ from what you stated in your asylum interview?

Sometimes those questions may be legitimate. There is nothing objectionable about investigating deliberately fabricated trafficking claims. Credibility is relevant and genuine contradictions can require explanation. But another question must be asked with equal force: why did the authorities not identify the victim earlier?

Conclusion

Parliament should be extremely cautious about legislating that delay, material inaccuracies, inconsistencies and omissions are damaging to credibility when the Home Office’s own specialist guidance recognises that genuine trafficking victims may display precisely those characteristics. The ‘good reasons’ exception does not entirely resolve that contradiction because the Bill leaves its meaning to guidance.

Victims should not be expected to diagnose their own legal status and should not lose credibility because someone finally asked the right question. And where the state failed to recognise what a victim was telling them the first time, the victim should not bear the consequences of that failure later.

text:
The federal lawsuit brought by a Baldwin County construction worker repeatedly detained by immigration officers now identifies the Homeland Security Investigations agent accused of detaining him the first time: Kent Blacklidge.

Blacklidge is now facing nine felony sex-crime charges in an unrelated Baldwin County case involving a juvenile.

Leonardo Garcia Venegas, a U.S. citizen from Baldwin County, filed the lawsuit after being detained multiple times by immigration officers despite showing an Alabama STAR ID and telling agents he was born in Florida.

A first amended complaint filed this month names Blacklidge as an individual defendant. It alleges he participated in Venegas’ detention during a May 21, 2025, immigration operation at a private Foley construction site.

According to the complaint, Venegas was walking toward his brother, who was being detained, while recording on his phone when Blacklidge blocked his path. The complaint alleges Blacklidge grabbed Venegas’ arm, forced it behind his back and pushed him toward the ground without first asking him questions.

Venegas repeatedly told agents he was a U.S. citizen and offered to show identification, according to the filing. The complaint says agents searched his pocket, found his Alabama STAR ID, but continued to detain him for more than an hour.

The amended complaint alleges officers targeted Latino workers while passing by white and Black workers at the site. Those are allegations in the lawsuit, which remain pending in federal court.

A federal judge has since issued a preliminary order limiting certain warrantless immigration raids and detentions at Alabama construction sites while the case continues.

Blacklidge was working as a Homeland Security Investigations special agent when the May 2025 detention occurred, according to the amended complaint. HSI is the investigative arm of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

In September, Blacklidge was charged in Baldwin County with first- and second-degree rape, first- and second-degree sodomy, two counts each of first- and second-degree sexual abuse, and incest. The charges involve a juvenile, according to the Alabama Attorney General’s Office and prior NBC 15 reporting.

Prosecutors had sought an Aniah’s Law hearing that could have resulted in Blacklidge being held without bond. That request was later withdrawn after prosecutors said the defense had subpoenaed the juvenile alleged victim to testify at the hearing.

text:
California officials are calling for an investigation after they say a man was injured while being detained by federal immigration agents, who were captured on video pinning him down against a curb as he yelled for help during the encounter in Long Beach over the weekend.

California Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia, whose district includes Long Beach, called the incident "incredibly disturbing" and said the man is a U.S. citizen.

ABC News has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment.

In a formal complaint to the Department of Homeland Security, Long Beach Mayor Rex Richardson said the man "reportedly was subjected to repeated Taser use, forcibly restrained, and sustained significant injuries" during Saturday's encounter.

Long Beach police officers who responded to the scene Saturday saw a "large group disturbance" involving Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents and located the man handcuffed and bleeding while being detained by ICE, the Long Beach Police Department said in a statement.

The mayor identified the man in a statement on Monday as Ricardo Gonzalez, referring to him as a "Long Beach resident, father, and former City employee."

In a video posted on social media by StopICE.net, Gonzalez can be heard yelling, "Help me!" while being pinned on the street against a curb. He repeatedly said his arm was broken and could be heard moaning in pain while being detained.

Officers brought him to a local fire station, where they removed his handcuffs and then transported him to a local hospital for medical treatment, according to the police department.

It is unclear what specific injuries Gonzalez sustained or what led up to ICE detaining him. A family member told ABC News on Monday that they do not have any comment at this time.

According to Richardson's complaint to DHS, Gonzalez contacted the Long Beach Police Department "seeking assistance during a confrontation with federal immigration agents."

Long Beach police said their officers responded after ICE personnel requested emergency assistance from local authorities "due to vehicle vandalism taking place and a subject in need of medical aid."

"LBPD officers were not involved in any immigration enforcement and LBPD personnel did not make any arrests," the police department said.

Garcia, the ranking Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, called for an investigation into the incident.

"There is no reporting that he was doing anything wrong, no public reporting," he said during a press conference on Monday. "Certainly, I have not received any information from our own police department that he was somehow causing some sort of criminal activity."

The Long Beach mayor said he submitted a formal complaint to DHS on Monday "demanding accountability for the actions of federal immigration agents in Long Beach."

"What happened to Ricardo is outrageous and unacceptable," Richardson said in a statement while calling for an independent investigation into the incident. "Long Beach will not stay silent when our neighbors are harmed. A federal badge is not a license to brutalize people or disregard their constitutional rights. If you are entrusted with enforcing the law, you must answer to it."

title: 2 ICE arrests in Oakland and Emeryville Friday result in hospitalization
description:

ACILEP, the statement reads, “today condemned the violent manner of two ICE arrests this past weekend of Alameda County residents.
The agency denied that ICE agents used excessive force and said his injuries predated his arrest.

text:
Agents from Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, detained two people in the East Bay late last week, including one in Oakland.

Both individuals landed in the hospital after their arrests. According to statements from ICE and ACILEP, the Alameda County Immigration Legal Education Partnership, a county program launched last year in response to the Trump Administration’s escalation of immigration enforcement, the arrests occurred on Friday, Oct. 16.

ACILEP said agents used excessive force in both arrests. The first took place that morning at San Antonio Park in East Oakland, and the other later in the afternoon in Emeryville, near 45th and Adeline streets.

In an email statement to The Oaklandside, also posted on ACILEP’s social media channels, ACILEP said the person arrested at San Antonio Park was taken to an unspecified local hospital, while the person detained in Emeryville was taken to Highland Hospital.

ACILEP, the statement reads, “today condemned the violent manner of two ICE arrests this past weekend of Alameda County residents. In both cases, federal agents appear to have used excessive force against the people they detained, leaving them injured and in need of hospital care.”

A spokesperson at the Department of Homeland Security confirmed the Emeryville arrest to The Oaklandside, saying that ICE arrested a man from Honduras during a targeted enforcement operation there. The agency denied that ICE agents used excessive force and said his injuries predated his arrest. And DHS made no comment on the Oakland arrest.

“During the arrest, he attempted to assault officers and refused their lawful commands,” the statement said of the man ICE detained. “Officers relied on their training to control the situation.”

The spokesperson said the man, whom the agency said was undocumented, “was taken to the hospital for evaluation, and he disclosed a preexisting injury from falling from a ladder two days prior. If we have a detainee we need to take to the hospital for medical care, we have officers accompany them for their monitoring, safety of the staff, and the public. This is standard procedure.”

Many of the hundreds of claims by ICE that immigrants have assaulted agents during arrests have later fallen apart. “ICE law enforcement officers are trained to use the minimum amount of force necessary to resolve dangerous situations to prioritize the safety of the public and our officers,” the DHS spokesperson said.

In response to queries about the patient, the Alameda Health System, which operates Highland Hospital, released a statement saying that “protecting patient privacy is a fundamental responsibility.”

The statement said AHS has activated an Incident Command Center to coordinate its response.

“Security personnel are on-site monitoring developments and supporting a safe environment for all. Hospital operations and patient care continue uninterrupted,” the statement said.

“We recognize that these events may cause concern among patients, staff and community members,” said James Jackson, the health system’s chief executive officer. “We want to reassure the community that our priority remains providing care to everyone who needs it while protecting patient privacy, safety and dignity.”

“AHS is following all immigration protocols,” Jackson said.

Protests at Highland Hospital

On Sunday, Oct. 18, ACILEP shared on social media that the person detained in Emeryville remained hospitalized at Highland. That announcement prompted activists to show up at the hospital to alert community members of the agency’s presence in the neighborhood and confront both ICE agents leaving the hospital, and sheriff’s deputies who were present outside of the parking lot.

Roberto Morales, a public information officer with the Alameda County Sheriff’s Office, told The Oaklandside that Highland Hospital is an assigned duty station for the sheriff’s office, which provides security for the hospital.

The Alameda County Sheriff’s Office and the Oakland Police Department are prohibited by city and county laws from cooperating with ICE agents.

According to videos shared on social media, protesters showed up once again on Monday, Oct. 19, as early as 5 a.m. to confront ICE agents as they left the hospital’s parking lot.

“At this time, we have no information suggesting that ICE is conducting enforcement operations at the hospitals or in the surrounding community,” ACILEP said in the statement. “Their reported presence appears to be connected to the individuals in custody.”

Earlier this month, the conservative publication the Washington Examiner broke the news that the Trump Administration would launch “Operation Safe California,” a 45-day operation across the state to arrest immigrants without legal status. Governor Gavin Newsom responded to the reports with a public statement saying, “Trump is using mass deportations to TERRORIZE diverse communities out of legally voting — ordering his secret police to ‘go after everybody.’”

The arrests over the weekend follow a spate of ICE pursuits or detentions of Oakland community members over the past year. On Aug. 12, 2025, six people were arrested at a home in East Oakland. On September 15, 2025, a man was arrested inside Oakland’s Wiley W. Manuel Courthouse. On Nov. 19, 2025, federal agents targeted a man dropping off his grandchild at school in West Oakland. On Dec. 4, 2025, Leandro Oliveira Xavier, a member of SambaFunk!, the renowned Oakland-based cultural organization, was detained at a routine immigration check-in in San Francisco. Then, on July 20 of this year, Chantal Morales Rojas was taken by ICE in the Denver airport before boarding a flight back home to Oakland. She was released a week later.

When asked for more information about the people who were arrested on Friday, ACILEP said in the email statement that both individuals have asked for privacy.

“These incidents are part of a troubling pattern of escalating force in immigration enforcement, putting immigrant families and the broader community at risk,” ACILEP said in the statement. “To protect the privacy and safety of the individuals involved, ACILEP cannot share details about either case. Response efforts are ongoing, and we are continuing to follow up on both.”

text:
The 56-year-old Mexican man who died Saturday while in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody was a lawful permanent resident in the country, the agency said in a statement a day after The Texas Tribune reported about his death.

Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias, 56, was found unconscious in his bed at the Rio Grande Processing Center on Saturday morning. ICE said staff performed chest compressions and called emergency services, but he was declared dead about 20 minutes after being found unresponsive. He had been in immigration detention since June.

ICE on Monday said Andrade-Covarrubias’ cause of death is still unknown, as the autopsy was still pending with the Webb County Medical Examiner. The agency also said he received proper medical care and was seen by medical professionals.

In the statement, ICE said Andrade-Covarrubias was returning to Texas from Mexico at a port of entry in Laredo when immigration officers detained him on June 26. ICE added that he was detained because officers believed he obtained his legal status in the U.S. fraudulently because he failed to disclose a 2004 arrest for theft during the review process.

The agency was also seeking to deport him, saying that he was in removal proceedings before an immigration judge. Andrade-Covarrubias was supposed to appear at an immigration court hearing on Nov. 2, according to online records.

Andrade-Covarrubias’ daughter, Estefani Andrade, told the Tribune that her father did bring up his criminal record during the application process — and that immigration officials approved his green card application.

Andrade-Covarrubias had lived for decades in Dallas, where he raised three children who were all born in the U.S. He painted apartments and townhomes for a living, and his daughter said he was planning to return to Mexico. He traveled to Mexico often because he was building a house there, she added.

Her dad had a heart condition, she said, along with diabetes and high blood pressure. He had medicine with him when he was detained, but she said staff at the center wouldn’t “give him his medications.”

When he said he felt sick and had a cough, she said her family was especially worried because he was hospitalized for COVID-19 in 2021 and the illness took a lasting toll on his health. He sought help from the facility’s medical staff, but he told her that “they would just ignore him.”

She said her dad told her that medical staff at the center brushed off his concerns, even when he told them he was having trouble breathing and felt tightness in his chest.

U.S. Rep. Henry Cuellar, D-Laredo, told the Tribune that he inspected the detention facility on Sunday and asked staff about the facility’s medical procedures, but they could not provide specific details about Andrade-Covarrubias’ case because his death was still under investigation. The Democrat said he has sent ICE written questions to get more information on the case.

“Any death in federal custody is a serious matter, and we need to know what happened,” Cuellar said in a Monday statement.

Andrade-Covarrubias is the seventh person to die while detained by ICE in Texas this year — the first being Geraldo Lunas Campos, whose death was ruled a homicide by the El Paso Medical Examiner’s office in January.

Andrade-Covarrubias is also the second to die in an ICE facility in Laredo this year. Felix Alcorta-Rodriguez, a 63-year-old Mexican who was being held at Webb County Detention Center, died on June 19 after being found unresponsive, according to the agency.

In June, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers at ports of entry were allowed to prevent people with legal permanent residency — commonly known as green card holders — from reentering the U.S. if they had any history of criminal arrests or convictions.

In an opinion written by Justice Clarence Thomas, the Supreme Court ruled in a 6-3 vote that immigration officials at ports of entry don’t need “clear and convincing evidence that a lawful permanent resident has committed a crime involving moral turpitude.” Immigration officers would be allowed to detain the person from reentering the country, but an immigration judge would have the final say on whether that person would be stripped of their green card and ordered deported.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented, writing that the court’s opinion undermines “the benefits and security that come with having a green card.” She also wrote that she is worried the court “handed the Government a massive blank check” to put lawful permanent residents in “immigration limbo.”

text:
A federal judge raked President Donald Trump’s administration over the coals on Monday in a case involving his plans to renovate a public golf course in Washington, DC.

After the administration cut down more than 430 trees without properly notifying US District Judge Ana Reyes, she said last week she was “furious” and issued a court order to stop it.

Then, after Trump on Sunday said construction would begin “immediately” despite the judge’s order, she forced officials to testify on Monday and sought to highlight the apparent unwillingness of Justice Department lawyers to vouch for the administration’s claims in court.

All of this comes as the administration accuses the judge of “egregious” behavior and seeks to remove her from the case.

It’s been quite the scene. But it’s also been a long time coming.

Reyes’ exasperated displays come after a series of similar examples of the administration flouting and even violating court orders.

District judges like Reyes ruled that the administration had violated court orders in at least 31 lawsuits over 15 months, according to an Associated Press investigation in May. That’s in addition to more than 250 other examples of noncompliance that judges have found related to immigration cases.

And the judges finding these violations are often Republican-nominated ones.

Any one of these examples could be understood as a mistake or a mishap. But the growing volume of them — along with Trump and those around him often speaking openly about violating court orders, as Trump did Sunday — suggest there’s something more going on. (A whistleblower last year also claimed that a top DOJ official explicitly spoke about the possible need to ignore court orders.)

At the same time, there’s been no accountability that is seeming to make the administration change its approach. Because this just keeps happening.

Let’s recap some of the high-profile examples of the administration flouting or violating court orders, and what became of them.

The government funding freeze

Mere weeks into Trump’s second term, a federal judge in Rhode Island found the administration had violated a court order by failing to un-freeze many of the federal grants it blocked after he ordered it to do so.

The conclusion: The judge opted not to hold the administration in contempt of court, but he did issue a warning. He quoted from a 1975 Supreme Court ruling that said: “Persons who make private determinations of the law and refuse to obey an order generally risk criminal contempt even if the order is ultimately ruled incorrect.”

The Alien Enemies Act flights

US District Judge James Boasberg ordered the administration to turn around planes that were deporting migrants to a notorious prison in El Salvador under the Alien Enemies Act. But the flights continued.

The conclusion: Boasberg initiated contempt hearings, saying that “probable cause exists to find the Government in criminal contempt.” But after a lengthy process that included plenty of stops and starts, two Trump-nominated judges on a divided appeals court ended the inquiry and called it a “clear abuse of discretion.”

Kilmar Abrego Garcia

US District Judge Paula Xinis found the administration had engaged in “willful and intentional noncompliance” with her orders related to the deportation of Kilmar Abrego Garcia, whom the administration wrongfully deported to El Salvador, later charged criminally and tried to deport again.

The conclusion: Xinis also repeatedly floated possible contempt. But eventually, in June 2025, Abrego Garcia was returned, despite the administration having previously claimed it didn’t have the power to make that happen.

Third-country deportations

Around the same time, US District Judge Brian Murphy of Massachusetts said that the administration’s rapid third-country deportations of migrants despite his injunction were “unquestionably violative of this court’s order.” He also accused the administration of manufacturing chaos and trying to evade court orders.

The conclusion: Murphy said he would leave the contempt question “for another day,” but he didn’t proceed with such an inquiry.

The many immigration orders

Other judges have found hundreds of instances of immigration authorities failing to comply with immigration-related court orders. Patrick Schiltz, the GOP-nominated chief US district judge in Minnesota, said he found more than 200 such instances.

The conclusion: Schiltz at one point took the extraordinary step of summoning Todd Lyons, then the acting director of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and threatening him with contempt. But Schiltz canceled the contempt hearing after ICE complied with an order to release a wrongly detained man from Ecuador.

The media ban

Despite a court order blocking Trump from barring media outlets whose coverage he didn’t like, including CNN, from the White House grounds, those journalists were initially unable to access the grounds. And Trump has since then barred CNN from traveling with him on Air Force One.

The conclusion: The access to the grounds was soon restored as the case proceeds. The access on Air Force One wasn’t explicitly mentioned in the court order, and the White House has continued to block CNN from boarding on its assigned pool days.

The political ads

Despite another federal judge ruling that the administration had to cancel all future airings of Trump’s controversial taxpayer-funded political ads, the administration was again slow to comply. The ads aired hundreds more times, CNN reported last week.

The conclusion: A Justice Department lawyer apologized “to the court and the plaintiffs,” and no further legal action has been taken.

The young deportees

Trump-appointed US District Judge Stephanie Gallagher of Maryland has found that ICE wrongfully deported more than 50 unaccompanied minors who had blanket court orders barring their removal. And in a separate case, she found it twice wrongfully deported an asylum-seeker to El Salvador, in violation of three court orders.

The conclusion: These two examples appear to be the only ones in which a judge has found the administration in contempt. Gallagher held the administration in contempt for the first one in August, according to Law360, and for the second one a few weeks ago.

Despite those two rulings, the administration has flouted or delayed complying with court orders in three other cases — the media ban, the political ads and now the golf course — since then.

title: Mahmoud Khalil Asks Supreme Court to Overturn Ruling That Could Put Him Back in ICE Custody
description:
Khalil, a lawful permanent resident, is challenging a federal appeals court decision that overturned a judge's order releasing him from detention.
The appeals court subsequently stayed its ruling to allow Khalil to seek Supreme Court review, temporarily preserving the orders protecting him from renewed detention.
His Supreme Court petition also cites conflicting appellate rulings over when immigrants can challenge their detention in federal court.
The dispute follows other federal court challenges involving foreign students and scholars targeted over pro-Palestinian advocacy.

text:
Mahmoud Khalil, the former Columbia University graduate student who spent 104 days in immigration detention over his pro-Palestinian activism, asked the U.S. Supreme Court on October 19, 2026, to overturn a ruling that could send him back into ICE custody as the Trump administration pursues his deportation.

Khalil, a lawful permanent resident, is challenging a federal appeals court decision that overturned a judge's order releasing him from detention. His attorneys argue that the ruling could force immigrants to remain imprisoned for months or years before federal judges can review claims that their confinement violates the Constitution.

The petition asks the justices to decide whether federal district courts can hear constitutional challenges to immigration detention through habeas corpus, a legal procedure allowing people to contest unlawful confinement.

Immigration agents arrested Khalil on March 8, 2025, at his Columbia University residence in New York. Authorities transferred him to Louisiana, where he remained detained until U.S. District Judge Michael Farbiarz ordered his release on June 20, 2025, after finding that his continued confinement was likely unconstitutional.

Farbiarz had previously ruled that Khalil was likely to succeed in challenging the administration's use of a foreign policy provision to justify his detention. The government appealed, arguing that federal immigration law required Khalil to pursue his claims through the deportation process.

On January 15, 2026, a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit sided with the administration and overturned the district court's orders. The panel found that the Immigration and Nationality Act required Khalil to pursue judicial review through the immigration system, with federal appellate review available after a final removal order. The decision effectively barred his constitutional detention claims from proceeding before the district judge.

Khalil's attorneys say the ruling could allow immigration authorities to keep people in custody while constitutional challenges move through lengthy deportation proceedings. They argue that federal judges must retain the authority to promptly review claims of detention imposed in retaliation for protected political speech.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio invoked a rarely used immigration provision to seek Khalil's removal, determining that his activities threatened U.S. foreign policy interests. Federal officials accused him of contributing to an antisemitic environment at Columbia during demonstrations against Israel's military campaign in Gaza.

Khalil denies the allegations and maintains that the administration targeted him for political advocacy protected by the First Amendment. His case has become a prominent legal challenge to the administration's use of immigration enforcement against foreign students and activists involved in pro-Palestinian demonstrations.

Khalil suffered another setback on May 22, 2026, when the Third Circuit rejected his request for a full-court rehearing in a 6-5 vote. Five judges supported reconsidering the decision, with Judge Cheryl Ann Krause warning in a dissent joined by Judges Luis Felipe Restrepo and Arianna Freeman that the ruling improperly restricted federal courts' authority to protect constitutional rights.

The appeals court subsequently stayed its ruling to allow Khalil to seek Supreme Court review, temporarily preserving the orders protecting him from renewed detention.

His Supreme Court petition also cites conflicting appellate rulings over when immigrants can challenge their detention in federal court. Khalil's lawyers argue that the disagreement requires the justices to clarify whether immigration authorities can keep people confined while their constitutional claims await review through the removal process.

The dispute follows other federal court challenges involving foreign students and scholars targeted over pro-Palestinian advocacy. In a separate case, a federal judge ruled against efforts to deport international students because of political expression protected by the First Amendment.

Khalil is also fighting a separate deportation order. An immigration judge ordered his removal, and the Board of Immigration Appeals upheld that decision. He is contesting the order before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit while asking the Supreme Court to restore the district court's authority to review his detention claims.
