text:
A San Francisco civil rights group and a national immigration nonprofit are suing the federal government to obtain records related to “mega master” hearings, where upward of 100 immigration cases may be slated for a single hearing.

The suit, filed on Oct. 15, compels the federal government to release records explaining why the government is now scheduling these kinds of mass hearings where dozens of cases are being heard at a time.

“Mega master” hearings have proliferated at the Concord immigration court since June, as reported by Mission Local. They present serious due process issues, immigration attorneys say, because immigrants often learn of their hearings just weeks in advance, if at all.

In many cases, immigrants who had hearings scheduled years in the future have them abruptly pushed forward without what attorneys argue is the time to prepare. According to the lawsuit, the Executive Office for Immigration Review, the Justice Department agency that runs immigration courts, recommended in its own standards back in 2017 that no more than 25 people be included in a group hearing.

If an immigrant fails to appear, they can be ordered removed in absentia, which means they are subject to deportation. Hundreds have been ordered deported in this way, Mission Local has reported. Failure to appear in court also ends an immigrant’s ability to seek legal status in this country.

The attorneys behind the case argue that immigrants do not always receive the translation services they need at these mega hearings, nor do they receive individual review from immigration judges during what are crowded procedures.

“We want to make sure laws are being applied in a fair way such that people have notice and can actually defend themselves,” said Jacob Gonzalez, an attorney with Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights of the San Francisco Bay Area, which filed the suit alongside attorneys from the National Immigration Project.

Gonzalez said he has heard examples from around the country of immigrants who attended these mega hearings and were ordered deported because they did not hear the judge call their name due to a language barrier.

The lawsuit is over information related to the hearings. It argues that the federal government has not released records within deadlines set by the Freedom of Information Act after the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights submitted a records request on July 15.

The group requested records like policies, communications, scheduling data, affected immigration courts, and data on in-absentia removal orders issued during these mass hearings, according to the lawsuit.

So far, the federal government has not released a single record, attorneys say.

The Office for Immigration Review did not respond to Mission Local’s questions about why it began holding master calendar hearings and why it has not responded to the records requests. Instead, it said it “declines to comment on litigation-related matters.”

The Bay Area’s immigration court in Concord, where San Francisco immigrants have had to attend court since the fall, continues to hold these “mega” master calendar hearings. There were 17 such hearings in September, according to the latest data collected by Concord court observer and data analyst Jere Ramsey.

In Concord, between June and September, there have been an average of 80 immigrants scheduled for mega master hearings, according to Ramsey’s data.

The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, asks a federal judge to order the Executive Office for Immigration Review to release the records.

The plaintiffs hope to receive a response by early next year, according to Gonzalez.

Ultimately, he said, they would like the mega master calendar hearings to stop. But first, they need to receive initial records from the federal government to understand the facts of what is going on and why.

“The immigration system needs to be fundamentally fair,” said Gonzalez, “regardless of your stance on immigration.”

Appearing on Fox News over the weekend, border czar Tom Homan gave the starkest indication yet that the administration is moving forward with plans to “denaturalize” Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minnesota), stripping her of U.S. citizenship status that she’s had since she was 17 years old.

Last week, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) raided Omar’s residence in Washington D.C., seizing her phone, notebooks, personal computers, and passport. Members of her family have also received subpoenas relating to the investigation. So far, the details of the inquiry have not officially been made public, but sources with knowledge of it say it stems from paperwork Omar’s father submitted when she applied to become a citizen in 2000, at age 17.

Homan appeared to confirm that is the investigation’s focus.

“If you lie during the naturalization process, there is a process to denaturalize somebody. We’ve done it before … And certainly, if the evidence points that way, that could happen” to Omar, he said on the program.

The border czar left some rhetorical wiggle room, but reiterated that the administration was looking into fraudulent behavior by the Minnesota lawmaker or her family members.

“I’m not going to get ahead of the bureau or HSI, but I’ve been told they have a strong case, and we’ll let the evidence lead where it leads,” Homan said.

A person can be denaturalized, or have their citizenship status revoked, only in extreme circumstances — generally, when evidence of fraud is discovered later on. Several conservative conspiracy theorists have alleged that Omar’s father lied about her age when she applied for citizenship, pointing to evidence that she once changed her birth year from 1981 to 1982 in official records, which would have made her 18 when her application was submitted.

But that change was made to correct another error, Omar maintains, and fact-checking websites have demonstrated there is no evidence that the change was for malicious reasons. For denaturalization to occur, there must be evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that fraud actually happened.

Notably, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) examined accusations of fraud relating to Omar’s citizenship several years ago, and found no evidence to justify moving forward on the matter. But President Donald Trump has targeted Omar for over a decade, including demanding that she and other lawmakers of color “go back” to their own countries after they criticized him in 2019. All four of those members of Congress, collectively known as “the Squad,” are U.S. citizens.

Trump reiterated that demand for Omar during a Newsmax interview this past week.

“I think she hates our country. She is a person that truly hates our country. … I’ve said it many times before, she ought to go back to her own country,” Trump said.

Responding to the raid on her home, Omar blasted the administration, decrying the action as “an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”

“For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” Omar said, adding: “I will not be silenced.”

Several critics described the raid as outright fascism. But some Democratic lawmakers, including party leaders, have been more muted in their response, including Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-New York), who appears not to have said anything publicly on the matter at all.

text:
LEXINGTON, S.C. (WIS) - Democratic nominee Zyon Khalifa and Republican incumbent U.S. Rep. Joe Wilson offered sharply different views on affordability, immigration, health care, education and American military involvement abroad Monday in a student-led debate at River Bluff High School.

The hourlong forum, hosted by the school’s student government and its Center for Law and Global Policy Development, put high school students at the microphones to question the candidates seeking to represent South Carolina’s 2nd Congressional District.

Khalifa, an Aiken native, Air Force veteran and attorney, framed his campaign as a call for change, arguing families are struggling with the cost of food, gas, housing and health care.

“It’s time for us to be able to afford our gas. It’s time for us to be able to afford our groceries,” Khalifa said in his opening statement. “It’s time for the next generation to be able to purchase their first home.”

Wilson, who has held the congressional seat since 2001, highlighted his work on national security, infrastructure and bipartisan initiatives. He told students he was grateful for the opportunity to represent the district and said the country benefits from what he called “peace through strength.”

The candidates sometimes found common ground, including on the need for border security and on encouraging students to participate in civic life. But the debate also included pointed exchanges over the role of government, the conduct of past and current administrations, congressional oversight and federal spending.

Immigration and border security

Student Renee Fox opened the policy portion of the debate by asking how the candidates would balance immigration enforcement with due process and human-rights concerns.

Khalifa said he supports adding immigration judges and argued that people in the United States deserve due process before officials determine their immigration status. He said the country should enforce its laws while recognizing its history as a nation of immigrants.

“We are a land of laws,” Khalifa said. “But we are also a land of immigrants.”

Wilson said existing immigration laws should be enforced. He said people who enter the country illegally and commit crimes should be removed, while describing his past legal work representing people seeking to immigrate legally to the United States.

On a later question about fentanyl, both candidates said the border should be secure.

Khalifa said the government should know who enters the country and should not allow criminals in. He distinguished between enforcement and the treatment of immigrants who are not criminals.

Wilson said federal officials should work to stop drug trafficking and human trafficking at the border. He also pointed to treatment and law-enforcement efforts to address fentanyl addiction.

Khalifa called addiction an illness and said resources should be focused on treatment while people dealing drugs face punishment.

Health care, affordability and education

The candidates also offered different diagnoses for rising household costs.

Asked about health care access, Khalifa called health care a necessity for all Americans and said South Carolina’s decision not to expand Medicaid had made access more difficult in rural communities. He called for more competition in health care and stronger oversight of insurance companies.

Wilson praised the health care systems and community health centers in the district. He said no one should “fall through the cracks,” while adding that Medicaid fraud must be addressed.

A River Bluff student later asked about inflation and structural costs for working families.

Khalifa blamed federal policy decisions for high prices and called for legislation that gives people “a hand up, not a handout.” He said the government should help people manage the effects of rising costs for housing, health care, gasoline and groceries.

Wilson attributed inflation to federal overspending and energy policy. He said he supports an “all-of-the-above” energy approach, reduced government spending and a balanced-budget amendment.

On the cost of college, Wilson said he would work with universities to hold down tuition and encourage vocational and career training. He also cited tuition tax credits and programs that allow families to set aside money for a child’s education.

Khalifa criticized cuts to student-loan programs and said he would push to restore Pell Grant funding and revisit financial-aid rules that rely on a parent’s income. He said students should not be steered away from college if that is their chosen path.

Foreign policy and congressional oversight

Foreign policy prompted some of the day’s strongest disagreements.

Students asked about congressional oversight of military operations and the cost of U.S. involvement in Iran.

Wilson, a member of the House Armed Services and Foreign Affairs committees, said congressional hearings and committee work provide checks and balances. He defended President Donald Trump’s actions toward Iran, arguing they were necessary to protect Americans from a potential nuclear threat.

Khalifa said Congress needs to reassert its oversight role and argued that the country should not spend money on a war he said Americans did not want. He said federal dollars could instead be used to help families facing high costs at home.

Several assertions made during the exchange — including claims related to intelligence assessments, military operations, spending and foreign threats — were not independently verified during the debate.

Infrastructure and political division

On infrastructure, Khalifa argued that both federal and state governments have a responsibility to maintain roads and bridges because taxpayers contribute through federal and state gas taxes. He criticized Wilson’s voting record on a 2021 infrastructure measure and said a representative should fight to bring federal dollars back to the district.

Wilson said infrastructure is primarily a state responsibility but that the federal government can help. He pointed to work on airport runways, Interstate 20 and Interstate 26 improvements, and the Advanced Manufacturing Collaborative at the University of South Carolina Aiken.

The candidates also differed on what is driving political polarization.

Wilson cited his bipartisan work with members of both parties, including on transportation and health care issues. Khalifa said elected officials should regularly hold town halls and listen to constituents across party lines. He criticized Wilson’s past conduct and said divisive rhetoric has contributed to the nation’s political climate.

In his closing statement, Khalifa said South Carolinians share goals such as good schools, jobs, roads and affordable gas, and called for less division. Wilson said he supports bipartisanship, limited government, expanded freedom and national security.

Students say debate gave future voters a voice

For the students who developed and asked the questions, the forum was an opportunity to participate in the democratic process before many of them are eligible to vote.

Fox said she was excited both candidates agreed to appear and answer student questions.

“It’s very great to know that they’re interested in speaking not only to their constituents, but to students,” Fox said. “It was an amazing opportunity for our students to speak to future legislators about what they’re most passionate about and get involved in the process.”

Student questioner Brett Winchester said the event mattered regardless of which candidate students supported.

“That definitely shows some character from both of the candidates, that they were willing to come out here on their random Monday morning and speak to a bunch of high school students,” Winchester said. “We’re not just including current voters, but we’re also including future voters as well.”

Both candidates praised the students after the debate.

Khalifa said young people need to be engaged now so they can understand the political process later. Wilson, who said he began his own civic involvement as a teenager, called the event a “remarkable opportunity” and encouraged students to stay involved.

Early voting began Monday. Election Day is Nov. 3.

Dayna Alane Smith, representing the Workers Party, is also on the November ballot.

LONG BEACH, Calif. (KABC) -- Video showing federal immigration agents taking a man to the ground during an arrest in Long Beach has drawn scrutiny from local leaders and advocacy groups, with one congressman now demanding an investigation.

According to witnesses, Ricardo Gonzalez, a former Long Beach city worker, was riding a bicycle Saturday when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents pursued him in SUVs and took him to the ground in a neighborhood.

Neither ICE nor the Department of Homeland Security has publicly said why Gonzalez was arrested. Advocates say the man seen being detained is a U.S. citizen. Eyewitness News has not confirmed his citizenship status.

During the arrest, Gonzalez could be heard yelling that his arm was broken.

The advocacy group StopICE.net reported that agents had positioned their vehicles in the middle of a Long Beach neighborhood and issued an alert. More than a dozen activists subsequently arrived at the scene and confronted the agents.

U.S. Rep. Robert Garcia, whose district includes Long Beach, held a news conference Monday and called for an investigation into the arrest. Garcia also said that ICE agents involved in illegal behavior would face accountability if Democrats regain control of the congressional oversight committee.

"ICE and DHS are completely out of control," Garcia said. "They are terrorizing communities."

Meanwhile, U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli criticized Garcia for supporting groups that confronted ICE agents during the incident. In a post online, Essayli wrote:

"These incidents would be less common if the targets complied with lawful commands. You're intentionally fanning the flames and increasing danger for the community and officers."

Gonzalez was later released and treated at a local hospital. His family said he is not speaking to the media.

text:
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said Monday that her government would file a complaint with US authorities over the death of a Mexican national in Texas immigration detention while condemning racism against Mexican migrants and pledging support for Mexicans living in the United States.

“We are also going to file a complaint in the United States because there must be protection for human rights,” Sheinbaum said during her morning press conference.

Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias, 56, died in US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody at the Rio Grande Processing Center in Laredo, Texas.

Andrade-Covarrubias, who reportedly suffered from a heart condition, diabetes and high blood pressure, was found unconscious in his cell and later pronounced dead. For months, he had complained to his daughter about the lack of medical care at the facility.

Mexico's Foreign Ministry has demanded a prompt, thorough and transparent investigation to establish the circumstances of his death and determine whether any authorities bear responsibility.

The ministry said the Mexican Consulate General in Laredo activated its protection protocol after being notified of the death, contacted the family and provided consular assistance.

The Mexican government will submit a complaint to the prosecutor in Webb County, where Laredo is located, while Mexico's embassy will also seek guarantees of consular access to immigration detention facilities.

Sheinbaum said her administration would strengthen consular efforts to protect the rights of Mexican nationals detained abroad.

She also reiterated her rejection of all forms of racism against Mexican migrants and pledged continued support for the Mexican community in the United States.

“Mexico's government and its president will always be their ally,” she said.

The death brings to 18 the number of Mexican nationals who have died in ICE custody or during immigration enforcement operations since US President Donald Trump returned to office on Jan. 20, 2025, according to Mexican media reports.

The cause of Andrade's death has not been officially established. Mexican authorities have called for transparency and accountability as investigations proceed.

text:
U.S. Representative Salud Carbajal (D-CA-24), Top Democrat of the House Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation, sent a letter to Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin raising concerns over the department's administration and oversight of Jones Act waivers.

Carbajal’s inquiry follows recent reports indicating that foreign-flagged vessels have transported more than $40 million in petroleum products between U.S. ports without required disclosures, raising critical questions about whether federal tax, labor, and immigration laws are being properly enforced on foreign operators.

“I am writing to express concern regarding the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) administration and oversight of Jones Act waivers, particularly in light of recent reporting that foreign-flagged vessels have transported more than $40 million in petroleum products between U.S. ports without required disclosures, among other potential violations,” wrote Rep. Carbajal. “These reports raise significant questions about whether DHS and its component agencies are adequately enforcing federal law with respect to foreign vessels operating in U.S. domestic commerce.”

The full letter is available HERE and below.

Dear Secretary Mullin:

I am writing to express concern regarding the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) administration and oversight of Jones Act waivers, particularly in light of recent reporting that foreign-flagged vessels have transported more than $40 million in petroleum products between U.S. ports without required disclosures, among other potential violations. These reports raise significant questions about whether DHS and its component agencies are adequately enforcing federal law with respect to foreign vessels operating in U.S. domestic commerce.

As you know, the Jones Act generally prohibits the transportation of merchandise between U.S. points unless a vessel is U.S.-owned, U.S.-documented, and U.S.-built. Recent waivers have been issued under 46 U.S.C. § 501(a), which permits the waiver of certain navigation and vessel-inspection laws only when necessary in the interest of national defense to address an immediate adverse effect on military operations. The statute does not, however, provide an exemption from any other federal requirements applicable to foreign vessels, vessel owners, operators, employers, or crewmembers.

Publicly available information indicates that more than 25 domestic voyages by foreign-flagged vessels have been completed under the current waiver, with some vessels conducting multiple voyages. Given the scale and duration of this activity, there must be a clear framework for ensuring continued compliance with federal law.

Recent IRS guidance further establishes that income earned by foreign corporations from operating vessels between U.S. ports under a Jones Act waiver constitutes domestic-source income and is not eligible for the international shipping exclusion under Section 883 of the Internal Revenue Code or related treaty benefits. This raises additional questions about DHS’s role in facilitating and enforcing compliance with federal tax requirements.

Accordingly, I respectfully request the following information:

Tax compliance. What steps has DHS taken, independently or in coordination with the Department of the Treasury and IRS, to ensure compliance with applicable federal tax requirements by foreign vessel owners, operators, charterers, and other waiver users? Has DHS provided Treasury or IRS with information identifying waiver users, vessel owners and operators, charterers, cargo interests, voyage dates, cargo movements, or other information necessary to identify potential tax obligations? Please describe the information provided, the frequency of transmission, and any related interagency agreements or procedures.

Immigration and crewmember status. Federal regulations generally provide that nonimmigrant crewmen admitted in D status may not be employed in connection with domestic movements of a vessel. How is DHS/CBP interpreting and applying this restriction to foreign officers and crewmembers serving aboard vessels engaged in domestic transportation under the waiver? What immigration classifications or other legal authorities permit such service? Has DHS/CBP identified instances in which a crewmember’s immigration status was inconsistent with domestic service, or in which a crewmember absconded? If so, what corrective or enforcement actions were taken? Please provide any guidance, memoranda, legal opinions, or internal directives addressing these issues.

Other federal requirements. Please describe the steps DHS and its component agencies have taken to ensure compliance with other applicable federal requirements, including maritime security, environmental protection, vessel safety and inspection, wage and hour, labor and employment, payroll and withholding taxes, harbor maintenance, customs, and any other requirements applicable to foreign vessels operating between U.S. points.

Interagency coordination and oversight. Please provide a description of all coordination between DHS and the Departments of Defense, Transportation, and Treasury; the IRS; U.S. Coast Guard; and other relevant agencies concerning operations under the waiver, including coordination regarding compliance with federal law and whether the statutory requirements for continued waiver authority remain satisfied.

The Administration has now authorized the waiver for an aggregate period of approximately 250 days, making oversight particularly important. Congress has a responsibility to ensure that a national-defense waiver is not being treated as a broader exemption from federal law. I therefore request a response addressing the matters above by October 31, 2026.

Background

Carbajal serves as Ranking Member of the House Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation Subcommittee.

text:
Ukrainian and Sudanese immigrants in the United States with Temporary Protected Status (TPS) will keep their protections for at least another six months, after the Trump administration left decisions on both countries' designations unresolved Monday.

The development comes a couple weeks before the midterm elections and follows bipartisan concerns, including from Republican Senators Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Susan Collins of Maine, about the fate of Ukrainians who fled Russia's 2022 invasion and have been living legally in the U.S. since.

The Trump administration has largely sought to end TPS for various countries as their statuses came to an end over the past 21 months, with hundreds of thousands of people losing work permits and protections from deportation, despite concerns of ongoing conflicts and unstable conditions in their home countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, and Afghanistan.

Read More on Politics

Both Ukraine and Sudan's TPS designations were set to expire Monday, with no official announcement on an extension or termination from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), meaning a by-default six-month extension.

A spokesperson for the department told Newsweek Monday that decisions for both countries would be made "at the appropriate time," and until that happens, TPS holders from both countries can remain in the U.S. under TPS protections.

While protections can continue for now, some advocates have warned that the lack of a clear decision beyond the next few months leaves thousands of people in limbo.

"If the Trump administration doesn't want to end TPS for Ukraine and Sudan, it could have done so by following the law and announcing an extension for as few as 6 months," Dara Lind, senior fellow at the American Immigration Council, told Newsweek Monday. "By choosing not to follow the law, it's throwing immigrants and employers into a state of day-to-day existential uncertainty. It's long past time for Congress to step in and allow TPS holders who've been complying with the law for years to apply for permanent status."

Immigration Policy and the Midterms

The move comes as immigration remains one of the most closely watched issues heading into next month's midterms.

A Pew Research Center survey in May found 52 percent of Americans said the Trump administration was doing too much to deport immigrants living in the country illegally, while 31 percent said it was doing the right amount. In June, Gallup found 73 percent of Americans viewed immigration as a good thing for the country, although this was down on 79 percent a year earlier.

In an ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos survey, conducted October 9-13, the GOP's former advantage over Democrats on the issue had vanished, with the latter taking a 2-point lead when it came to voter trust on the matter—37 percent to 35 percent.

Concerns grew about the administration's handling of a core issue that saw President Donald Trump return to office when protests spread across the U.S. following the fatal shootings of two American citizens during protests against sweeping immigration enforcement in Minneapolis in January.

Trump has seen pushback within his own party in recent months when it comes to immigration, including from Collins following a fatal shooting in Maine, and Florida Representative Maria Salazar, who posted a video filmed outside the White House in which she said some of the president's policies had gone too far.

What Are Conditions Like in Ukraine, Sudan?

When terminating TPS for other countries, DHS has cited improved conditions in countries which originally obtained TPS because of the outbreak of war, an environmental disaster, or political instability, among other reasons.

Despite situations remaining volatile in Haiti, Venezuela, Afghanistan, Somalia, Syria, and other nations which still saw high-risk travel warnings from the Department of State, DHS opted to end the protections.

In some cases, this led to legal challenges that made their way to the Supreme Court, which ultimately sided with the Trump administration.

For Ukraine and Sudan, as El Salvador, which also saw its status lapse into a six-month extension in September, the same framing was not used to seek to end TPS.

Ukraine is still at war with Russia, and the U.S. is still actively involved in negotiations to seek to end the conflict. Millions of Ukrainians were displaced following the outbreak of the war, with around 101,000 heading to the U.S. and benefiting from TPS.

In their September letter, Murkowski and Collins said human rights abuses and widespread destruction of TPS holders' home communities was still apparent, writing, "sending Ukrainians back now would risk returning them to life threatening conditions."

Sudan is still in the midst of a humanitarian crisis and a civil war which has been underway since April 2023. The conflict has displaced millions of people, devastated infrastructure, and triggered what the United Nations described as one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. Around 1,700 Sudanese are estimated to be in the U.S. with TPS.

"The appropriate time to act was weeks ago. Families who depend on this status to stay safe and keep working deserve a formal decision in writing, not a weekend statement to press," Krish O'Mara Vignarajah, president and CEO of Global Refuge, said in a press release Monday. "Keeping protections in place is the right call, but a promise to a reporter is not a policy."

What Happens Next

Both countries should keep hold of their TPS designations for another six months, with DHS required to make a decision at least 60 days before the default expiration date in April.

text:
A new court decision stretches Monell to the point of absurdity, holding that the county’s top official does not set official county policy. Boone County, Illinois’s Coroner Wesley Hyland committed a constitutional violation of an uncommonly disturbing sort. He “kept several skulls as trophies from the deceased he examined,” according to the Seventh Circuit. One of them belonged to a high school student who was kidnapped, raped, and murdered. Forty-five years later, her brothers learned that Hyland had held onto her skull. They recovered it, exhumed her other remains, and reburied them together. Then, they sued Boone County.

They lost. The Seventh Circuit noted that a plaintiff can satisfy Monell by showing that a constitutional violation was “an act by a person with final policymaking authority.” Yet, the court determined, Hyland’s actions were illegal under state law, requiring that remains be released to the deceased’s next of kin. So in spite of his role as coroner, he “frustrated” official policy rather than deciding it. That means Boone County bears no responsibility for his acts—even though Hyland was Boone County’s decisionmaker concerning the treatment of remains.

If the girl’s family lived in the Third, Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, Tenth, or Eleventh Circuits, they would be able to recover from their local government under Section 1983. But because they live in the Seventh Circuit, they cannot.

Cato, assisted by the University of Virginia School of Law Supreme Court Litigation Clinic and joined by the Due Process Institute, Public Accountability, and the Rutherford Institute, filed an amicus brief asking the Supreme Court to reverse the Seventh Circuit’s decision. The ability to pursue compensation—under federal statute—for violations of federal constitutional rights should not vary by state.

text:
MANHATTAN (CN) — A group of immigrant youth pressed a Second Circuit panel Monday to restore deportation safeguards they say were unlawfully scrapped by the Trump administration.

The plaintiffs are Special Immigrant Juveniles (SIJ), a classification for migrants under age 21 who have been abused, neglected or abandoned by their parents. In the past, this immigration status would allow beneficiaries to live and work in the United States without the imminent threat of removal.

But the Trump administration quietly reversed course in 2025 by no longer treating SIJ eligibility as a “strong factor” to grant these protections. A lower court agreed with the plaintiffs that this was unlawful, but only ordered a return to the status quo for those granted SIJ status in a fixed time period — between April and June 2025.

Catherine Weiss, a public interest lawyer for Lowenstein Sandler representing the plaintiffs, told the panel Monday that this unfairly endangers thousands around the country.

“The district court was wrong to jettison the strong factors standard for tens of thousands of young people who were abused, neglected, or abandoned by their parents,” she told the court.

The contested lower court ruling comes from U.S. District Judge Eric Komittee, a Donald Trump appointee in the Eastern District of New York. In briefing, the plaintiffs contend Komittee’s narrow relief does not truly restore the status quo and can’t work.

“People applying for SIJ had a reason to anticipate that they would not be subject to removal,” Weiss said. “And so they did things like start school, begin degree programs, pay for higher education because they were able to lawfully work.”

The government contends the appeal should be moot amid new 2026 guidance on the issue. Department of Justice lawyer William Silvis told the court it is speculative to assume the plaintiffs need any further relief — a statement that prompted some pushback from the panel.

“But what you’re calling speculative, they’re calling uncertain and transitory,” said U.S. Circuit Judge Myrna Pérez, adding statistics show it is indeed more difficult to get these protections after the administration’s changes.

Pérez, a Joe Biden appointee, remained skeptical of Komittee’s ruling throughout Monday’s hearing, at one point scrutinizing the narrow time frame for which he granted the relief.

“How can that be?” she asked. “The status quo was either the status quo or it wasn’t.”

U.S. Circuit Judges Raymond Lohier, a Barack Obama appointee and Barrington Parker, a George W. Bush appointee, rounded out the panel, which did not indicate when or how it will rule.

Congress created the SIJ designation in 1990 under the Immigration and Nationality Act to offer immigrant minors abused or neglected by a parent a path to permanent residency. The plaintiffs in this case filed suit last summer after the Trump administration formally ended protections against deportation for these youths.

One of the named plaintiffs, identified only as A.C.R., said the policy shift endangered her dreams of becoming an astronaut.

“Without the protection of deferred action, I won’t be able to attend school and pursue my dreams, and I’ll live in constant fear of deportation,” she said in a statement accompanying the suit. “I felt that I was finally in a safe environment, but if I had to return to [Guatemala], I would be very afraid of the violence and abuse from my mother and father.”

text:
Sacramento, CA — Senator Eloise Gómez Reyes today issued the following statement in response to Attorney General Rob Bonta’s lawsuit challenging ICE’s civil immigration arrests in and around California courthouses. The complaint cites Senate Bill 873, authored by Senator Gómez Reyes, which strengthens protections against civil arrests for people traveling to, attending, or returning from court, including within 1,000 feet of a courthouse.

Senator Eloise Gómez Reyes said:

“No one should have to choose between seeking justice and risking separation from their family. When a survivor is afraid to seek protection, a witness is afraid to testify, or a parent is afraid to attend a hearing, our entire community pays the price.

“I authored SB 873 to strengthen protections against civil arrests for people traveling to, attending, or returning from court. I welcome Attorney General Bonta’s lawsuit challenging the Trump Administration’s courthouse immigration arrests and defending California’s ability to administer justice.

“The enforcement quotas and sweeping arrest directives described in the complaint show a disturbing disregard for the people behind those numbers—and for the harm these tactics cause families and communities.

“To our immigrant neighbors and the organizations standing beside them: you deserve safety, dignity, and access to justice. We will continue using every lawful tool available to protect those rights.”

Javier Hernandez, Executive Director for the Inland Coalition for Immigrant Justice (IC4IJ), a sponsor of SB 873 serving Inland Empire communities, also welcomed the lawsuit:

“Every day, we witness the fear and harm ICE’s enforcement activities inflict on immigrant communities across our region and throughout California. No one should have to choose between showing up to court to seek justice, testify as a victim or witness, or support a loved one and risking detention.

“Courthouses must remain places where people can access justice without fear. This lawsuit is an important step toward accountability and challenging the unchecked power ICE has exercised in our communities. Our justice system cannot function when the very people it is meant to protect are too afraid to walk through its doors.

“We will continue fighting to ensure that immigrant communities can access the courts, exercise their rights, and live with dignity and without fear.”

text:
The son of a man who died while in ICE custody earlier this year at Miami Correctional Facility has filed a lawsuit against Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Department of Homeland Security.

Court documents state Lorth Sim, a 59-year-old immigrant from Cambodia, died in February while being held in ICE custody. Sim's son said his father did not receive proper medical care while at Miami Correctional and was not given medication to treat Type II Diabetes, which contributed to Sim's death.

His son, Viccheat Sim, further claimed that ICE and DHS violated the Freedom of Information Act by broadly withholding documents, including medical records, he requested that are related to his father's death.

A press release given by Immigration and Customs Enforcement earlier this year stated Sim said was found unresponsive in his cell on February 16. Despite lifesaving efforts by facility staff and EMS, Sim was officially pronounced dead that morning.

The ICE press release further stated Lorth Sim first entered the United States legally in 1983 and became a lawful permanent resident in 1986. Sim was arrested for multiple crimes over the next decade, however, including disorderly conduct in 1989, indecent exposure in 1996 and larceny in 2005. Sim surrendered himself into ICE custody in Boston on December 30, 2025 after receiving a notice of revocation of release.

He was transferred from ICE Boston custody to ICE Chicago custody on Jan. 5, 2026. From there, he was directly transported from the ICE facility to the Miami Correctional Facility in Bunker Hill.

According to court documents, Sim informed medical staff at the facility of his diabetes diagnosis and the medication he had received for treatment. Court documents note that Sim did not receive any medication to treat his diabetes while in ICE custody.

A forensic pathologist who conducted the postmortem examination found that Sim's glucose levels had been elevated in the hours before his death and reported his cause of death as "atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease with other significant conditions of diabetes mellitus."

The lawsuit was first launched in August in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. The federal judge gave the defendants until Oct. 22 to respond to the complaint.

Protesters interrupt Trump at start of Kansas rally

Trump was interrupted at least two times less than five minutes into rally remarks tonight in Park City, Kansas.

Some protesters were removed from the venue. Trump called them “paid protesters.”

Sen. Roger Marshall focuses more on Democratic opponent than Kansas in rally remarks

Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., used his speaking slot at tonight's campaign rally in Park City to talk more about his opponent and events overseas than his home state of Kansas.

Marshall, who is in an unexpectedly tight race for re-election, talked about “radical Islam” and the rioting in France while claiming his opponent, Adam Hamilton, and Democrats would open the border, weaken the military and charge higher taxes.

Marshall said Republicans will “give you secure borders, a strong military and lower taxes,” but he did not talk about what he would do for Kansas if he is re-elected.

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report has shifted the race toward Democrat and characterized it as a “toss-up.” NBC News characterizes it as competitive but leaning toward the GOP.

Hamilton has picked up several endorsements from past GOP and Democratic governors.

Trump again suggests renaming New Mexico as ‘New America’

Trump has once again suggested giving New Mexico a new moniker.

He urged the state on Truth Social this afternoon to “immediately change its name to New America.”

Trump said the name change would "add great value and prestige" to New Mexico, adding without evidence that home values and people's incomes would increase as a result.

“Maybe even the Crooked Elections, that New Mexico is known for, would become honest again!” he wrote.

New Mexico Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver responded to Trump's suggestion of voter fraud, calling it "tired and patently false."

"He must stop insulting the intelligence of this state's voters. New Mexicans know that we have repeatedly received high national rankings for administering some of the most secure and accessible elections in the country," Toulouse Oliver wrote in a statement on X.

This isn’t the first time Trump has called for renaming New Mexico.

Trump wrote on Truth Social last month that many people have suggested the name change, saying “New America” would be “much more prestigious and beautiful for the people of that potentially incredible State.” In another September Truth Social post, he posted an image of a map of the state with “New Mexico” crossed out with a red X and the words “New America” written below.

Trump signed an executive order in January 2025 to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America” and another executive order in August to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America” during the trade war with Canada.

The “Gulf of America” and “Lake America” name changes apply to the U.S. government and its agencies; American businesses and other countries aren’t required to follow the executive orders.

Indiana Democrat who went viral for candidate interview says she had 3 beers before forum

An Indiana Democrat running for local office who went viral last week for a televised rant during a candidate forum in which she called for “firing all Republicans” and reminded voters that “we have guns, too,” said in an interview today that she may have had a drink or two or three before the event.

“I had three beers, OK?” Jaime West, who is running for the Fayette County Council, said in an interview with Piers Morgan when she was asked exactly how many drinks she had had after she admitting drinking a Coors Light before the Oct. 9 forum.

“I was nervous,” West, who appeared to slur her words during the forum, told Morgan today.

West added that she was “not that intoxicated” during the interview, and “I do know what I’m talking about.”

She raised eyebrows this month after she was asked at the forum for an unpopular policy position she held.

“Firing all Republicans. I wouldn’t let them, I mean, I don’t even talk to them. I don’t like them. There, there are good Republicans out there, but then there’s these MAGAs who are just racist and aren’t very intelligent at all,” West said in response.

Asked for “a few last words to the voters,” West said, “We have guns, too.”

West said today she would not take her inflammatory remarks about Republicans back.

“No, I say it all the time. I’m not friends with them. I don’t like them,” West said, blasting the Trump administration for the Iran war and what she called a “constitutional crisis.”

“I have every right to be angry, and so does every American,” she said.

West, who said she owns a cleaning service, is running to represent the 4th District on the Fayette County Council, the local government for the largely rural Indiana district. The Indianapolis Star reported that it was unclear whether she had sought public office before.

First to NBC News: Sen. Elissa Slotkin to campaign with Democrats in South Carolina, the first 2028 primary state

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., will campaign for Democratic candidates Wednesday in South Carolina, her team confirmed with details shared first with NBC News.

The trip is sure to intensify speculation about Slotkin’s White House ambitions. Though red South Carolina isn’t traditionally home to swing races, the state is scheduled to hold the first Democratic presidential primary in 2028.

On Wednesday, Slotkin will join Nancy Lacore, who is running for the open seat in the state’s 1st Congressional District, as well as three downballot hopefuls: state House contender Sonja Ogletree Satani, lieutenant governor candidate Sam Skardon and DeShawn Blanding, who is running for state agriculture commissioner.

From there, Slotkin will head to Georgia, where she is scheduled to campaign with Sen. Jon Ossoff in Savannah on Thursday. Ossoff, who is locked in a re-election bid against Republican Rep. Mike Collins, is also seen as a 2028 presidential prospect. Slotkin will participate in other events with the Georgia Democratic Party and thank volunteers at Democratic field offices.

Slotkin, who was elected to a six-year term in 2024, has been traveling the country for months to drum up support for Democrats and lay the groundwork for a possible 2028 campaign.

“I’m literally not arrogant enough to think that I’m the only person who can do this,” Slotkin told NBC News in April during a trip to Iowa. “If there was someone who I really felt had what it takes to win, I’d get behind that person. I’m a new senator. I’m new to this level of elected office. But if we get through the midterms and I don’t see it emerging from other leaders as they start to announce and people decide and don’t decide, you know, I wouldn’t rule it out.”

Texas Democratic candidate for governor sues to review emails between Elon Musk and Greg Abbott

Texas state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic nominee for governor, announced a lawsuit today against Gov. Greg Abbott over emails between his office and Republican ally Elon Musk.

Hinojosa — who is challenging Abbott in a tight contest — said at a news conference that she filed the suit to obtain redacted documents that “Abbott refused to release,” claiming they were being withheld because they are “intimate and embarrassing.”

A spokesperson for Abbott called the lawsuit “baseless” and “nothing more than an act of desperation.”

“Even worse, State Representative Gina Hinojosa is abusing her official capacity as an outgoing lawmaker to generate headlines for political purposes,” Abbott’s press secretary, Andrew Mahaleris, said in a statement. “Texans see this for what it is: a political stunt.”

Musk, who is CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Miami bakery condemns socialism after critics turn up the heat over Hakeem Jeffries campaign stop

A small bakery in Miami has found itself on the defensive after it hosted House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., last week for a surprise campaign stop as national Democrats pour resources into the tightening congressional race between Democrat Eliott Rodriguez and Republican Rep. María Elvira Salazar.

CAO Bakery, which stands for Cuban American Original, partner and chief marketing officer Yvette Cao said in a statement last night that she understood “why Friday hurts.”

“Let me start off by saying opening our doors was not an endorsement of any candidate, party or platform,” Cao wrote, adding that the bakery “stands with our Cuban American community for a free Cuba and condemns Socialism. That will never change.”

Cao went on to say “a congressional campaign” asked it last week whether its candidate could stop by for “a cafecito and to greet the community,” adding that she “didn’t know it would turn into a press conference.” A local political influencer criticized the bakery over the weekend for hosting Rodriguez and Jeffries, blasting it for opening "its doors and platform this week to leadership of a political party that works with democratic socialists."

Meanwhile, a Cuban American bakery started by Cao’s grandparents distanced itself from CAO Bakery and voiced its opposition to socialism in a separate statement.

Rodriguez, a Cuban American former news anchor, is running to unseat Salazar, who has found herself on the outs with Trump over her criticism of his immigration enforcement tactics. The candidates are running in a congressional district where 74% of the population is Hispanic, the vast majority of which has ties to Cuba.

Republicans in Miami-Dade County have sought to tie Democrats to socialism and the Democratic Socialists of America movement in an effort to sway voters whose families once fled authoritarian regimes.

Salazar told reporters Friday that Jeffries and Rodriguez would be “dragged” by “the socialist radical forces that are infiltrating the Democratic Party.” Jeffries has said he does not support the DSA’s agenda, and Rodriguez has rejected the label.

The district has taken dramatic swings in recent presidential elections, going for former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton by 20 percentage points in 2016 and then for Trump by 15 points in 2024. Salazar has represented the district since 2021.

Trump and Republicans battle to protect the midterms’ most surprising battleground

No other state has shut out one party in U.S. Senate races for as long as Kansas. But with days to go in the 2026 midterm elections, Trump is headlining a rally near Wichita today in a bid to head off the biggest threat in years to the GOP’s local winning streak.

Megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton hopes to make history as the first Democrat elected to the Senate in ruby-red Kansas in nearly a century. And Republican Sen. Roger Marshall is fighting for his political life in a state he won by over 11 points in 2020, with polls showing a toss-up.

Trump says Zelenskyy shouldn't negotiate on behalf of Ukraine

Trump told reporters today that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy should step aside from negotiating for his country.

“To be honest, I think it’s time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine,” Trump said. “Maybe it’s time for Zelenskyy to get somebody else to negotiate.”

A reporter had asked Trump for his reaction to Zelenskyy’s saying Trump was on the wrong side of history. Zelenskyy told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” yesterday that if Trump sided with Russia, it would be a “historic mistake.”

On Friday, Trump waived sweeping sanctions against Russia that Congress passed with bipartisan support — and he had signed into law last month. Trump defended his move on Truth Social yesterday, saying he did not want to drive Russia away from the bargaining table.

Trump reiterated that defense today, saying he did not want to “break up negotiations right in the middle.”

He said he would be open to a trilateral meeting with Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin. He also did not discount the possibility of cutting Zelenskyy out of a negotiation when he was asked whether he would be open to meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, even if Zelenskyy were not there.

“Well, I would meet in order anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody’s there or not, whatever I can do to end the war, and they do want to have a meeting at my suggestion, because I’m going to be over in China in November on the denuclearization, and if we can do denuclearization, I will have done the world a big, big favor,” Trump said.

Man charged with threatening Trump in Kansas, where he is set to rally tonight

A man today was charged with threatening Trump in Kansas, where he is set to hold a rally tonight to campaign for GOP Sen. Roger Marshall in a tightening re-election race.

The man, Jaden John Read, is charged with threatening to take the life of the president of the United States.

The complaint, signed by a Secret Service special agent, alleges Reade published posts on Facebook on or about Thursday calling to “shoot Trump” in Kansas, where he said he “already mapped out roofs around.”

How Flock’s cameras spread through government deals that bypassed public scrutiny

In less than a decade, Flock Safety’s license plate-reading cameras have spread across the U.S. In dozens of communities, residents and their elected representatives never voted on whether to install them.

An NBC News review of local government contracts and public records found that police departments and other officials regularly purchased Flock surveillance technology through deals that avoided competitive bidding or fell just below spending thresholds that require approval by elected representatives.

Read the full story here.

BBC seeks to depose Jack Smith to push back on Trump's Jan. 6 claims

Attorneys for the BBC have subpoenaed former special counsel Jack Smith to testify about Trump's state of mind on Jan. 6, 2021.

"It is difficult to imagine a more authoritative source on these issues than Mr. Smith, who spent years gathering evidence on those topics with the force of the Justice Department and the power of the grand jury behind him," the BBC said in a court filing.

Trump filed a $10 billion suit against the British news organization last year, alleging it aired a "false, defamatory, deceptive, disparaging, inflammatory, and malicious depiction of President Trump" in a documentary that spliced together comments from his speech at the Ellipse on Jan. 6. He argues the network falsely implied he incited violence in the speech.

The judge has said that to defend itself, the BBC "is entitled to discover the contours of the message and impression” behind Trump's speech that day.

Trump's attorneys want the judge to quash the subpoena, contending "Smith does not have any personal knowledge regarding President Trump’s state of mind at the time the Speech was given. Any evidence that Smith gathered during his investigation consists of secondhand knowledge based on materials that he and other third parties collected from various sources."

The BBC is separately asking the judge for help getting Trump to sit for his deposition in the case. He agreed to sit for a deposition last Friday but canceled in late September because of “matters of national importance.” The BBC lawyers note that he wound up going to a campaign rally in Georgia and then a fundraiser in Florida.

‘Astounded’: DOJ vets shocked by timing of Ilhan Omar search

It was early Columbus Day morning when a group of armed officers showed up on a quiet residential street in Northeast Washington, D.C., to seize the phone and boxes of belongings from one of Trump’s biggest critics and political targets: Rep. Ilhan Omar.

The move and the timing were highly unusual. Search warrants aren’t normally executed on federal holidays, since that could trigger overtime pay, three former officials said. Even more shocking to longtime Justice Department observers: Election Day was three weeks away.

Read the full story here.

Massachusetts GOP lieutenant governor candidate suspends campaign after OUI arrest

A candidate for lieutenant governor of Massachusetts, Republican Shawn Oliver, was arrested on drunken driving charges after a crash late Saturday that left several parked vehicles damaged and his own overturned, police said.

Yesterday, Oliver, a New Bedford City Council member, announced he was suspending his campaign, as his running mate, Mike Minogue, had called for him to do.

Read the full story here.

Trump signs executive order to establish new women's health division at the National Institutes of Health

Thrump signed an executive order this morning to direct the Department of Health and Human Services to create a women's health division at the National Institutes of Health and a task force to address women's health.

First lady Melania Trump spoke before Trump signed the order.

"Beginning today, we will change the reality of women’s health," she said. "Previous generations fought for women’s rights. Our generation will fight to discover the cures that will ensure a woman can live her life in health and to the fullest."

The first lady said the executive order "establishes a new standard for women's health in America." She pointed to the country's ability to draw upon artificial intelligence, biotechnology and "groundbreaking therapies."

The first task force meeting will take place today, she said. The president said later that White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. would lead the task force.

In remarks after his wife, the president said the initiative would "promote new research and really go after the understudied diseases affecting women and promote innovative technologies to diagnose conditions sooner and improve treatment using the best available science."

The text of the executive order has not yet been posted to the White House's website. The National Institutes of Health has an existing Office of Research on Women's Health. USA Today reported that the new division would have a mandate that extends beyond research and will not replace the existing office.

Schumer urges FCC to reject bid to ease AI robocall rules before midterms

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., called on the Federal Communications Commission to turn down a petition from the conservative group Club for Growth that would allow robocalls to voters' cellphones without consent, including messages with AI-generated voices.

"Not only is it bothersome to receive these calls — it can have major, misleading implications on elections. Under this change, campaigns could use their opponents’ voice to send out a message that is, at best, disingenuous and, at worst, a blatant lie," Schumer said in a comment on the FCC's public docket Monday.

An FCC spokesperson said in response to Schumer that the regulatory agency did not plan to advance any such proposal.

“There is no one at the FCC that has expressed any interest in moving to an order on this or any of the petitions and there are zero plans to do so," the spokesperson said in a statement. "The FCC seeks comment on petitions that come in as a matter of normal procedure.”

The agency's public comment period on the topic expires today.

Club for Growth last month formally asked the FCC for an expedited waiver from federal rules that would allow it to to send out robocalls "using an artificial or prerecorded voice — including an ​AI-generated voice — without obtaining prior express consent" from the recipient.

"There is absolutely no excuse to relax these standards and allow special interests to flood our cellphone lines with deepfakes or dark-money-funded AI voices. I am going to fight to make sure the FCC doesn’t change this rule this October or ever," Schumer said in a statement.

High spirits: Supreme Court to decide fate of federal ban on home distilling

In a boost for those who want to make whiskey in their bathtubs or gin in their kitchens, the Supreme Court today announced it will consider whether to strike down a long-standing federal ban on distilling spirits at home.

Although interest in the home distilling of hooch has continued despite the 150-year old ban, advocates hope the court will remove the threat of criminal sanctions, which can include a fine of up to $10,000 and a maximum sentence of five years in prison.

Read the full story here.

GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick says he will speak with Zelenskyy this week

Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., co-chair of the Ukraine Caucus, said today that he will speak with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy this week about the country's use of Starshield, the military version of the Starlink service.

Zelenskyy has warned that Ukraine is dealing with a speed restriction with Starshield. Fitzpatrick said in a post on X that “anyone who attempts to limit the use of Starshield for Ukraine will be fully investigated and will be held fully accountable.”

The Republican lawmaker, who also serves as co-chair of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus, said that the U.S. “must provide any and all defensive equipment that Ukraine needs to defend itself” and that America “must not import a single drop of Russian oil.”

"Congress will unequivocally reaffirm that Ukraine is an indispensable ally to the United States, that Russia is a self-declared enemy of the United States, and that the United States will 100% support and defend the people of Ukraine in their fight for their own freedom against this brutal, illegal, and unprovoked Russian invasion," he said.

Trump has lashed out at Zelenskyy in recent days after the Ukrainian president accused the U.S. of betraying his country with recent policy shifts, which have included allowing imports of Russian diesel and pressuring Ukraine to cease attacks on Russia's energy infrastructure. Last Friday, Trump also waived sanctions against Russia that Congress passed in September.

Fitzpatrick's race for re-election against Democrat Bob Harvie is considered a toss-up by NBC News.

Supreme Court to hear a new case on race and school admissions, this time in Maryland

The Supreme Court today agreed to hear a new challenge to school admissions policies aimed at fostering diversity, taking up a case targeting a lottery-based process for magnet programs in a Maryland county.

The court agreed to take up an appeal brought by the Association for Education Fairness seeking to revive a lawsuit it filed against the Montgomery County Board of Education. Montgomery County is a large and diverse county in the suburbs of Washington, D.C

Read the full story here.

Obama calls Trump officials’ investigation of Ilhan Omar ‘appalling’

Former President Barack Obama yesterday condemned federal agents’ raid on the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., calling it a “transparent” effort by the Trump administration to “intimidate” her.

“The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president,” Obama wrote on X.

Read the full story here.

Trump to sign an executive order on women's health

Trump will sign an executive order today to establish a new division at the National Institutes of Health and a task force on women's health.

The executive order was spearheaded by first lady Melania Trump, who will join the president at the signing this morning. She's expected to deliver remarks at the event, which will take place in the Rose Garden.

The White House task force will be led by the president's chief of staff, Susie Wiles, and hold its first meeting today. Wiles announced in March that she was diagnosed with breast cancer. Last month, she said she was cancer free.

The text of the executive order has not yet been released. The NIH currently operates the Office of Research on Women's Health, but USA Today reported that the new division would not replace the existing office and would have a mandate that extends beyond research.

Former President Joe Biden also signed an executive order in the last year of his administration to advance women's health initiatives in several areas and called on Congress to establish a $12 billion fund at NIH for related research.

Judge denies Trump administration's request to remove herself from the D.C. golf course case

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes denied the administration's request to recuse herself from the case surrounding Trump's push to redo a D.C. golf course.

The administration had argued that Reyes' "histrionics in prior hearings have clearly demonstrated she is no longer impartial."

In a filing last night, Reyes countered several of the administration's arguments, saying her being "furious" over the administration removing hundreds of trees from the course was not "sudden onset bias." Rather, it was the result of the administration's decision to wait until nearly 5 p.m. on the Friday ahead of the Columbus Day weekend to provide notice that it would start removing the trees within 15 hours, she said.

Reyes also pointed out several instances of her praising the government's lawyers, including her siding with the administration against plaintiffs who requested a temporary restraining order. She wrote that "no reasonable person could believe" after she denied plaintiffs' requests that "the Court exercised favoritism in a manner supporting disqualification."

In the conclusion of her filing, Reyes said, "It is easy to weaponize selective quotations to bring a baseless recusal motion. But it is much harder to meet the demanding legal standard against a full record. By any objective measure, the Government fails to meet the standard for recusal."

Trump called Reyes "a crazed lunatic" on Truth Social this morning and argued that the administration did not "need an approval" for renovations.

"Work is scheduled to begin IMMEDIATELY!" he wrote. "The finished product will be World Class, and bring income and great prestige back to D.C."

Trump said yesterday in a Truth Social post that he would renovating the public East Potomac Golf Links into a championship-level course.

Treasury secretary refuses to say if the U.S. sees Ukraine as an ally

Amid escalating tensions between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent yesterday dodged three times when asked whether Ukraine is an ally of the United States.

“We provide the three different things ... to Ukraine, so that’s what you do for an ally. We’re not providing those to Russia,” Bessent told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” the second time he was asked whether the U.S. considers Ukraine an ally.

Read the full story here.

Poll: Americans are anxious, pessimistic and deeply unhappy with Trump ahead of the midterms

Weeks ahead of Election Day, 71% of U.S. adults think the country is on the “wrong track.” It’s the highest share yet in Trump’s second term, illustrating the grim national mood his party faces in the midterm elections, according to a new NBC News Decision Desk Poll powered by SurveyMonkey.

Poll respondents expressed deep unhappiness over economic conditions and widespread distrust toward both major political parties, but Trump and Republicans bore the brunt. For the first time in Trump’s second term, the poll has found the “right track” sinking into the 20s.

A majority of Americans view the president’s administration as uniquely corrupt, even as they look skeptically at corruption in both parties. And they say Trump is failing to improve their material financial conditions.

Read the full story here.

Trump to travel to Kansas to boost GOP candidates in the final midterm stretch

Trump will hold a rally tonight in Kansas to campaign for Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, the latest of his midterm campaign stops.

Trump secured Kansas, a solidly red state, by more than 16 points in the 2024 presidential election. But Marshall and Democrat Adam Hamilton are locked in a close race this year.

In the governor's race, Republican Ty Masterson and Democrat Cindy Holscher are vying to replace Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly, who is term-limited.

Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, will travel to North Carolina today for a midterm rally to support Jennifer Balkcom, a Republican running in the 11th Congressional District against Democrat Jamie Ager, one of the most competitive House races.

Rep. Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., ended his re-election campaign in the district after he was accused of sexual harassment, which he has denied.

North Carolina also has a battleground Senate race, with Democrat Roy Cooper facing Republican Michael Whatley.

text:
Project now accepting case referrals nationwide and recruiting volunteer attorneys

WASHINGTON, D.C. — The National Immigration Project and the End SIJS Backlog Coalition launched the SIJS Habeas Project, a national effort to win the release of young people with Special Immigrant Juvenile Status (SIJS) who are being held in ICE detention. The Project is now accepting case referrals from anywhere in the country and recruiting pro bono attorneys to file federal habeas petitions for SIJS youth in ICE custody, with trainings beginning later this week.

The SIJS Habeas Project matches detained SIJS youth with pro bono lawyers, then trains and mentors those lawyers through habeas corpus litigation in federal court. Staff also advise attorneys already working on these cases and, in some cases, take on representation themselves. Coalition advocates and youth leaders track arrests of SIJS youth around the country, and what they find shapes the Project's legal strategy. The Project has been informally placing cases since September and has already found representation for several detained SIJS youth and advised more than a dozen attorneys working on similar cases. With new staff and a finalized intake process, the Project can now take referrals directly and bring on new volunteers.

“Most of the SIJS youth we work with came to this country as children, and a lot of them had already lived through more than anyone should by the time they got here,” said Diana Marin, SIJS Habeas Project Senior Attorney. “The SIJS Habeas Project can be a lifeline for youth with this protection who are unjustly being detained. While we know that access to a lawyer can greatly increase someone’s chances of being released, the demand we are seeing far exceeds what any of us can take on alone. We need charitable lawyers to step up and help us meet this moment.”

Every young person with SIJS has been through a state court that found they experienced parental abuse, abandonment, or neglect, and that it wasn't in their best interest to be sent back to the country they came from. Federal immigration authorities then also approved their petitions. But because of the visa backlog, many will be forced to wait years before they can apply for a green card. Since the start of this Trump administration, ICE has been arresting and detaining more SIJS beneficiaries than ever, including many who have deferred action preventing their deportation.

“Living with the uncertainty of the SIJS backlog is incredibly stressful, especially when our future depends on our immigration status,” said Amber, a young person with SIJS. “Knowing that the SIJS Habeas Project exists and is helping find attorneys who genuinely care about SIJS youth and are willing to dedicate their time and effort to fighting for our freedom and future means so much to me."

The SIJS Habeas Project takes referrals for anyone with an approved SIJS petition (Form I-360) who is being held in ICE detention in the United States. Family members, advocates, and attorneys can submit a referral through this case referral form. Attorneys who are litigating or considering a habeas case for a SIJS youth can ask for a consultation through the technical assistance form. Staff aim to respond within 2-3 business days, and urgent cases, such as when deportation is imminent, can be flagged on either form. Attorneys interested in volunteering to litigate a SIJS habeas case–regardless of prior experience–can sign up through this volunteer form.

“I have years of experience in immigration law but am newer to the federal litigation that is required to most effectively assist our clients in this climate,” said Grace Benton, Benton Immigration Legal Services PLLC. “The Project’s attorneys had multiple strategy calls with me, provided quick, helpful feedback on filings, and offered a wealth of resources and expertise to help my client and me navigate a scary, rapidly changing situation.”

title: More Said Than Done: Migrants Need Lawyers, Not Speeches (The National Law Journal)
description:
In an op-ed published by The National Law Journal, Stephen J. Brogan, Managing Partner of Jones Day from 2002 through 2022, posits that the legal profession's response to immigrants' growing legal needs has been a case of "more is said than done," a concern he first raised in 2015 in the Houston Chronicle and The National Law Journal.
With immigration court backlogs above 4 million cases, faster timelines, more detention, and less funded counsel for unaccompanied minors, he calls on lawyers to do "less talking and more doing."
Mr. Brogan points to Jones Day's own commitment since the 2015 border crisis: 2,214 lawyers and 392 staff working on immigration matters, a Laredo office devoted only to immigration and asylum cases, "know your rights" presentations to more than 30,000 migrants, a success rate above 80% in 170 asylum trials, and a habeas corpus program for people held in custody unlawfully.
