title: 'Unhinged' Immigration Judge Abused Power in Woodland Park, Sources Say
authors: Logan M. Davis, consultant based in Denver, public speaking, information ecosystems
description:
His name is David W. Illingworth, and his tenure on the Woodland Park school board between 2021 and 2023 was marked by lawbreaking, aggression towards district parents, and alleged abuse of power.
In 2023, Illingworth’s time as a school board member was brought to an abrupt halt by the voters of the Woodland Park School District (WPSD).
His time as a deputy district attorney ended around the same time, shortly after his former boss, District Attorney Michael Allen, was reached for comment regarding Illingworth’s behavior in Woodland Park.
Now, the man whose behavior in Woodland Park led sources to describe him as “unhinged” and “psychologically disturbed” is deciding the fate of migrant families.
“From November 2023 to December 2025, [Illingworth] was in private practice as a sole practitioner in Woodland Park, Colorado,” the bio reads.
text:
Last month, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche appointed 47 new immigration judges to oversee enforcement and removal cases. One of the new appointees formerly held elected office in Colorado, though his official Department of Justice biography makes no mention of that fact. His name is David W. Illingworth, and his tenure on the Woodland Park school board between 2021 and 2023 was marked by lawbreaking, aggression towards district parents, and alleged abuse of power. The new judge’s temper, along with his willingness to flex his roles as both a school board member and a deputy district attorney in repeated efforts to intimidate detractors, even resulted in the wrongful arrest and imprisonment – and eventual complete exoneration – of one district mother.

In 2023, Illingworth’s time as a school board member was brought to an abrupt halt by the voters of the Woodland Park School District (WPSD). His time as a deputy district attorney ended around the same time, shortly after his former boss, District Attorney Michael Allen, was reached for comment regarding Illingworth’s behavior in Woodland Park. “It is important to note that this office does not tolerate any employee misusing their authority,” Allen told me in September 2023, shortly before Illingworth’s departure from the office. Allen is currently the Republican nominee to be Colorado’s next attorney general.

Now, the man whose behavior in Woodland Park led sources to describe him as “unhinged” and “psychologically disturbed” is deciding the fate of migrant families.

“My heart breaks for the American people,” former district parent Samantha Peck told me upon hearing the news of Illingworth’s judgeship. “God have mercy on the souls of those who will encounter the consequences of his wrath,” Peck said – and she is in a position to know: nobody else in Woodland Park bore the brunt of Illingworth’s wrath as acutely as Peck.

I have reported on Peck’s story before, and covered the drama surrounding the WPSD board extensively during Illingworth’s tenure. In light of his new role as a federal judge, parts of that tenure bear reexamination, reflecting as they do on his fitness – or lack thereof – for the bench. The Executive Office of Immigration Review did not reply to multiple requests for comment on this story, or to the allegations against Illingworth.

The trouble started in 2021. That year, a slate of far-right candidates won a majority on the Woodland Park RE-2 Board of Education, a local government body which had been so uncontroversial in the preceding decades that there were rarely as many candidates as open seats. The sleepy environment surrounding the school board dissipated almost immediately upon Illingworth and his colleagues declaring victory. Before their first meeting as a new school board, emails obtained via public records requests show that Illingworth was already aggressively pushing two agenda items: disciplining the district’s teachers, whom Illingworth called “the enemy,” and pushing the district to officially grant a charter to Merit Academy, where his wife was on the board.

The first of those priorities led to widespread discontent among district teachers and parents, and proved to be just the first stone in a landslide that ultimately led to the district losing 40% of its teaching staff. The second of those priorities, chartering Merit Academy, which Illingworth and his colleagues pursued by violating Colorado’s Open Meetings Law, resulted in a years-long lawsuit which the district ultimately lost. Before Illingworth’s tenure on the board came to an end in late 2023, the district had attracted a number of additional lawsuits, and its annual legal expenses had increased by more than 900%.

Erin O’Connell, the district parent who filed the first lawsuit over the board’s Open Meetings Law violation, took the case all the way to the Colorado Supreme Court, where she won. Like Peck, she was shocked to learn of Illingworth’s judicial appointment.

“Illingworth is intensely unqualified to make decisions that affect vulnerable populations,” she told me, citing his history of “violating the law, ignoring policy as a board member, creating intentional division with the people he is supposed to represent, and publicly shaming citizens who oppose him.”

During his time on the Woodland Park school board, Illingworth formed ties with the Woodland Park-based ministry and political operation of evangelist Andrew Wommack, who has commented that a second civil war in the United States would be “worth it.”

Illingworth also used his board seat to successfully advocate for the adoption of the controversial American Birthright social studies curriculum which actively rejected “so-called ‘anti-racism,’” making WPSD the only district in the nation to adopt the program.

Amid Illingworth’s many controversies, a group of district parents launched an effort to recall him and his colleagues from the school board. In Colorado, if voters collect enough petition signatures, a recall election is triggered, in which the recalled elected official must run to maintain his or her seat. In Woodland Park, the effort was organized chiefly by O’Connell and Peck. Along with other district parents, they started collecting signatures.

On the evening of July 24, 2022, while collecting signatures in the Safeway parking lot, Peck noticed a woman closely inspecting the other signature gatherers. Seeming impaired and aggressive, the woman struck Peck as a threat. In the weeks leading up to that evening, the recall had become highly contentious in local circles, with threats and intimidation being deployed at Peck, O’Connell, and the other volunteers – an atmosphere which had led the Woodland Park Police Department to instruct Peck to give them a call if anything seemed amiss. Following that instruction, Peck called the local police to report the incident.

After concluding her shift collecting signatures and making sure her volunteers were okay, Peck went home. The police, meanwhile, arrived at the Safeway and questioned the woman Peck had called about. The woman turned out to be Katie Illingworth, whom Peck had never met.

A week later, in the middle of the night, Peck – a West Point graduate and Army veteran – was hauled out of her house by Teller County Sheriff’s deputies, leaving her children alone in the home. She was not given the opportunity to get dressed or put on shoes before she was locked in a cell overnight. The charge: filing a false police report and two felony counts of attempting to influence a public servant. What happened during the week between her call to the police and her arrest by sheriff’s deputies only became clear as the trial progressed, but not before Peck was dragged through the mud, not before her mugshot was published in the local paper.

The details of Peck’s arrest, and Illingworth’s role in it, have been reported extensively. Illingworth, outraged that Peck would report his wife to the authorities, spoke to local law enforcement officers. Identifying himself as a deputy district attorney in the district that would be prosecuting the case, Illingworth convinced the sheriff’s office that Peck called the police purely to intimidate him in his role as a school board member. Illingworth even instructed an officer on how to elevate the charges against Peck to felony level. The entire exchange was captured on the officer’s body-worn camera, the footage from which has since been released.

In July 2023, after being dragged through a trial on the felony charges Illingworth concocted, Peck was quickly and unanimously exonerated of all charges by the jury. One of the jurors allegedly commented that he had “never seen a bigger abuse of power ever.”

Peck’s only crime, in the end, was offending David Illingworth.

“The fact that he colluded with law enforcement to target a citizen makes him uniquely unqualified for this position,” said O’Connell of Illingworth’s new judgeship. It was O’Connell who bailed Peck out of jail the morning after her arrest.

It was in relation to Peck’s case, in the months after her exoneration, that I contacted Colorados’ 4th Judicial District Attorney’s Office to make inquiries about their knowledge of Illingworth’s involvement in the case. District Attorney Michael Allen said that his office had zero tolerance for employees abusing their power. At some point in the next two months, Illingworth’s employment with Allen ended.

The Illingworth biography provided by the Department of Justice upon his appointment last month notes his tenure working for Allen, but omits his time as an elected official altogether. “From November 2023 to December 2025, [Illingworth] was in private practice as a sole practitioner in Woodland Park, Colorado,” the bio reads. “From August 2018 to November 2023, he served as a deputy district attorney for the Fourth Judicial District Attorney in Colorado Springs, Colorado.”

Now, Illingworth is serving on the San Diego Immigration Court, where his job is to decide which migrants to deport and which should be allowed to remain in the country.

“This adds to my deep concerns about the ethics of our current administration,” Peck told me. “When leadership cannot find honorable people to make difficult and consequential decisions, and instead chooses to fill sensitive positions with individuals who have been found by our judicial system to have engaged in illegal activity—all for the sake of power and control—that is when you know we have reached an ultimate ethical low.”

WASHINGTON (OSV News) — The Trump administration on Oct. 18 extended protections from deportation to people from Ukraine and Sudan, allowing them to continue living legally in the U.S. for now.

Temporary Protected Status grants the U.S. government the power to shield eligible migrants from deportation if they are from countries experiencing dangerous conditions such as war, disaster, or other unrest. The Trump administration has sought to end TPS for several countries, notably Haiti, which is racked by extreme levels of gang violence, but it also recently granted an extension to migrants from El Salvador.

In a written statement provided to OSV News, a spokesperson for DHS confirmed the extension without sharing a rationale. The spokesperson stated an announcement on each country’s TPS “will be made at the appropriate time,” and until such announcements are made, nationals of those countries “present in the U.S. under TPS retain protection.”

David Spicer, director of policy and engagement for migration at the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, told OSV News Oct. 19 the conference “is closely monitoring the situation facing people relying on TPS without clarity on the future of their designations.”

“These include hundreds of thousands of Salvadorans, Ukrainians, and Sudanese who are lawfully present in the United States, but face the reality of suddenly having their protection and work authorization revoked,” Spicer said. “The conference continues to urge the administration to abide by the requirements of the TPS statute, to carefully consider conditions in countries of origin and the threats to human life that could come with forcibly repatriating people, and to provide meaningful notice about the future of these designations so that families, employers, and communities can plan accordingly.”

Uncertainty remains for TPS holders

Ashley Feasley, the legal expert in residence at the Immigration Law and Policy Initiative at The Catholic University of America Columbus School of Law, told OSV News that while the DHS statement “is a welcome reprieve to TPS holders from Ukraine and Sudan,” it “does little to clarify the growing confusion and uncertainty they face with regards to their lives here in the U.S.”

“In addition to enduring growing conflict and war in their home countries, these individuals must continue to navigate an unpredictable day-to-day existence here in the U.S. given so much recent uncertainty over TPS generally,” Feasley said.

“Congress created TPS and codified it into law and the Executive is required to implement that process accordingly,” she continued. “For both Ukraine and Sudan, it is clear that both countries face ‘ongoing armed conflict,’ as is described in the statute designating TPS. It is absolutely not safe for these individuals to return to their home country.”

TPS extension requested for Haiti

Earlier this year, the U.S. Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to end TPS designation for Haitian and Syrian nationals. Catholic leaders have also urged protection for people from those countries who would be subject to dangerous conditions in their countries of origin.

The Trump administration terminated TPS for Haiti after that ruling, and has since carried out mass deportations of Haitians back to Haiti, which is among the immigration policies the U.S. bishops have criticized, calling it incompatible with their God-given right to life, human dignity, and unity of the family.

text:
[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – Today, U.S. Senators Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), Richard J. Durbin (D-IL), Ron Wyden (D-OR), Adam Schiff (D-CA), Edward J. Markey (D-MA) and Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) urged Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. to reverse the decisionThis link opens in new window or tab. for HHS attorneys to represent unaccompanied children against the Trump Administration’s own deportation machine and restore independent legal counsel immediately. In the letter to Secretary Kennedy, the Senators underscored how failing to reverse this decision would result in a clear conflict of interest, especially since HHS has a responsibility to care for these kids in custody and already shares personal information with immigration enforcement. The Senators’ letter comes after Duckworth held a press conference in Chicago lambasting the Trump Administration for this latest attempt to violate these children’s due process rights and called for the reversal of these egregious plans.

“HHS holds these children in custody, decides where they live and shares information about them and their families with immigration enforcement. HHS cannot also be their lawyer,” wrote the Senators. “The immigration judge works for the Trump Administration. So does the prosecutor. Under your plan, so would the child’s lawyer. That is unacceptable.”

As a direct result of the Trump Administration cuttingThis link opens in new window or tab. funding to facilitate independent legal aid for unaccompanied migrant children, this year tens of thousands of children facedThis link opens in new window or tab. immigration judges with no legal representation. In their letter, the Senators cited how the bipartisan Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008 legally requires HHS to make every effort to secure pro bono counsel that will provide independent representation and protect the kids from mistreatment or exploitation. By appointing HHS attorneys to these cases instead, the Administration intends to place these children in removal proceedings led by judges working for the U.S. Department of Justice with legal representation that is anything but independent.

The Senators continued, “Reunifying children with their families is HHS’s job. Legally representing an unaccompanied child, including against HHS in legal proceedings, is not. It is a job for an experienced, expert and independent attorney trained to represent unaccompanied children who are often experiencing extreme stress and trauma.”

Additionally, the Senators highlighted that HHS’s decision would discourage these kids from reporting abuse, trafficking and dangerous family circumstances to their lawyers for fear of the information reaching immigration enforcement. Notably, HHS’s announcement mentions no procedures for screening conflicts, protecting client confidentiality or insulating attorneys from HHS’s custodial functions.

“HHS cannot serve as both custodian and counsel. You must meet your statutory obligation to these children. Unaccompanied children deserve lawyers whose only loyalty is to them. We demand that you rescind this harmful policy before a single HHS attorney stands beside a child in immigration court,” the Senators concluded.

The full text of the letter is available on Senator Duckworth’s website and below.

We call on you to rescind your decision to have U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) attorneys represent unaccompanied children in immigration proceedings through the newly created Unaccompanied Alien Children Legal Representation Division (UACLRD). HHS holds these children in custody, decides where they live and shares information about them and their families with immigration enforcement. HHS cannot also be their lawyer.

The immigration judge works for the Trump administration. So does the prosecutor. Under your plan, so would the child’s lawyer. That is unacceptable. We demand that you:

Rescind the decision creating the UACLRD and confirm in writing, no later than October 30, 2026, that no HHS attorney will represent an unaccompanied child in immigration proceedings; and

Restore independent counsel for these children by making every effort to utilize pro bono counsel, as section 235(c)(5) of the William Wilberforce Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008 (TVPRA) (8 U.S.C. 1232(c)(5)) requires, and by funding experienced, independent legal service providers, as 45 CFR 410.1309 provides, through competitive, merit-based awards.

On September 29, 2026, HHS published a notice in the Federal Register that places the UACLRD within its Office of the General Counsel (OGC). According to the notice, the division “provides direct legal services to unaccompanied alien children,” including “introductory legal orientation concerning immigration proceedings” and representation in immigration court. The division reports to the General Counsel through a designated Deputy General Counsel and “may coordinate with other OGC components and appropriate Federal entities as necessary” to carry out its work. The notice says the division will not advise the Administration for Children and Families or the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) on matters involving its clients, but it sets out no procedures for screening conflicts, protecting client confidentiality or insulating attorneys from HHS’s custodial functions.

HHS has described the division as “an additional mechanism to provide these children direct legal support while dedicated public servants work around the clock to safely reunify them with their families.” Reunifying children with their families is HHS’s job. Legally representing an unaccompanied child, including against HHS in legal proceedings, is not. It is a job for an experienced, expert and independent attorney trained to represent unaccompanied children who are often experiencing extreme stress and trauma.

Congress was clear in the bipartisan TVPRA. HHS must ensure, to the greatest extent practicable, that unaccompanied children who are or have been in Federal custody have counsel “to represent them in legal proceedings or matters and protect them from mistreatment, exploitation, and trafficking,” and it must make every effort to utilize the services of pro bono counsel who agree to represent these children without charge.

HHS’s own regulations require that the legal orientation children in ORR custody receive “be provided by an independent legal service provider,” and they provide for funding legal service providers to represent children directly when pro bono counsel is not practicable. The September 29 notice assigns legal orientation to attorneys in your General Counsel’s office. An HHS employee is not an independent legal service provider. For nearly two decades, under administrations of both parties, HHS met these obligations by funding outside legal service providers with the expertise and independence these cases require. HHS has spent more than a year dismantling that system.

ORR withheld payments to legal service providers in late 2025 after they declined to hand over confidential client information, and in August a Federal court ordered HHS to pay more than $65 million in overdue invoices. HHS let the contract covering more than 20,000 children expire on July 31, 2026. Your Department then turned to a small law firm with little immigration experience, which withdrew, and to Our Rescue, a controversial nonprofit with no apparent experience representing children in immigration court, whose $158 million no-bid sole source contract is stayed.

Today, children are left with an ineffective temporary provider, the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants, whose representatives have reportedly sat silent at some children’s hearings and missed others. Many children in custody have reportedly not received the legal orientation HHS’s regulations require, and in August a one-year-old appeared in an Arizona immigration court without a lawyer. Having created this gap, HHS now proposes not to fix it but to fill it with its own employees.

The conflict of interest is clear. UACLRD attorneys would be HHS employees supervised by the HHS General Counsel, who answers to you, the official responsible for every custody, placement and release decision HHS makes. In immigration court, they would face U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) attorneys seeking the child’s removal, before an immigration judge who answers to the Attorney General of the United States.

Professional conduct rules in Illinois and across the country prohibit a lawyer from letting the person who employs or pays the lawyer direct or regulate the lawyer’s professional judgment on a client’s behalf. Federal public defenders, sometimes cited as precedent for government-paid counsel, operate under the Federal judiciary, independent of the Department of Justice that prosecutes their clients.

The UACLRD would sit inside the agency that holds its clients in custody. Consider a child abused while in ORR care. Will a UACLRD attorney zealously gather evidence and litigate against HHS colleagues or HHS grantees? If the child may be eligible for a U visa as the victim of a qualifying crime, will the HHS attorney pursue that relief when it exposes failures in HHS’s own program? Will the attorney challenge Executive Office for Immigration Review decisions in Federal court, or argue for an interpretation of immigration law that contradicts the Attorney General?

The conflict is sharpest for children seeking Special Immigrant Juvenile (SIJ) status, a path to lawful permanent residence for children who cannot reunify with one or both parents because of abuse, neglect, abandonment or a similar basis under State law. A child in ORR care in Illinois, as elsewhere, may petition a State court for the findings SIJ status requires. But Federal law bars a juvenile court from determining the custody status or placement of a child in HHS custody unless you specifically consent to that jurisdiction, and ORR decides where each child is placed, including whether to transfer a child to a State where those findings are harder to obtain. A UACLRD attorney would have to ask the attorney’s own employer for that consent and challenge that employer’s placement and release decisions to keep the child’s case alive and win the child’s release to a safe, vetted sponsor. An independent lawyer faces no such conflict.

Children must also be able to tell their lawyers about abuse, trafficking and family circumstances, with confidence that the information will be properly reported and without fear that the information will reach immigration enforcement. Independent legal advocates can play an important role in referring cases with indication of trafficking directly to the Office of Trafficking in Persons (OTIP). But without independent legal advocates, HHS’s recent policy change requiring care providers to refer cases to ORR instead of directly to OTIP in 24 hours, as mandated by Federal regulation, could endanger children at risk of trafficking even more than it already does.

HHS has shown it cannot be trusted to protect children who report abuse or trafficking. According to internal Federal data reported by Reuters, immigration authorities have arrested more than 12,000 people, including children and their sponsors, after tips from ORR. No child can be expected to confide in a lawyer employed by the agency that supplied those tips. The notice does not bar the UACLRD from sharing client information with the Department of Homeland Security. It permits coordination with “appropriate Federal entities,” limited only by the attorneys’ “professional responsibilities” to their clients.

HHS cannot serve as both custodian and counsel. You must meet your statutory obligation to these children. Unaccompanied children deserve lawyers whose only loyalty is to them. We demand that you rescind this harmful policy before a single HHS attorney stands beside a child in immigration court.

text:
A federal court has ordered the U.S. State Department to open registration for the Diversity Visa Lottery for fiscal year 2027. The Trump administration failed to open registration by the deadline, even though the program offers a pathway to a green card, according to the International Legal and Business Services Group (ILBSG).

On October 14, 2026, Federal District Court Judge Jinsook Ota issued a preliminary injunction and ordered the State Department to set the registration deadline for fiscal year 2027. Anyone can now apply for the lottery. The State Department must continue processing applications until all 55,000 visas are issued or fiscal year 2027 ends.

According to Curtis Morrison, an attorney with Red Eagle Law LC, the law firm that filed the lawsuit, the judge ordered the State Department to publicly announce the registration process and open it no later than midnight Eastern Time on October 15, 2026. The registration process must take at least 30 days. A State Department spokesperson stated that the agency delayed the process to prioritize the interests of the American people. He added that the State Department prefers not to comment on ongoing or pending litigation.

On the subject: The State Department has finally clarified what will happen next with the green card lottery.

The Trump administration has openly opposed the Diversity Visa program. Authorities claimed they were unable to open the 2027 lottery until the end of the previous fiscal year due to inconsistencies in the rules governing the program's timing.

Red Eagle Law subsequently filed a lawsuit against US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, challenging the government's arguments under the Administrative Procedure Act. The law firm claimed the delay caused it financial harm. Its work depends on representing Diversity Visa applicants. Because the previous fiscal year ended without new applications being accepted, potential lottery applicants were effectively prevented from applying. As a result, the firm suffered financial losses for which it will not be able to recoup.

Judge Ota concluded that the failure to open registration effectively suspended the program without sufficient explanation. The government argued that reopening the lottery after missing the regular registration deadline would violate the federal rule requiring applications to be accepted for 30 days. Red Eagle Law argued that missing the required deadline should not prevent the court from ordering the State Department to conduct the lottery. The judge rejected the government's arguments.

Ota acknowledged that Red Eagle Law has the right to pursue legal action in this case. The firm's financial losses could lead to irreparable damages that would be impossible to recover.

This decision reversed the outcome of the previous phase of the case. Ota had previously denied Red Eagle Law's motion for a temporary restraining order that would have compelled the State Department to immediately open registration. The denial was made without foreclosing the firm's right to resubmit such a request. Now, under the new injunction, the State Department is required to begin registering lottery participants for 2027. The court will retain authority to oversee compliance with the order.

Fresno City Councilmember Miguel Arias is proposing a $1 million immigration legal defense fund to help city residents facing deportation proceedings, following increased federal immigration enforcement activity in the Central Valley.

The proposal is scheduled for consideration at the Fresno City Council’s Thursday, Oct. 22, meeting. According to city records, the resolution would reestablish the Immigration Legal Defense Fund and direct the city to identify funding for legal services.

The measure, listed as Agenda Item 2-BB, would direct the city manager’s administration to prioritize identifying $1 million for the program through the fiscal year 2027 midyear budget process. The resolution is subject to a mayoral veto.

The proposal calls for the City Attorney’s Office to administer the program, with qualified outside legal service providers representing eligible Fresno residents in immigration-related proceedings.

Arias announced the proposal Monday, Oct. 19, citing recent enforcement operations by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement that he said have disrupted daily life for immigrant families.

“Over the last two weeks, we have seen ICE terrorize our community, leaving families afraid to go to work, take their children to school, or shop for groceries,” Arias said in a statement.

“Residents across the Valley have called on leaders to take action. This action would provide immigrant residents with legal support to protect their constitutional rights and defend them against ICE’s unconstitutional actions,” he added.

The proposed fund would cover immigration-related legal defense services for Fresno residents, according to Arias’ announcement.

However, approval of the resolution would not necessarily make the full $1 million immediately available. The proposal directs city officials to identify available funding, with any allocation subject to the city’s budget process.

The proposal does not identify a specific funding source.

Details about eligibility requirements, the number of residents who could receive assistance and the selection of legal service providers have not been fully established.

Arias scheduled a news conference Monday afternoon at Fresno City Hall to discuss the proposal.

The Fresno City Council is scheduled to meet Thursday at 9 a.m.

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement could hire more workers at its offices in Vermont as part of a $100 million plan to boost intelligence-gathering for the branch of the agency that carries out arrests and deportations, federal records show.

The plan, which is not final, calls for 24 positions evenly split between ICE’s Law Enforcement Support Center and its National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center, both of which are in Williston. They’re among 142 total positions proposed for ICE offices around the country, all of which would be staffed by a government contractor.

The workers would provide “intelligence research and analytical support” for ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations division, often abbreviated ERO, according to a contracting document published online last month. That includes “understanding emerging trends, identifying potential threats, recognizing intelligence gaps, assessing relationships and patterns” and a number of other duties.

The contractors would work with a mix of classified and unclassified information, and at least some of them would need “top secret” government security clearance, according to the document. ICE estimates the total cost of the nationwide plan, called ERO Overwatch and National Security Enforcement, would be more than $100 million, according to another federal record published last month.

The government has been “conducting market research” for the plan and issued a request for information to potential contractors, which was due late last month, according to the published records. A final contract could be awarded around February, the magazine The American Prospect reported last week, citing intelligence contracting experts.

One of the Williston centers, the Law Enforcement Support Center, is located on Harvest Lane. It operates a round-the-clock service for police nationwide to get information on a person’s immigration status, as well as a tip line for the public. Workers there also generate leads for immigration enforcement agents and process biometric data for other federal law enforcement agencies including the U.S. Secret Service, according to ICE’s website.

Less than a 10-minute drive away on Industrial Avenue, the National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center also develops leads for ICE operations, using an array of digital tools to provide “critical investigative support for daily arrest efforts” according to an agency webpage.

Together, the centers are a major node in ERO’s national intelligence-gathering network. Another key facility, the Pacific Enforcement Response Center, is located in Southern California. That center would get nine contract workers under the plan outlined last month.

The plan marks at least the third time ICE has considered increasing its staffing at Vermont’s facilities since President Donald Trump took office a second time last year, but the agency has disclosed little information publicly about those earlier efforts.

Both Vermont centers have been regular sites for protests in Trump’s second term. Some of those demonstrators have been arrested and are now facing trespassing charges.

The demonstrations in Vermont have been a far cry from the violent clashes that have erupted between protesters and federal agents in other parts of the country. Earlier this month, protesters wrote anti-ICE messages with chalk on the facade of the Law Enforcement Support Center and blocked the road in front of the building using garden beds.

ICE did not immediately respond to a request for more information Monday about its plans for the facilities in Vermont.

WASHINGTON – On Friday, United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) Commissioner Rodney Scott toured a cargo processing facility in Arizona, seeing firsthand how CBP keeps harmful contraband from entering the United States.

At the cargo inspection facility at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport, CBP personnel inspect imported goods for illegal drugs, fraudulent labeling, and other national security threats. Among the items that were seen during the visit were baseball jerseys that were labeled as being manufactured in Mexico, but were actually manufactured in China.

“The hardworking men and women of CBP look at almost every package that comes in, so that dangerous drugs, counterfeit products, and other harmful contraband does not come into our country,” said Secretary Mullin. “The patriots at CBP understand these criminals’ patterns, how the traffickers and cartels try to get around the duties and customs, and the way they try to ship things into our country. That’s why experience matters.”

text:
Right now, tens of thousands of people across the United States are in immigration detention, where rights violations are rampant, and the Trump administration is signaling that it intends to accelerate its detention and deportation campaign. “We came here hoping to find safety,” said 45 men who are detained in a privately owned detention center in Folkston, Georgia in an open letter. “Instead we found ourselves in prison.” Many of the people held in the Folkston facility have been on hunger strike since October 6 to protest their prolonged detention and the violation of their rights.

On October 6, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) reportedly raised its arrest goal by 1,000 people each day, following record arrests this summer. In the longer term, public federal procurement documents reveal that ICE plans to scale up its detention capacity by operationalizing a vast network of facilities, transportation, and personnel – almost entirely run by private contractors – and using “mobile detention facilities” to hold individuals after their arrest.

As the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) expands its vast immigration detention system, conditions within detention facilities remain abysmal. Reporters and advocates continue to document harrowing stories of life inside of detention centers, including physical abuse and inadequate food and medical care. Meanwhile, many of the agencies designed to provide oversight over detention conditions have all but collapsed.

Using the tool below, call and email your Members of Congress to urge them to exercise oversight and demand accountability for the Trump administration’s lawless campaign of mass detention and deportation.

EMAIL YOUR MEMBERS OF CONGRESS

Using the tool above, you can send an email to your federal elected officials.

Sample email: My name is [insert name], and as your constituent from [City/Town] and a [person of faith/refugee/member of community], I am horrified by the scale and cruelty of the Trump administration’s mass detention and deportation campaign.

With the signing of H.R. 1 in July 2025, Congress appropriated a record-setting $170 billion for immigration enforcement and detention. Less than a year later, in June 2026, Congress gave the administration another $70 billion to support its mass deportation agenda. I urge you to rescind the over $240 billion in congressional funding that is enabling the administration to arrest, detain, and deport members of our communities on an unprecedented scale.

I also urge you to take the following steps to pressure the administration to change course and provide needed oversight into the immigration detention system:

Speak out about detention conditions and demand the closure of detention facilities: Immigrants – including families and children – are facing harrowing conditions in immigration detention. Inadequate food, limited medical care, and other abuses are rampant. Access to counsel is often extremely restricted, and many people report being coerced into accepting “voluntary departure.”

Promote rigorous oversight: I urge you to conduct oversight by visiting Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention centers, Customs and Border Protection (CBP) facilities, and administrative buildings where immigrants are being held. Visiting detention facilities is especially crucial because the administration has gutted and defunded many of the offices designed to provide oversight into immigration detention. Congress also can and must prevent future abuses by funding and upholding the oversight functions of the Office of Inspector General (OIG), Office of the Immigration Detention Ombudsman (OIDO), Office of Civil Rights and Civil Liberties (CRCL), and Citizenship and Immigration Services Ombudsman.

Hold the administration accountable for its overreach: Pass legislative guardrails to prevent harmful ICE practices such as arresting individuals who are attending court hearings or immigration check ins in fulfillment of their legal obligations; deliberately targeting sensitive locations like schools, medical settings, and houses of worship; erasing immigrants with final orders of removal from the detainee locator database; and refouling people to places where they will face danger, including third countries.

Push back against efforts to further expand detention and deportation: Congress must hold oversight hearings to hold the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) accountable for the abuses it has already committed and to investigate its plans for expansion. DHS has stripped hundreds of thousands of people who fled violence and persecution of their legal protections and continues to deliberately target them for arrest, detention, and refoulement to danger – including over 300,000 Haitians who were previously protected by TPS. ICE has reinterpreted longstanding law to massively expand mandatory detention, and many people who have been ordered released from detention remain detained. The Office of Refugee Resettlement is holding unaccompanied children in custody until they age out of the system and then immediately transferring them to ICE custody. DHS recently raised its daily arrest goal, and in the long term, public documents show that ICE intends to expand detention and deportation by operationalizing a network of private contractor-run facilities, transportation, and personnel.

Immigrants and refugees make major contributions to our local communities and economies. Evidence demonstrates that the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign has harmed businesses, increased unemployment, and weakened worker protections. A path to citizenship would stabilize jobs and prices across key industries to help communities flourish.

Again, I urge you to investigate and condemn the administration’s campaign to detain and deport immigrants, and to pass a path to citizenship and support legislative guardrails to prevent future abuses. text:
DHS did not respond to a question about whether they can keep their work permits, but TPS generally allows people to work while their protections remain in effect.

The decision Monday marks another incident where the Trump administration, which has previously sought to end these temporary protections from deportation and send people back to their home countries, has allowed people covered by the temporary status to stay in the country but without giving any guidance as to how long.

Yuriy Boyechko, CEO of Hope For Ukraine, a nonprofit that provides humanitarian aid in Ukraine and helps resettle newcomers in the U.S., described the government's announcement as "last-minute patches."

It is a "bandage that has been placed on a wound that does not solve the real issue," he said. "It's time for U.S. to come up with some normal path to permanent residency for all these people," Boyechko noted. He emphasized that they cannot safely return to Ukraine.

The context of the decisions to keep the protections

Watch the segment in the player above.

The Trump administration has already terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria.

But in a change in practice roughly a month ago, the administration kept protections in place for nearly 200,000 Salvadorans whose TPS was set to expire Sept. 9. In that case they also said that they were going to make a decision at the appropriate time and that in the meantime, people from El Salvador could continue to work and live in the U.S.

Activists and a bipartisan group of lawmakers have been raising the alarm over the upcoming deadline for TPS to expire for Ukrainians, arguing that conditions remain unsafe for them to return home amid the war with Russia.

Ukraine was first designated for TPS in April 2022, following Russia's full-scale invasion two months earlier. The Biden administration subsequently extended the designation, most recently in January 2025, when DHS authorized an additional 18 months of protection through October 2026.

The TPS program for Sudan was established in 1997, and since then, successive U.S. administrations have extended it due to the armed conflict and political instability that have plagued the African nation.

The decision Monday comes two weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Trump's hard line immigration policies will face a test at the ballot box.

The TPS program has offered protections for decades but is controversial

The U.S. Congress created TPS in 1990 to prevent deportations to countries suffering from natural disasters or civil strife.

It allows people already in the country to remain and work, for renewable periods if the homeland security secretary determines conditions are unsafe for their return. But it doesn't give them a pathway to permanent residency.

Supporters say that using this tool protects people from being returned to dangerous situations and that uprooting people covered by TPS after years of living in the U.S. is cruel. Critics, especially in the Trump administration, say successive administrations have extended these protections for years regardless of what has happened in the home countries.

Federal rules say TPS is automatically extended for six months if the secretary doesn't make a determination at least 60 days before the designation expires.

Advocates are grateful for DHS decision, warn about the war

"We're grateful for an extension, however temporary, for TPS holders from Ukraine and Sudan," said Myal Greene, president and CEO of World Relief, an organization that has provided humanitarian assistance in both countries. "We encourage the administration and Congress to consider longer term relief for women, men and children trying to carve out stability while their countries of origin remain in upheaval."

Krish O'Mara Vignarajah, president and CEO of Global Refuge, noted Ukraine and Sudan are not safe and meet the legal conditions for TPS to be extended.

"Russia's war on Ukraine is nearing its fifth year, and Ukrainians are bracing for another winter under drone and missile strikes, driving civilian casualties and devastating critical infrastructure. Sudan remains locked in a brutal civil war marked by famine, widespread human rights abuses and the hallmarks of genocide," Vignarajah said. "It is not safe for these families to go home."

Associated Press reporter Rebecca Santana contributed from Washington.

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil asked the Supreme Court on Monday to let federal judges quickly determine the legality of immigration-related detentions so that individuals cannot be held for months or years without judicial oversight.

In papers filed with the high court, Khalil asked it to overturn a ruling earlier this year by the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Philadelphia that found federal courts do not have jurisdiction to review the legality of the detentions until immigration courts had fully considered each case.

Khalil, a lawful permanent U.S. resident, was detained by immigration authorities last year because of his participation in pro-Palestinian demonstrations at Columbia University in the spring of 2024.

The U.S. government argued at the time that Khalil's presence in the U.S. was harmful to the country's foreign policy interests.

As a result, the former Columbia graduate student spent over three months in detention before a federal judge in New Jersey ordered him freed after finding that the federal government had acted unconstitutionally.

READ MORE: Mahmoud Khalil lawsuit says Columbia University failed to protect pro-Palestinian activists

In a statement Monday, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said: "It is a privilege to be granted a visa or green card to live and study in the United States of America. The Trump Administration acted well within its statutory and constitutional authority with respect to Khalil, as it does with any alien who advocates for violence, glorifies and supports terrorists, harasses Jews, and damages property. We would encourage him to use the CBP Home app and self-deport."

The 3rd Circuit has put its ruling on hold so that Khalil could appeal to the Supreme Court. He remains free.

Although the Supreme Court typically agrees to grant only a small percentage of appeals requests, the U.S. government has already asked the high court to overturn a federal appeals court decision that upheld a judge's decision to release Georgetown University scholar Badar Khan Suri. That ruling by the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Richmond, Virginia, directly conflicted with the 3rd Circuit decision in the Khalil case.

Sometimes, conflicting appeals court rulings can increase the chances that the Supreme Court agrees to hear a case. If it does, oral arguments before the justices would likely occur sometime next year.

text:
Former Columbia grad student and pro-Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil, whom the Trump administration detained and sought to deport from the U.S. on foreign policy grounds last year, has appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court, seeking to sue the government for allegedly violating his First Amendment rights.

A divided federal appeals court ruled earlier this year that Khalil, a green card-holder married to an American citizen, could not litigate his claims before a judge unless and until immigration proceedings against him had been completed.

He was arrested by federal agents in New York City in March 2025 and held more than 100 days in ICE custody ahead of deportation after Secretary of State Marco Rubio signed an unusual determination that Khalil's pro-Palestinian activities "compromise a compelling U.S. foreign policy interest."

Khalil, who has not been charged with any crime, contends that he was deliberately targeted by Trump as part of a scheme to crackdown on pro-Palestinian protests and debate over Israel’s war in Gaza that had swept college campuses shortly after the president took office.

After a legal challenge, Khalil was released from custody pending the outcome of his petition.

"This fight is not only about whether I get to stay in this country," Khalil said during a remote press conference Monday. "It’s about whether anyone in this country can speak out for Palestinians without being punished for it."

Asked for comment on Khalil's appeal, a White House spokeswoman said the executive branch has the authority to take actions that protect the country and the immigration system.

"Khalil obtained his visa by willfully and intentionally failing to accurately report information relevant to his background. Those who lie to the government to obtain entry into the United States will face justice,” spokeswoman Lauren Bis said.

The legal question at the heart of the case involves the writ of habeas corpus, the legal procedure that allows a person detained by the government to challenge his confinement before a judge.

If the high court takes up the case -- and says Khalil can access the procedure -- his case alleging targeted retaliation by the government over disfavored speech can go forward. If the court denies the appeal, Khalil could be deported before getting the chance to make his case.

"It’s clear and conceited that Mahmoud has never committed a crime and that his detention and removal are only because of the speech the government dislikes," said Khalil's attorney Baher Azmy. This is "unprecedented weaponization of immigration power ... The question is whether the federal courts can address this egregious action."

Khalil has a separate legal challenge pending in the 5th Circuit Court of appeals focusing on U.S. immigration law.

"It's way bigger than me," Khalil said. "I can afford to lose … unlike the thousands of immigrants in this country who really cannot lose this fight. Whatever I’m going through is a drop in the sea of what other families are experiencing."

The justices are likely to consider the petition during a formal private meeting in January. If they agree to hear Khalil's case, it would likely be set for oral argument sometime in the spring and decided by the end of June.

text:
Masked Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents broke the arm of a U.S. citizen during a detention attempt Saturday in Long Beach, California, Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., said Sunday.

Ricardo Gonzalez, a former Long Beach city employee, was found handcuffed, bleeding and being detained by several ICE officers when local authorities arrived at the scene, according to a statement from the Long Beach Police Department.

Videos of the encounter taken by bystanders appeared to show Gonzalez lying face down in a gutter while several ICE agents kneeled on his back. In several videos, Gonzalez is heard yelling repeatedly, “Help me, my arm is broken,” and “Call a paramedic.”

Gonzalez’s daughter, Leslie Gonzalez, said her father was “struck by an unmarked vehicle of federal agents while riding his E-Bike.” He was then tased twice and pinned to the ground, according to her description on a GoFundMe page created to help with her father’s medical expenses.

“ICE agents brutally attacked and broke the arm of a North Long Beach resident and U.S. citizen,” Garcia, whose district includes Long Beach and parts of Orange County, wrote in a statement Sunday posted to X. “The videos are horrific and should concern not just our community but the country.”

Long Beach police said in a statement Monday to MS NOW that officers arrived after receiving a request for emergency assistance from the ICE officers due to “vehicle vandalism taking place and a subject in need of medical aid.”

According to police, officers saw “a large group disturbance involving the ICE agents” and a man in handcuffs who was bleeding.

“First responders from the Long Beach Fire Department took the man to a nearby fire station,” according to the statement. There, Gonzalez’s handcuffs were removed, and he was taken to a hospital.

ICE and the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to MS NOW’s requests for comment Monday.

Police officers cleared a crowd of protesters who had gathered near the scene Sunday.

Gonzalez is believed to have been one of several community members who called 911 when he “saw a circumstance escalating,” Long Beach Mayor Rex Richardson told CNN in a statement Sunday.

More articles

“When the police arrived, we know that he was detained. He was on a curb. He was injured,” Richardson said.

The incident drew outcry over the federal agency’s frequent use of force, which has often turned violent.

In a statement released on social media, Richardson said, “ICE doesn’t belong in our city and this activity undermines community safety and public trust.”

The situation involving Gonzalez is among the latest in a series of violent incidents and high-profile killings that have roiled the federal immigration agency. An ICE agent was placed on leave earlier this month after striking an undocumented immigrant with his vehicle in Houston.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta filed a lawsuit on Oct. 15 alleging ICE agents were unconstitutionally taking people into custody near state courthouses. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani demanded ICE end its operations in the city after an agent shot and wounded a Dominican man earlier this month while trying to arrest him as his 5-year-old child sat in the backseat.

Scores of high-profile national Democrats have demanded that the immigration agency be abolished in the wake of the deadly shootings of two U.S. citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, by federal immigration agents in Minneapolis earlier this year.

“I’m proud of the neighbors who documented and stood up for the family being terrorized by ICE,” Garcia wrote in his statement Sunday. “Donald Trump and his inhumane and illegal deportation machine must be stopped. Long Beach stands with our community and our immigrant families. ICE is not welcome in Long Beach. Abolish ICE.”

text:
The Trump administration is shifting its strategy for building out a nationwide network of immigration detention facilities, and litigators say challengers may have a harder time blocking them from opening under environmental law.

The US Department of Homeland Security is acquiring private prisons and working with contractors to bring previously shuttered facilities online while scaling back efforts to convert commercial warehouse properties into detention centers.

States, local governments, and environmental groups successfully blocked immediate renovations to the warehouses under the National Environmental Policy Act, securing preliminary injunctions and agreements with DHS to compel months-long environmental reviews.

Now, bolstered by a $45 billion detention center allocation from last year’s budget reconciliation bill, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement is signing contracts to reopen dormant private prisons across the country.

By paying for space in an existing incarceration infrastructure, the Trump administration can argue its contract “doesn’t really have any environmental effects, or the environmental effects are a lot smaller,” said Justin Pidot, a law professor at the University of Arizona and former counsel for the White House Council on Environmental Quality.

“It certainly makes NEPA claims more complicated than when it’s the federal agency doing something directly that changes the physical built environment,” Pidot said.

Acquisition Shield

Earlier lawsuits over the warehouses hinged on infrastructure restrictions at the properties ICE acquired. Warehouses built to store commercial goods didn’t have the sewage and water systems to meet the agency’s own standards for detaining hundreds, if not thousands of people, environmental groups and local officials argued in court filings.

The agency has since pivoted to purchasing or leasing what the agency’s bid proposal called “turn-key facilities,” or prison properties with existing beds and security infrastructure. DHS bought prisons operated by CoreCivic and The GEO Group Inc. in California, Minnesota, and Kansas, and now leases a facility in Colorado.

The agreements outline companies maintaining the day-to-day operations of such facilities, a caveat similar to Florida’s role in constructing the detention facility dubbed Alligator Alcatraz, according to Pidot.

The US Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit ultimately ruled DHS didn’t need to prepare a NEPA review for the makeshift detention facility because it was Florida’s decision to put up the funds and construct the center in the first place.

In this kind of contract, “the state or the prison company is on its own building or rebuilding a facility, so any environmental effects from that are not related to the federal decision to enter into a contract,” Pidot said.

Courts will have to examine the timeline of when companies decided to reopen prisons or undergo renovations to determine if the environmental effects of a prison operation are far enough removed from the contracts DHS signed, according to Laurel Jobe, an attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity.

“They’re going to have to really be careful and look really closely at the communications and the directives between, for example, GEO and DHS,” Jobe said.

In a statement, a DHS spokesperson said ICE complies with NEPA, and the agency “maintains a robust, multi-layered compliance program” to promote “contractually obligated detention standards.”

Only one contract has drawn lawsuits so far. Colorado and environmental groups challenged the $500 million five-year contract DHS signed with The GEO Group Inc. to renovate and operate a prison that hasn’t housed anyone for approximately 13 years. The lawsuit alleged the agency should have considered how reopening the facility would nearly double the population of Hudson, Colo., and strain local resources and infrastructure.

“What will be interesting to see is how courts respond is that when you have a facility that has been sitting vacant and has been dormant for the amount of time that these facilities have been empty, you almost reset to zero,” said Carmen Iguina González, deputy director for immigration detention at the ACLU’s national prison project. “For a long time you haven’t had that facility be a burden on the water system or the sewer system or the emergency response system or roads.”

DHS’s legal response is due in federal court Monday. In the statement the agency spokesperson said opposition to the agency adding detention capacity “isn’t about the environment.”

For the outright prison acquisitions, states have a lot less ground to challenge ICE detention expansions or provide oversight for prison conditions, according to Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, a senior fellow at the American Immigration Council.

“The supremacy clause is a very big issue here,” Reichlin-Melnick said, referring to the priority of federal law in the US Constitution.

“States have very limited ability to tell the federal government how to operate facilities that the federal government owns,” he said.

ICE Portfolio

DHS remains close-lipped about its detention strategy and its current holding numbers, according to several immigration advocates, but the agency hasn’t entirely shrugged off its initial warehouse real estate portfolio. Former acting director of ICE Todd Lyons said at a Phoenix border security conference in 2025 that he envisioned the agency running its deportation process like Amazon “Prime, but with human beings,” according to the Arizona Mirror.

The department has told courts it continues environmental reviews for several warehouses, and the latest filings in New Jersey’s lawsuit against the agency suggest one warehouse has been used “in connection with immigration enforcement” in possible violation of a court order. San Antonio filed a NEPA lawsuit last week to compel an environmental review for a proposed detention warehouse in its jurisdiction after ICE awarded a $17 million contract to GardaWorld Federal Services to renovate the property.

According to a Government Accountability Office report issued last month, ICE is selling seven of the 11 warehouses acquired in the last year, a move the auditing agency said has resulted in millions in unnecessary costs.

The same report said ICE hasn’t developed a “comprehensive strategy plan,” and the agency “has not assessed the long-term affordability of facilities it purchased or the risks and benefits of using facilities with high operating costs.”

A 56-year-old Mexican man held at a federal immigration facility in Laredo was found dead in his cell Saturday morning, his daughter and U.S. Rep. Henry Cuellar, D-Laredo, confirmed to The Texas Tribune.

Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias was found unresponsive by staff at the Rio Grande Processing Center during a security check at around 10 a.m. Saturday, Cuellar said. Staff performed CPR and called emergency services.

Andrade-Covarrubias is the seventh person to die while detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Texas this year - the first being Geraldo Lunas Campos, whose death was ruled a homicide by the El Paso Medical Examiner's office in January.

He's also the second to die in an ICE facility in Laredo this year. Felix Alcorta-Rodriguez, a 63-year-old Mexican who was being held at Webb County Detention Center, died on June 19 after being found unresponsive, according to the agency.

GEO Group and officials with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to requests for comment sent Sunday.

Andrade-Covarrubias' daughter, Estefani Andrade, told the Tribune that her family has not yet been contacted by federal agencies. Instead, she said, they heard about his death on Saturday through the Webb County Medical Examiner, which is performing his autopsy.

Estefani Andrade, 29 and a U.S. citizen, said the family is going to visit the detention facility on Monday to get his belongings.

Andrade-Covarrubias lived in Dallas for decades, had three adult children who were all born in the country and worked as a contractor painting apartments and townhomes, his daughter said. He wanted to eventually return to Mexico and had been travelling back and forth to build a house there, his daughter added.

She said her dad was detained in June at the border after coming back from Mexico by bus. She added that during his months in detention, "he lost weight because he didn't look the same as when we were doing, like, the video calls with him."

Cuellar said he planned to visit the facility Sunday afternoon.

"I'll ask the basic questions: What happened?" he said. "What were the conditions? [Was] there medical? Is there anybody ill? I'm gonna talk to the medical folks there."

Estefani Andrade said her dad had a heart condition, along with diabetes and high blood pressure. He had medicine with him when he was detained, but she said staff at the center wouldn't "give him his medications."

She also said her dad was sick at the detention facility. He had a cough - which she said was concerning since he was hospitalized for COVID-19 in 2021 and that took a lasting toll on his health - and told her that he wasn't feeling good. He sought help from the facility's medical staff but he told her that "they would just ignore him."

She said her dad told her that he felt like medical staff at the center was brushing off his concerns, even when he told the staff that he was having trouble breathing and feeling tightness in his chest.

Estefani Andrade said she is now trying to be strong for her mom, who is devastated.

"When she got the news, she wasn't all there," she said. "It's hitting her really hard."

text:
Congressional Democrats sent a letter to Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Monday, urging him to rescind a new policy they say violates the rights of unaccompanied immigrant children and makes them vulnerable to deportation.

Under the policy, unaccompanied minors would be represented in court by HHS lawyers instead of independent attorneys, a change the lawmakers say creates a conflict of interest, given the administration’s desire to deport as many immigrants as possible and the health department’s role in detaining the children.

“The immigration judge works for the Trump administration. So does the prosecutor. Under your plan, so would the child’s lawyer. That is unacceptable,” wrote Sens. Tammy Duckworth and Dick Durbin (Ill.), Elizabeth Warren and Edward Markey (Mass.), Adam Schiff (Calif.), and Ron Wyden (Ore.).

As I reported earlier this month, HHS had quietly announced the creation of a new division, the Unaccompanied Alien Children Legal Representation Division, to perform this legal work. Kennedy’s agency also oversees the Office of Refugee Resettlement, which is responsible for placing kids in shelters after they cross the border alone and deciding when to release them to relatives in the United States.

Under President Trump, ORR is holding kids significantly longer than it had under Biden—about six months on average; it also is sharing information with ICE. “HHS holds these children in custody, decides where they live, and shares information about them and their families with immigration enforcement. HHS cannot also be their lawyer,” the lawmakers wrote.

Federal law gives unaccompanied minors a right to an attorney, and HHS’ own regulations stipulate they should receive a legal orientation from an independent provider. Historically, that’s been done by a network of experienced nonprofits, led most recently by the Acacia Center for Justice. But the Trump administration let the network’s contract expire over the summer. It then awarded the job to Burke Law Group, a small firm with far less experience in these matters, but greater ties to Trump: One of Burke’s co-founders served in the first Trump administration and one of its founding partners works for the second.

Facing backlash, Burke Law Group pulled out. Next, the contract went to Our Rescue, a nonprofit founded by a former ICE agent. A court put that deal on hold after the Acacia Center filed a protest against it. In the meantime, the administration gave a temporary contract to the US Committee for Refugees and Immigrants, whose personnel, according to court filings, often sit silently in court and have only represented 12 children so far; by contrast, the nonprofit network had been representing more than 20,000.

The network’s advocates doubt the government’s lawyers will have their clients’ best interests in mind if they take over the cases. “The idea that HHS, the same agency that’s detaining the children, would be able to provide the kind of child-centered, zealous and trauma-informed, independent legal services that were mandated by Congress is frankly absurd,” says Shaina Aber, the Acacia Center’s executive director. Aber questions whether HHS attorneys would help children who are wrongly detained or abused or mistreated while in government custody.

“It’s a major conflict of interest and ethical concern,” adds Adina Appelbaum, an attorney with the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, part of the nonprofit network.

Some independent attorneys have continued representing kids without pay, but they can’t afford to pick up new cases and say the administration is hampering their work in other ways. For one, immigration judges in the Justice Department are fast-tracking children’s cases, requiring them to attend hearings with little time for counsel to prepare, according to a lawsuit filed this month. “They’re just ordering everybody removed—even good asylum claims where the kids are genuinely going to be killed” if they return to their countries of origin, says Laura Smith, an attorney at the Children’s Legal Center in Illinois.

In recent weeks, the administration has also transferred children’s cases to courts far from where they are living, their attorneys say, thus forcing the children and their lawyers to appear virtually, even when there is courtroom space in the jurisdiction where they are located, where they could otherwise attend in person. Meanwhile, the Department of Homeland Security lawyers seeking to deport the children can often show up at the new location, putting the children at a disadvantage.

Attorney Lauren Fisher Flores, who represents kids at the American Bar Association ProBAR in Texas, says she and a young client logged into one hearing but could not see the judge on the screen, which made it difficult for the child to follow what was happening.

“Part of due process is having to look at the child they’re deporting and explain things to that child, and have the child be able to ask questions,” she says. “When you have a child looking at an empty court room, and you have no real ability for all the parties to be in the same space, it’s contrary to child-friendly best practices, and it means children are just churned through this deportation machine.”

When I reached out to the Executive Office for Immigration Review, the Justice Department office that handles immigration cases, it said it was not “fast-tracking” cases but rather working efficiently, and it defended the virtual hearings. The office “prioritizes the timely completion of all cases and makes scheduling adjustments as needed to ensure cases do not languish,” a spokesperson said. HHS did not respond to my questions about its lawyers representing unaccompanied minors, but told the Associated Press that the lawyers would “give the Department an additional mechanism to provide these children direct legal support while dedicated public servants work around the clock to safely reunify them with their families.”

The senators who sent the letter on Monday aren’t buying it. They are calling on the administration to restore independent counsel for the kids. “Unaccompanied children deserve lawyers whose only loyalty is to them,” they wrote. “We demand that you rescind this harmful policy before a single HHS attorney stands beside a child in immigration court.”

text:
What Happened: A New Mexico Democrat in the House introduced a bill last week that would make it easier for U.S. citizens to sue immigration agents and the federal government over wrongful detentions and arrests.

Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández credited ProPublica’s reporting as the catalyst for the bill, the Justice for Citizens Wrongfully Detained by ICE Act. Earlier this month, we revealed that more than 500 U.S. citizens have been detained in warrantless arrests during the second Trump administration.

Leger Fernández said the legislation would roll back the protections from lawsuits that agents and the federal government currently have. It would also establish a minimum level of compensation for people who win their suits, and extend the statute of limitations for such cases.

The legislation would also take back any unspent Immigration and Customs Enforcement funding from President Donald Trump’s so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

Leger Fernández’s bill was introduced with co-sponsor Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, a New Jersey Democrat.

Why It Matters: It can be difficult to sue federal officers for wrongful arrests or excessive force, or for local prosecutors to bring charges. Federal agents can claim immunity in response to civil lawsuits or to state charges and can move their cases to federal court.

People who accuse immigration agents of wrongdoing can currently only sue in a narrow set of circumstances, and previous Democratic bills aiming to change that have not passed.

Some local prosecutors have announced investigations into the wrongful arrests of U.S. citizens or prosecuted federal agents accused of wrongdoing during immigration enforcement actions.

What They Said: In an interview with ProPublica, Leger Fernández emphasized that accountability could not only address past wrongs, it may also help head them off in the future. “We know that when there are consequences, bad actors start behaving better because they don’t want to face those consequences,” she said.

Without legislation, Leger Fernández said, agents “will continue to violate the law, to violate their own policy, and to violate the Constitution without any consequences.”

Asked about the legislation, the Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, repeated claims that it is not arresting U.S. citizens and defended its immigration operations as “highly targeted.”

Background: The federal government denies that there is any pattern of immigration agents detaining U.S. citizens, but according to ProPublica’s count, more than 100 citizens were held after agents questioned their citizenship. At least 70 children and teens were also detained.
