text:
Women are being forced out of employment through “sham redundancies”, losing shifts and facing hostile work environments after having a baby, according to a report by the Australian Human Rights Commission, which warns parental discrimination remains a major barrier to gender equality.

The commission’s report suggests pregnancy discrimination is more prominent for vulnerable groups, including immigrant and First Nations women, people with disability and LGBTQ+ people. The commission held roundtables with dozens of parents, legal and community advocates when compiling the report.

In one case study detailed in the Balancing Act report, Luisa*, an experienced HR manager in the healthcare industry, was made redundant one month after telling her employer she was pregnant.

“Her employer questioned who would support Luisa after the baby was born, because her family lived overseas,” the report noted.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

“Luisa explained that her husband would take parental leave and that she planned to return to work soon after the birth. Luisa also offered to continue working on a part-time basis, but the redundancy went ahead.”

The sex discrimination commissioner, Anna Cody, said urgent law reform was needed to the sex discrimination act to protect women and families, arguing legislation has not kept pace with a changing society. She said women delayed telling their employers about pregnancies for fear of losing work.

“Frequently, when a woman does tell that she is pregnant … she will experience either performance management, or suddenly – if she’s in insecure work, and we know that migrant women and women targeted by racism are more likely to be an insecure and shift work – then the shifts will dry up,” Cody said.

“The third thing that happens is redundancies – and they are ‘sham redundancies’. They’re not … because the job is no longer required or has been eliminated within the workplace, it’s because they no longer want that woman working in the job because she’s pregnant and is going to leave.”

A 2014 national review by the AHRC found 49% of mothers reported discrimination during pregnancy, parental leave or on their return to work.

Cody said discrimination remained widespread but it was hard to know whether the situation had improved. The commission would push the federal government to fund another survey, she said.

The chief executive of the Parenthood, Georgie Dent, told the national press club in September that another survey was critical.

“It must be reinstated,” she said at the time. “We can’t fix what we’ve stopped counting.”

A 2024 survey of 1,048 parent workers by the University of South Australia found 89% reported discrimination during pregnancy, 85% reported experiencing discrimination while on parental leave and 92% reported discrimination when returning to work.

The number of complaints to the human rights commission has increased from 52 in 2023 to 71 in 2025. Cody said complaints to the Fair Work Commission were higher but many parents didn’t report discrimination.

“If you make the loss of a job look like a redundancy, the employer is the one who has all the evidence to show whether or not the job has actually disappeared, and yet it’s the complainant, it’s the woman, who has the responsibility, that burden, of bringing a complaint,” Cody said.

“We know that when women are having their child, or are pregnant, that’s a really vulnerable time. And so then to put on top of that, ‘Now it’s your responsibility to make a complaint to either the Fair Work Commission or to the Australian Human Rights Commission,’ sometimes that’s just too much.”

The AHRC takes up to a year to allocate a conciliator after a complaint is lodged, meaning there is a backlog of cases.

The commission’s report, to be released this week, found some parents were given less responsibility at work after the birth of a child. Others were given fewer shifts or no opportunity for development.

New parents faced difficulty asking for flexibility and safe arrangements for breastfeeding.

Another case study, Michelle, told the AHRC she lost her job after asking to work longer shifts rather than multiple shorter shifts to care for her two young children and terminally ill father.

“Her workplace responded to her request by no longer offering her any shifts and dismissed her from her role,” the report wrote.

Meanwhile, Emily told the commission she was discouraged from taking lactation breaks while employed at a tech start-up despite its clean, accessible and secure breastfeeding area.

“She was expected to work uninterrupted, long hours and was unable to take her lactation breaks. Despite the available space and policies, the culture and attitudes in her workplace made Emily feel unsupported and led her to stop breastfeeding her child earlier than she wanted to.”

*Name changed by human rights commission in its report

title: Homan says investigators have 'strong case' against Ilhan Omar | Minnesota
authors: Elyse S. Apel, Elyse Apel, The Center Square
description: (The Center Square) – White House border czar Tom Homan said over the weekend that federal investigators have a “strong case” against U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar.
text:
Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., at a town hall in Las Vegas, Feb. 9, 2020. Photo: Gage Skidmore / Flickr / CC BY-SA 2.0 / Cropped from Original

(The Center Square) – White House border czar Tom Homan said over the weekend that federal investigators have a “strong case” against U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar.

These comments come less than a week after Homeland Security Investigations searched the Minnesota Democrat’s Washington, D.C., home. Reports have linked the search to an investigation into the circumstances surrounding her naturalization as a U.S. citizen.

In an interview on Saturday, Homan addressed whether Omar could face legal consequences.

“I’m not going to get ahead of the bureau,” Homan said. “We will let the evidence lead where it leads. But she will be held to the same standards you and I are held. If she violated law, then she will be held accountable.”

When asked what the investigation is examining and whether it extends beyond potential immigration fraud, Homan said he “knows things” but directed the question to the FBI.

The FBI did not respond to a request for comment from The Center Square.

Over the weekend, former President Barack Obama joined the many Democrats and civil rights groups condemning the raid.

“It is a basic principle of American democracy that the government can’t selectively target individuals simply because of their political beliefs or what they say,” Obama said in a social media post on Sunday. “But that’s exactly what the Trump Administration is doing to Congresswoman Ilhan Omar of Minnesota.”

The Democrat called claims regarding Omar’s immigration status “unsubstantiated,” also stating that this investigation is because the Trump administration is “actively trying to deport” Omar.

“The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president,” Obama said. “The fact that any president, or any administration, is willing to engage in such transparent efforts to intimidate someone should outrage all Americans.”

Federal officials searched Omar’s home early Monday morning, according to a statement the U.S. Department of Justice provided The Center Square.

“Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice,” said a spokesperson. “This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation.”

That same spokesperson declined to comment further on “investigations.”

Attorneys for Omar have demanded that items—including her phone—taken during the raid be returned to the congresswoman, stating its seizure was “neither justified nor lawful,” according to reports . Members of her family are among more than a dozen people who have been subpoenaed by a grand jury.

The raid came just a month after Homan confirmed that Omar is actively under investigation by DHS.

Omar, who immigrated to the United States in 1995, has faced scrutiny for years over the circumstances surrounding her naturalization as a citizen.

In September, Homan refused to reveal many details regarding the “ongoing criminal investigation,” besides that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement are the ones conducting it.

Since the raid, other federal officials have joined Homan in confirming the case is “strong,” adding that this is not a politically-motivated prosecution.

“We try to let the law follow the facts, rather than creating facts just to prosecute people we don’t like,” Vance said last week. “I do know there are some serious allegations against Ilhan Omar . . . If there's a real case there, we're going to follow the facts.”

The scrutiny includes longstanding allegations that Omar married her brother to facilitate immigration fraud. Omar denied the allegations in 2016, calling them “disgusting lies.”

In December, Omar called an effort to examine records pertaining to her immigration “sick.”

“I have no response because I don’t know what they'll be investigating,” Omar told a reporter. She added that investigators would “absolutely not” find anything.

According to federal officials, the investigation has been ongoing for some months.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin also discussed the issue in September, alleging that they’ve already determined that she married her brother.

“Something’s going to happen,” Mullin said. “We know that she married her brother to try to bring him to the United States. We know he now lives in London.”

Mullin also threw out the prospect of deportation, which would first require denaturalization.

“There may be more to this, the whole family migration and possibly some illegal activity for them to come to the United States to begin with,” Mullin said. “If we can prove it, that you shouldn’t have been here in the first place, we will deport you.”

Omar, who represents Minnesota’s 5th Congressional District, has served in Congress since 2019. She addressed the investigation last week.

“Thank you to everyone who stood with me over the years,” Omar said in a post on her personal social media. “It’s been a scary journey but I have always been grounded in my work and ability to provide exemplary service to my constituents.”

Omar added that she has felt targeted.

“Trump and his administration have been after me since I arrived in Congress,” she said. “I have always stood up to him and that will never change. The pedophile protector will never silence me.”

Elyse Apel, a graduate of Hillsdale College, is a reporter for The Center Square covering Minnesota and Michigan. Her work has appeared in a range of national outlets, including the Washington Examiner , The American Spectator , and The Daily Wire .

WASHINGTON – The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) released the following statement announcing that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has arrested more than 100 gang members in less than a week, including members of gangs such as MS-13 and Tren de Aragua (TDA).

From October 4 to October 10, ICE arrested 131 gang-affiliated individuals, including 129 arrests by ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) and two arrests by ICE Homeland Security Investigations (HSI). Among those arrested were 22 affiliates of MS-13 and 13 affiliates of TDA.

Since President Donald J. Trump returned to office on January 20, 2025, ICE has made 12,018 gang-related administrative arrests. This includes 1,965 MS-13 affiliates and 1,553 TDA affiliates.

“In less than a week, the brave patriots of ICE have arrested more than 100 gang members across the country, including members of MS-13 and Tren de Aragua,” said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. “The best that America has to offer are on the frontlines every day to ensure that the worst of humanity cannot threaten or harm innocent Americans. Under President Trump’s leadership, we are smashing the gangs and cartels, making it impossible for them to do business in America, and removing their members from our country. Arresting and deporting illegal aliens, especially gang members, is how we make America safe again.”

Among the gang members arrested in recent days are:

Image

Gustavo Adolfo Flores-Ramirez, an illegal alien from El Salvador and MS-13 member, arrested by ICE ERO in Las Vegas on October 14. He is wanted in his home country for charges of aggravated homicide, aggravated femicide, rape of a minor or incapacitated person, illegal or irresponsible handling, carrying, or possession of firearms, illicit grouping, and crimes involving public peace. Flores-Ramirez first illegally entered the United States at an unknown date and location, and was arrested by the U.S. Border Patrol in September 2021 and deported to Mexico. He then illegally re-entered the country – a felony – at an unknown date and location.

Image

Perez-Arrias illegally entered the United States through Texas in October 2023 and was arrested by the U.S. Border Patrol. He was then RELEASED into the country by the Biden Administration.

Image

Emerson Jossiel Calderon-Hernandez, an illegal alien from El Salvador and MS-13 member, arrested by ICE Washington D.C. on October 13. His criminal history includes a conviction for second-degree assault and arrests for attempted first-degree murder, attempted second-degree murder, armed robbery, first-degree assault, reckless endangerment, and false imprisonment. Calderon-Hernandez illegally entered the United States through Texas in August 2012 and was arrested by the U.S. Border Patrol. He was then RELEASED into the country by the Obama Administration.

On October 13, HSI Denver and ERO Denver arrested a 14-year-old illegal alien from Venezuela who is associated with Los Piratas Gang, a faction of Tren de Aragua, in Denver, Colorado. At the time of his arrest, he unlawfully had a Glock 48 pistol in his possession. The suspect is currently facing charges of first-degree murder – criminal attempt with extreme indifference, first-degree assault with extreme indifference, first-degree kidnapping, aggravated criminal extortion, illegal discharge of a weapon, and conspiracy.

SAN ANTONIO – Federal prosecutors in the Western District of Texas filed 476 new immigration and immigration-related criminal cases from October 2 through October 15, announced U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons. Charges were brought against alien smugglers and illegal aliens with past convictions for violent crimes, thefts, numerous DWIs, and multiple prior removals.

Among the new cases, in Austin, Alexi Tellez-Gonzalez, was charged with illegal re-entry. He has prior convictions for theft, burglary of a building, evading arrest, possession of marijuana, DWI, and assault causing bodily injury.

Hector Castro-Lopez, an illegal alien from Mexico, was also charged with illegal re-entry for the second time. Castro-Lopez has prior convictions for failure to identify and assault family violence. He has also twice been convicted of violating a protective order and burglary of a habitation.

Gerardo Torres-Sanchez was found in the Travis County Jail and identified as an illegal alien from Mexico. Torres-Sanchez has been deported 11 times and has five convictions for illegal re-entry.

Illegal alien from Mexico Raul Reyes-Hernandez aka Aurelio Reyes-Hernandez was found in the Washington County Jail in Brenham. Reyes-Hernandez was convicted in 2023 for alien smuggling and money laundering. He’s now charged with illegal re-entry.

Gutierres-Cruz has been deported a total of seven times and has multiple prior convictions, including driving without a license and possession of cocaine.

Amaurys Gutierrez-Nunez, an illegal alien from Cuba, was arrested near Eagle Pass and charged with illegal re-entry. Gutierrez-Nunez was previously deported for the first time in July 2025 but has an extensive criminal record that includes two convictions for grand theft, multiple petty theft convictions, resisting an officer, and driving with a suspended license.

Illegal alien from Mexico Julian Garcia-Soto was arrested near Carrizo Springs and charged with illegal re-entry. Garcia-Soto has been previously removed from the U.S. three times and has three DUI convictions, along with a conviction for possession of a controlled substance, and for obstructing a public officer.

Omar Alberto Sanchez-Briones, an illegal alien from Honduras, is charged with illegal re-entry following his arrest near Eagle Pass. Sanchez-Briones was convicted in California earlier this year of his third burglary charge and one battery count. He’s been deported twice, the last being in May 2025 through Phoenix, Arizona.

Illegal alien from Mexico Jose Miguel Aguilar aka Miguel Angel Aguilar Bustillo was arrested near Comstock after just being removed from the U.S. on Sept. 11 through Harlingen. Aguilar has been previously convicted of bringing in and harboring aliens, unlawful possession of a weapon by a felon, failure to identify, and assault causing bodily injury to a family member. He now faces a charge of illegal re-entry.

Illegal alien from Honduras Jose Luis Masias-Milla was arrested near Eagle Pass and charged with illegal reentry. He was deported for the first time on May 20 through Harlingen but has two DWI convictions and a conviction for unlawful carrying of a weapon on alcohol premises.

Luis Alberto Guajardo, an illegal alien from Mexico, was arrested near Eagle Pass and faces his second illegal re-entry charge. He’s been deported from the U.S. five times, the last being in August 2022, and has been convicted of three DWIs as well as making a terroristic threat against a public servant and possession of a controlled substance.

In San Antonio, Melvin Acosta-Martinez was encountered at the Bexar County Jail after he was arrested for theft of property greater than $30,000 and less than $150,000, according to a criminal complaint filed on Oct. 9. Acosta-Martinez is an illegal alien from Honduras whose criminal record includes a conviction for assaulting a federal officer, which resulted in a 237-day prison sentence. He has also been previously convicted of a DWI and illegal re-entry. He now faces his second illegal re-entry charge.

These cases were referred or supported by federal law enforcement partners, including ICE, U.S. Border Patrol, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), the FBI, the U.S. Marshals Service (USMS), and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), with additional assistance from state and local law enforcement partners.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Texas comprises 68 counties located in the central and western areas of Texas, encompasses nearly 93,000 square miles and an estimated population of 7.6 million people. The district includes three of the five largest cities in Texas—San Antonio, Austin and El Paso—and shares 660 miles of common border with the Republic of Mexico.

Indictments and criminal complaints are merely allegations and all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

These cases are part of Operation Take Back America a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

text:
The Trump administration will keep deportation protections in place covering more than a 100,000 Ukrainians in the US.

Temporary Protected Status designations were set to expire Monday for both Ukraine and Sudan. But a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said announcements for both countries “will be made at the appropriate time.”

Until then, TPS protections for Ukrainians and another 2,000 people from Sudan will remain in place. The continuation of TPS designations was first reported by CBS.

The Department of Homeland Security first designated Ukraine for Temporary Protected Status in 2022 following a Russian invasion of the country. More than four years later, a war that’s led 6.7 million people to flee the country continues.

An armed conflict in Sudan has also created a humanitarian crisis, displacing 11.4 million people.

The TPS program allows foreign nationals to remain in the US for up to 18 months when circumstances such as armed conflict in their home country prevent a safe return. TPS holders are also eligible for work permits and have filled jobs in the restaurant, construction, and healthcare fields.

Dismantling the program has been a key piece of the administration’s larger mass deportation agenda. DHS has terminated TPS designations covering nearly a million people from 13 nations so far, an effort aided by a US Supreme Court decision in June finding those decisions aren’t subject to judicial review.

TPS protections for 170,000 Salvadorans were set to expire Sept. 9., but DHS made no formal announcement. It instead posted an update to its website stating that an announcement “will be made at the appropriate time.”

title: College options shrink for undocumented students as Trump targets higher education
authors: Lily Altavena, Michael Elsen-Rooney, Alex Nitkin, Illinois Answers Project, Bri Hatch, Molly DeVore, Block Club Chicago, NaBeela Washington, www.chalkbeat.org, lily-altavena

text:
Did you know search engines like Google are changing the way you see news? Keep Chalkbeat’s valuable education coverage at the top of your feeds by clicking here and checking the box next to our name.

In the thick of college application season, some undocumented students are discovering they’ve lost eligibility for in-state tuition.

Other students’ eligibility for lower tuition at state colleges and universities may be up in the air as litigation winds through federal court. And in Florida, state authorities have banned them from enrolling in a public college or university at all.

“It has been a little bit bleak and disappointing,” said Martinez, a college counselor in north Texas, one of the states that has backtracked on in-state tuition for undocumented students. (Chalkbeat is only using her last name because she is in the process of gaining citizenship and concerned about immigration enforcement.)

While children have a right to a public K-12 education in the U.S. regardless of their immigration status, undocumented students’ access to higher education is shrinking due to actions by states and the federal government. The consequences extend beyond college campuses. The changes not only create confusion for high schoolers, but some worry they might discourage more undocumented students from even finishing high school due to pessimism about their long-term prospects.

Over two decades, states created policies that allowed graduates of their high schools who were undocumented to pay the same lower college tuition as their classmates who were U.S. citizens. The federal government also gave young people who arrived as children a pathway to work authorization and protection from deportation through the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, commonly known as DACA.

Now, the Trump administration is trying to close those doors. It has sued two dozen states to end in-state tuition policies and pressured states to end access to career and technical education for undocumented students. Students, meanwhile, cannot currently get DACA status amid ongoing legal challenges.

Immigration hardliners argue that granting benefits like in-state tuition to undocumented students unfairly displaces students who are citizens from attending state universities.

“It’s easy to put a human face on that illegal alien student … but for most middle class families, a seat at a state university is the only real option,” said Ira Mehlman, media director of the Federation for American Immigration Reform, which has filed briefs in support of the federal government’s lawsuits.

But supporters of immigrant students — including an estimated 525,000 undocumented students enrolled in U.S. colleges — say they are as deserving as citizens, and many have received much of their education in the states where they would receive the in-state benefit.

“I don’t think anybody was expecting the federal government to sue every single state in such a short period of time,” said Diego Sánchez, vice president of policy and strategy for the President’s Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration. “We’re seeing the pathway from high school into college and the workforce is narrowing in different ways.”

New political pressure limits access to higher education

Policies giving undocumented students access to in-state tuition started under Republican state leadership.

In 2001 under Gov. Rick Perry, Texas granted the benefit to undocumented students who had lived in Texas for at least three years. Other states passed similar legislation. Perry defended that policy a decade later when he was a presidential candidate, calling the ethos behind the law the “American way.”

But the second Trump administration has targeted almost every state with a tuition-equity law, at the same time that it’s ramped up immigration enforcement activity.

Challenges to those policies in other states have yielded mixed results this year. But when the Department of Justice sued Texas in June 2025 to overturn its in-state tuition policy, state Attorney General Ken Paxton agreed to end it instead of going to court. Kansas, Kentucky, and Nebraska officials also agreed to ending their policies.

The impact on tens of thousands of Texas students and institutions serving them was swift and confusing, said Will Davies, director of policy and research at Breakthrough Central Texas, a college access nonprofit that works directly with students.

“Most of these kids grew up here,” he said. “They went to high school under the impression that if they, like their peers, got good grades and had a high rank in their high school, they were going to have affordable and high quality post-secondary options to pursue, and for a lot of those people, that promise was broken pretty much immediately.”

In addition, universities didn’t have clear direction for how to enforce the change, he said.

Conservatives have targeted other postsecondary education opportunities. Florida prohibited undocumented students from certain career-technical education programs in September. A Chalkbeat review found that Iowa, Virginia, and Georgia have taken steps to restrict undocumented students’ access to dual enrollment courses and career-technical education programs. Virginia later abandoned the policy.

While undocumented students have a right to a public education under the U.S. Supreme Court’s Plyler v. Doe ruling, seeing postsecondary doors close may send them a discouraging message about their prospects, said Julie Sugarman, associate director for K-12 research with the Migration Policy Institute.

“When students don’t feel like they see a future, they don’t end up staying in high school,” she said.

Counselor tells students to seek an education ‘sidequest’

In states where in-state tuition policies for undocumented students have recently ended, counselors have a delicate balance to strike when talking to students about their options.

Martinez said she often presents students with the idea of a “sidequest” if the degree they want might be too difficult or expensive to obtain due to their immigration status.

For example, a student who wants to go into nursing might think about pursuing a business degree first to help run a family business, because being a nurse might require a work permit in the future.

She said she tells students, “Life is happening. What are ways that you can grow as a person and develop yourself as a professional, so you can still make that one step forward for the career that you want?”

Their reactions are mixed, Martinez said. Some begin to brainstorm immediately. Others struggle to process the idea when she first raises it.

Davies of Breakthrough Central Texas said his organization has seen a number of students delay enrolling due to Texas’ policy change. He directs students to seek out aid and scholarships, some of which are tailored to help immigrant students. While some organizations have stepped in to try to narrow funding gaps, “it’s not enough to really address the broader problem.”

While financial barriers are significant for students, the current political climate is ultimately “a moment in time” — and a higher education is still worth pursuing, said Hyein Lee, chief operating officer of thedream.us, one of the largest scholarship funds for undocumented students.

“We also want to help our students understand and think more long term about how investing in their education now will pay dividends in the long term, even if it may not seem like this,” she said.

title: How the Fallout From an ICE Raid in Idaho Could Expand - TIME
description:
Yet on paper, this wasn’t an immigration raid at all.
The only warrant for the Wilder raid was secured by the FBI.
Twelve months later, the Wilder raid is at the center of a court fight that could shape ICE operations around the country.
Advocates argue that in Idaho, ICE unlawfully piggybacked on an FBI operation, rather than securing their own warrant, as they would be expected to do on this type of operation.
“Some community members don't even want to think about this anymore,” says Leo Morales, the executive director of the ACLU Idaho.
text:
Within minutes, the festival grounds descended into chaos. Backed by armored trucks and snipers, more than 200 members of law enforcement stormed the grounds, some shot rubber bullets into the crowd and hurled flash-bang grenades into vehicles where people had fled to hide. Hundreds of people, including teens as young as 14, were detained and zip-tied.

When it was all over, federal authorities had arrested 105 people for alleged immigration violations. Yet on paper, this wasn’t an immigration raid at all. The only warrant for the Wilder raid was secured by the FBI. Its target: the owner of the track and four others for alleged unlicensed gambling.

Twelve months later, the Wilder raid is at the center of a court fight that could shape ICE operations around the country. Advocates argue that in Idaho, ICE unlawfully piggybacked on an FBI operation, rather than securing their own warrant, as they would be expected to do on this type of operation. A lawsuit brought forth by the ACLU argues that federal authorities violated the Fourth Amendment, which protects against unreasonable searches and seizures, by using an unrelated search warrant as a “cover to go fishing for immigration arrests.”

Trump Administration officials insist that the arrests made that day were lawful. “The facts haven’t changed: ICE helped dismantle an illegal horse-racing, animal fighting, and a gambling enterprise operation out of a property known as La Cathedral Arena in Wilder, Idaho,” a DHS spokesperson told TIME. Idaho Gov. Brad Little also defended the raid, saying in a statement at the time that it is “common practice” to detain others present while processing the scene.

The ACLU and some of the families involved in the case released a documentary online on Monday called Wild Raids in which they discuss the raid’s impact, and why the legal challenge matters beyond people in Wilder.

“Some community members don't even want to think about this anymore,” says Leo Morales, the executive director of the ACLU Idaho. “But there are also folks who are also realizing how critical it is to be able to push back, to organize and to demand fairness and justice.”

Juana Rodriguez attended the festival with her three-year-old son. Despite both of them being U.S. citizens, they were zip-tied and detained for hours following the raid. Like many others who were detained, she described not being given access to food or water.

“For the longest time, my son begged me for food. He begged me for water,” Rodriguez says. She repeatedly asked the officers she could be untied so that she could feed and console her crying son, she says, but was rebuffed. “I wish I could have done more in the moment, but I couldn't.”

Detainees were eventually taken into a tent and questioned by ICE agents about their immigration status. Among the 105 people who were ultimately arrested, 75 are believed to have been deported to their home countries, according to local media, and 26 were released from ICE custody after their lawyers filed habeas corpus petitions. The whereabouts of the remaining four people are unclear. ICE did not provide an update on their case status.

A year later, Rodriguez says she is still scared to go to Latino cultural and other public events because of what happened at La Catedral. She also has nightmares about ICE officers taking her child away from her.

The ACLU filed a class-action complaint in February, charging that a variety of local, state and federal agencies violated the constitutional rights of those at the festival. Both sides are now waiting for a judge to rule on a motion by ICE and other agencies to dismiss, in which it argued that federal and state law enforcement are protected by qualified immunity, a longstanding legal doctrine when executing a federal warrant.

The Wilder case is one of multiple lawsuits the Trump Administration is fighting over its immigration enforcement operations. In Minnesota, none of the federal agents involved in the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti have been criminally charged, but a string of civil lawsuits is beginning to emerge. Earlier this month, the family of Renee Good, who was killed last January by a federal agent during the immigration enforcement surge in Minnesota, filed a pair of civil lawsuits against the federal government, according to their legal representative. Marimar Martinez, a U.S. citizen who was shot by a Border Patrol agent during a confrontation on a Chicago street last year, has also filed a lawsuit against the federal government.

Anyone seeking to hold federal agents accountable must be prepared for a long wait, says Borchetta. A lawsuit against the federal government can’t even be filed unless it’s been six months since a complainant filed a claim for compensation and the issue remains unresolved.

“If a federal employee is driving their car negligently on the job and hits you with their car, you can bring a claim for them for that negligence,” Borchetta says. “It also applies where an ICE agent is mistreating you or causing you harm.”

The Friends of Minidoka nonprofit will host its 2026 symposium, which will feature a film screening, legal discussion and lecture, “to consider the enduring importance of due process, equal protection, and civic engagement in protecting our civil liberties and strengthening democracy,” according to a press release from the organization.

The 2026 Civil Liberties Symposium, titled Law, Civil Liberties, and the Continuing Pursuit of Justice: From Wayne Collins to Today, will examine how “the unjust incarceration of Japanese Americans during World War II continues to inform contemporary debates surrounding immigration, detention, national security, and constitutional rights,” the press release said.

The series begins Thursday with a screening of “Wayne Collins: One Fighting Irishman,” a 30-minute documentary about the San Francisco attorney who spent more than two decades defending Japanese Americans who renounced their U.S. citizenship under duress while imprisoned at the Tule Lake Segregation Center during World War II.

The screening will be followed by a discussion with Emily Croston, staff attorney with the ACLU of Idaho, and Wendy Olson, former U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho and chairwoman of the Idaho State Bar’s Diversity Section.

On Nov. 5, the group will host its 2026 distinguished lecture: “Mass Deportation, Detention, and ICE: How We Got Here and What We Can Do,” presented by Kari Hong, the director of the Immigration Law Clinic at the University of Idaho College of Law.

Drawing on her experience as an immigration attorney, public interest lawyer, and legal scholar, Hong will examine the history and present-day realities of immigration enforcement and detention, along with opportunities to protect the rights of affected individuals. The lecture will be followed by a moderated Q&A session with the audience.

The symposium concludes Dec. 8 with an online presentation of Hong’s distinguished lecture, offering another opportunity for community members to participate and engage with these issues.

“History reminds us that civil liberties can be threatened when fear and claims of national security are used to justify the erosion of constitutional protections,” said Robyn Achilles, executive director of Friends of Minidoka. “By bringing historical perspectives into conversation with today’s legal challenges, the Civil Liberties Symposium creates opportunities for our community to learn, ask difficult questions, and consider our shared responsibility to uphold justice.”

All events are free and open to the public, with registration required. For event details and registration information, go to minidoka.org/2026-civil- liberties .



Friends of Minidoka worked with the University of Idaho College of Law, the ACLU of Idaho, Idaho State Bar Diversity Section, Boise State University, Boise State Public Radio, Boise Valley Japanese American Citizens League, and LED, to organize the symposium.

text:
More people are turning to the ACT Human Rights Commission for help, as they record a 21 per cent increase in complaints lodged last financial year.

The commission received 2,068 complaints in 2025-2026, and more than 2,100 enquiries.

Complaints about abuse, neglect and mistreatment of older people and people with a disability rose by a third, while complaints from Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people increased by 50 per cent.

"Unfortunately, some of the narratives in the community about vilification and racism are contributing to people wanting to bring more complaints," Karen Toohey, the Discrimination, Health Services, Disability and Community Services Commissioner, said.

"People [are] aware … that they don't have to take those behaviours, which we think is great.

Rise in vilification and racism complaints

The commission investigated 201 complaints from or on behalf of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, representing 10 per cent of the total number of complaints received last financial year.

"We do know from the parliamentary inquiry federally into violence and racism against Aboriginal people that, since the [Voice] referendum in particular, people are saying that they have experienced an increase in vilification and racism," Ms Toohey said.

Winnunga Nimmityjah Aboriginal Health and Community Services CEO Julie Tongs agrees.

But Ms Tongs said that while more First Nations people had been inclined to make a formal complaint to the commission, they were the ones who knew "how to navigate the system".

"There's still a gross under-representation from what I hear on the ground and what I see," she said.

"There are people out there that're frightened to report because sometimes when you report, if it's to do with maybe homelessness or housing or some sort of discrimination, then they're worried that then child protection or other services are going to get involved.

Abuse, neglect of vulnerable people

More than 150 vulnerable people complaints were made to the commission during the last financial year — a figure up 33 per cent on the previous financial year.

Ms Toohey is one of four commissioners who advocate for vulnerable people and help them resolve complaints across a broad range of service areas including health, older people, children and young people, disability and victims of crime.

She's seen complaints about disability services, aged care services, "but it's also about elder abuse within families or abuse of people with disabilities within their families".

"What we try and do is build community confidence that if [people] have an issue, it doesn't need to be about world peace."

Carers ACT Acting CEO Victoria Dolphin said she believed there were several elements at play when it came to the abuse and neglect of elderly people and people with disabilities, which could contribute to the rise in complaints.

"We know that carers are the people that are the backstop when systems fail, and they are holding up the pieces in the air, so to speak, in relation to delivering care to people with needs," Ms Dolphin said.

Disability discrimination complaints 'concerning'

Advocacy for Inclusion CEO Nicolas Lawler said the "concerning" increase in disability discrimination complaints "needs to be taken seriously".

"The ACT has strong human rights protections, and the Human Rights Commission plays an important role in helping people exercise those rights," Mr Lawler said.

"People with disability should not have to fight to be heard or rely on formal complaints and advocacy simply to have their basic rights respected."

But as more people turn to the commission for help, Human Rights Commissioner Penelope Mathew warned about resourcing.

"The commission should be a human rights resource for both the public service and the community, but the demand for information and support cannot be met given the current levels of staffing for the human rights team," Ms Mathew wrote in the annual report.

title: It wouldn't be easy to strip Rep. Ilhan Omar of her citizenship, legal experts say - CBS 58
description:

“She could help to MAKE SOMALIA GREAT AGAIN!” Omar has not been charged with a crime, and the Justice Department has not revealed any evidence against her.
But the path for the federal government to attempt denaturalization wouldn’t be an easy one, legal experts told CNN.
Between 2008 and 2024, 116 civil denaturalization lawsuits were filed, according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, an average of less than seven cases a year.
A case against Omar Omar has been under criminal investigations in recent years, including before Trump took office last year.
text:
By Michael Williams, Katelyn Polantz

(CNN) — The search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington, DC, home by federal law enforcement earlier this week was an extraordinary legal step taken against a sitting congresswoman who is facing reelection.

The Justice Department pushed for an unusually aggressive search of Omar’s home while the congresswoman has said she believes the administration is ultimately seeking to intimidate her.

The government has not yet indicated it will take steps to attempt to strip Omar of her citizenship. But the president himself has said he’d like to see Omar sent to Somalia.

“Fake “Congresswoman” Illhan Omar, a constant complainer who hates the USA, knows everything there is to know. She should be in jail, or even a worse punishment, sent back to Somalia, considered one of the absolutely worst countries in the World,” President Donald Trump posted on Truth social earlier this year. “She could help to MAKE SOMALIA GREAT AGAIN!”

Omar has not been charged with a crime, and the Justice Department has not revealed any evidence against her.

But the path for the federal government to attempt denaturalization wouldn’t be an easy one, legal experts told CNN.

Citizenship has long been considered “a kind of a safe harbor,” said Daniel Kanstroom, a Boston College professor who teaches immigration law. “It’s hard to get, but once you get it, the standard for the government to take it away is really, really high.”

Challenges ahead

Sources told CNN the search was related to an immigration-fraud probe investigating whether Omar’s father lied about her age when she obtained her citizenship in 2000.

Omar maintains she was born in Somalia in 1982 and spent the first years of her life in that country as it was embroiled in a deadly civil war. She has said she came to the US around age 12, and about five years later, she became a US citizen.

The federal investigators are looking at whether Omar lied about her age of 17 when she was applying for citizenship, and potentially whether that may have been a false statement repeated in recent years that could be prosecuted now.

Denaturalization, the process of stripping a naturalized citizen of their citizenship, is an arduous and, until recently, relatively rare process typically reserved for extraordinary lies or omissions made during the naturalization process.

It was used frequently to strip the US citizenships of former Nazis who lied about their wartime activities — the Department of Justice had a unit called the Office of Special Investigations that was formed specifically for this purpose — and has also been used against naturalized members of terrorist and other criminal organizations.

Since Trump took office last year, the Justice Department has said it would prioritize some denaturalization proceedings, which take place as lawsuits filed against citizens in federal court.

Between 2008 and June 12, 2026, 166 denaturalization complaints were filed, according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, an annual average of less than 10, and a miniscule fraction compared to the hundreds of thousands of people who became newly naturalized every year.

Under recent previous administrations, civil denaturalization cases were relatively rare. Between 2008 and 2024, 116 civil denaturalization lawsuits were filed, according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, an average of less than seven cases a year.

But the second Trump administration has significantly ramped up those numbers as part of its efforts to curb immigration, filing more than 160 civil denaturalization cases this year alone as of September 28, according to TRAC’s analysis.

“It’s a significant increase,” said Texas-based attorney Dan Gividen, a former Immigration and Customs Enforcement attorney during the Obama administration who is currently defending about 10 clients from denaturalization.

“For the government to go forward on either a criminal or civil denaturalization back then, the person had to warrant that kind of attention,” Gividen said.

The government could seek to denaturalize someone either through civil proceedings, or by obtaining a criminal conviction for naturalization fraud.

There is no statute of limitations for civil denaturalization proceedings.

The criminal offense, however, is generally subject to a 10-year window where it can be brought after a person becomes a citizen, so it would likely not be applicable in a case against Omar, who obtained her citizenship more than two decades ago.

A case against Omar

Omar has been under criminal investigations in recent years, including before Trump took office last year.

The current federal investigation is looking at whether Omar could have committed immigration fraud, and repeated false statements when filling out government documents, such as a passport, in recent years, and that could be considered a continuation of any suspected fraud.

Further detail of what prosecutors have gathered about Omar’s immigration and government records so far have been presented to a court confidentially and aren’t yet available to the public. However, more than a dozen media organizations and the right-leaning transparency advocacy group Judicial Watch asked a court this week to release more of investigators’ records that supported the search.

While the judge will hear from the Justice Department next week about those transparency requests, the criminal investigation continues.

Federal investigators gaining access to records found in Omar’s DC home is likely to progress slowly, as federal investigators could spend weeks or months trying to obtain some of the congresswoman’s documents.

If Omar were ever to be charged with a crime related to alleged immigration fraud, the Justice Department would have to prove that any misleading statements in immigration documents were made intentionally.

Process that could take years

The question of a possible deportation or denaturalization for Omar would also likely loom far in the future, even if there was evidence found of an immigration fraud crime.

Contested denaturalizations typically take between one to three years to process in district court, not including appeals, said Peter Loblack, an Orlando-based immigration attorney.

Even if a person has their citizenship stripped, deportation is not an immediate given.

A denaturalized citizen would revert to their most recent status — typically, a lawful permanent resident or green card holder — and then the government would have to seek to have them deported through an entirely different proceeding.

That also means that someone who is denaturalized could, theoretically, be renaturalized at a later date and under a different administration.

CNN’s Priscilla Alvarez and Catherine Shoichet contributed to this report.

I’d hoped to begin this article by naming the people who have died at the hands of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents.

But the number is too high for me to name every one of them.

In the first 500 days of Donald Trump’s second term, 52 people died in ICE custody. 52 fathers, mothers, sons and daughters died in detention as of June. 52 people rotted away in detention centers. 52 people showed signs of illness and were denied medical care. 52 people died and had their deaths ignored. 52 people died in silence, and the people responsible faced no consequences.

Since Trump took office, the mortality rate in ICE custody has more than doubled. More people are dying in detention centers than ever before, and in almost every case, there is evidence of delayed care and negligence. Individuals often had worsening symptoms, a history of illnesses or were visibly succumbing to illness, and they didn’t receive the medical care they needed

This is criminal negligence. This is purposeful ignorance. This is illegally ignoring the health of the people you are responsible for.

Soon it won’t be 52 people. It will be 60 or 80 or 100. People are dying because ICE isn’t following the law, and they are facing no repercussions.

It’s not just people dying silently. It’s not just people dying in the dark with no medical reports, no one notifying their families and no one giving them proper care or burial. It’s also public killings.

Since the new age of immigration enforcement began, there have been at least 25 shootings involving ICE agents firing at civilians.

Just over a week ago, an ICE agent fired at a man, Oscar Belgal, with his 5-year-old son in the back seat. Almost a year ago now, ICE shot and killed Renee Good, a US citizen. They then refused to allow medical help through. Weeks later, Alex Perretti was shot and killed while attempting to help another person. They claimed he was brandishing a weapon. A few months ago, ICE shot and killed Johan Durán Guerrero, who was working here legally. They then excused the death, saying that he wasn’t the target of their operation.

So, what justice has been served? In the age of technology, these deaths are videoed, posted and watched by millions. So, what justice has been obtained for the visible deaths? What comfort do the families who must watch their loved ones be shot, receive?

I say such things rhetorically, as I’m sure we all know the answer.

There are fundamental rights written into the Constitution, applicable to all who set foot into this country. There is due process. There is a right to a trial. There is a right to protest. There is a right to no cruel or unusual punishment. There is a right to no detainment without reasonable cause. If these rights are violated, there are consequences. If a death occurs at the hands of law enforcement, there is an investigation. There is justice for those who are treated unfairly.

These rights were written into the foundation of our country to protect us from tyrannical governments. You don’t need to be an expert on American history to know our founding fathers were afraid of this very thing. People being denied their rights has and will always be the great threat to democracy, and that is what President Trump’s administration is doing right now.

There should be consequences for this. We should expect consequences for this. Have we entered such a horrific era of American history that we have forgotten that there should be consequences for murder and corruption?

Every death that has occurred has been brushed off. Every death has been described as self-defense. Every death has been ignored.

These deaths never should have happened. These people should have been protected by the government, not killed by it. Not had their deaths covered up and excused by the state. Not been deprived of the dignity of an investigation into their killers by the same administration that claims to make their country great.

There are medical failings in the detention centers. There are ICE agents watching people die in their cells. There are shootings in the street. There are people dying in this country, documented and undocumented, and there have been no consequences.

This is illegal. This is unconstitutional. This should not be allowed to happen.

What have we become that even the most basic rights are no longer protected? What have we become that there are no trials and no due process? What have we become when government agents can murder someone in broad daylight and face no legal persecution?

A lost cause.

Food inspectors, fire safety officers and their colleagues work every day to protect us all from harm and are already seriously overstretched.

text:
A visit from a food hygiene inspector can make or break a business. A rating of five reassures customers that standards are very good. On the other hand, would you risk eating at a cafe or restaurant that’s rated a one or zero?

Inspections, as a result, are a stressful experience for business owners and their staff. Imagine, then, how much more fraught the process would be if, once they’d finished checking fridges and worktops, inspectors declared: “Right, let’s check your immigration status.”

That scenario is on the cards should Reform win power in Westminster.

As part of its plan to focus “every organ of the British state” on hunting down, detaining and deporting “illegal” migrants, a Reform government led by Nigel Farage would require food hygiene, fire safety, trading standards and many other inspectors to do immigration checks on top of their other duties.

The proposal, announced last week, has been described as “absurd and sinister” by the union Unison and an “intensification of the hostile environment” by the mayor of a London council which, earlier this year, became the first local authority in the UK to refuse to help the Home Office undertake immigration raids.

Reform claims that immigration checks could be “easily” incorporated into inspections undertaken by staff at local authorities and other public bodies, such as the Health and Safety Executive, because they “do not require highly technical qualifications”. Doing so, it estimates, would increase the immigration enforcement capacity by up to 40 times.

PCS, a union that represents UK government workers, told us immigration officers perform a “highly specialised” role that requires “extensive training, detailed knowledge of complex immigration legislation, as well as intel and the ability to make decisions with serious legal and human consequences”.

A spokesperson added: “Reform's suggestion that immigration checks do not require technical expertise and can simply be added to the responsibilities of any public sector inspector fundamentally misunderstands the nature of the work our members perform.

“It also demonstrates a clear disregard for the need for humane, lawful and properly-trained approaches to immigration enforcement.”

Councils would be encouraged to cooperate by receiving a share of fines handed out to those who employ illegal workers. That money would also pay for the recruitment of more inspectors.

Andrea Egan, Unison general secretary, said: “The idea of conscripting council workers to a Trump-style deportation police force is absurd and sinister in equal measure. Food inspectors, fire safety officers and their colleagues work every day to protect us all from harm and are already seriously overstretched.

“Reform’s back-of-a-fag-packet proposals would risk public safety. They’re part of a nasty campaign targeting our migrant friends, neighbours and colleagues. The very people who do so much to keep our public services, and our whole country, running.

“This racist agenda is completely contrary to the values of public service workers, and Unison will continue to oppose it every step of the way.”

Reform says these immigration inspectors would be expected to relay information to a new “Deportation Command” and the “Migrant Identification Centre”.

Council teams including trading standards and licensing officials occasionally take part in joint immigration operations led by the Home Office. Local authorities also share data with the government relating to a person’s right to work (when someone applies for housing or social care support, for example).

However, a growing number of councils, including seven in London, are refusing to cooperate with immigration raids where they legally can. Lewisham was the first to do so, passing a motion to that effect in July.

Mayor of Lewisham Liam Shrivastava said of Reform’s plan: “It is, in many respects, a continuation but intensification of the hostile environment [the name given to policies, aimed at undocumented migrants, introduced by then home secretary Theresa May in 2012] where ordinary workers, whether they’re council officers or teachers, are being made to behave like border guards.

“This sort of enforcement regime creates a climate of fear. Many workers and businesses are going to be terrified. This is obviously going to hit migrant businesses the hardest.”

Shrivastava said the council would resist any attempt to impose such a policy in Lewisham.

“There would be huge legal and practical questions around how you can compel officers to do that – I think we would be very against it,” he added.

Reform’s policy announcement also included plans to effectively end the asylum system for up to five years, and deport thousands of asylum seekers before their appeals to remain in the UK are heard.

text:
We previously wrote about the public inquiries into the proposed expansion of Campsfield and Haslar Immigration Removal Centres. To recap: the Home Office plans to create around 1,000 additional detention spaces, expanding the UK’s detention estate by approximately 40%.

We cannot let this happen, and Right to Remain is challenging this, with all of you.

Thanks to a large number of people who wrote to oppose the Campsfield planning application, there is now an public inquiry into this matter, and we will be formally giving evidence as an interested party. Our submission is based on the evidence provided by many of you in our community, especially by people who have first-hand experience of detention – thank you.

We must stand together to stop this expansion plan, as we work towards abolishing detention altogether. We are therefore absolutely delighted that JCWI (the Joint Council of Welfare for Immigrants) and Asylum Matters agreed to be the lead endorsers of Right to Remain submission.

Lavanya Pallapi, Chief Executive of the Joint Council for the Welfare of Immigrants said:

“We unequivocally support Right to Remain’s submission to the inquiry, and oppose the expansion of Campsfield.

Immigration detention is a cruel and inhumane punishment that this and successive governments have used against migrants and people seeking asylum, many of whom have faced horrific and traumatic journeys to seek safety in this country. This expansion is a costly, punitive and unnecessary solution to the government’s aggressive increase in forced removals.

People caged in these detention centres are not able to access the necessary trauma-informed healthcare that they need, leaving them with significantly worse physical and mental health if or when they are able to get out, as well as ruptures to their relationships, housing, education and employment. People detained are often also prevented or restricted from accessing proper legal advice, to which they are legally entitled. Despite this, most people detained are still ultimately released.

People have repeatedly been subject to violence and trauma in these dark prison-like institutions, where they can be held indefinitely, and which have repeatedly been found to systematically violate people’s human rights.

We must seek to invest in and build communities, not cages.”

Lou Calvey, Executive Director of Asylum Matters said:

“1,000 more beds at Haslar and Campsfield means thousands more people suffering completely unnecessarily. It means thousands more people trapped in fear and uncertainty; thousands more families, neighbourhoods and communities torn apart; thousands more people left trying to recover from the trauma of detention.

And, at a time when racist, anti-migrant sentiment is being spread aggressively in the UK, continuing to push for this expansion means our Government giving in to those who want to divide our communities. Expanding immigration detention harms all of us: so we all need to come together to prevent it.

We stand with everyone who has been directly harmed by immigration detention, and we support Right To Remain and all those intervening in the public inquiry against this plan – it’s vital that we all unite against this cruel expansion.”

If your group also would like to endorse our submission, alongside JCWI and Asylum Matters, please contact Ally(at)righttoremain.org.uk. You can find out more information about it here.

text:
Video showing a man being detained by ICE agents in Long Beach is drawing criticism from state and local leaders.

Neighbors say they rushed outside when they heard the commotion, and that's when they saw the man on the ground being held down by agents.

Cellphone video shows a man being detained on the ground by what appears to be ICE agents in North Long Beach Saturday afternoon. However, the video does not show what happened leading up to that moment.

Many neighbors say it was disturbing to watch and allege that the encounter was violent.

"They tased him, and it was just horrible," said Patty Villarrel, who lives in Long Beach.

"They were even kicking him when he was handcuffed on the ground," neighbor Ashley Brust said. "That was kind of crazy. That was kind of traumatic."

The encounter happened near the intersection of Locust Avenue and Ellis Street.

In the video, you can hear the man screaming that his arm is broken and asking for help. Neighbors are also seen in the street demanding federal agents leave the man alone.

The family confirmed to NBC Los Angeles on Sunday that the man is a U.S. citizen.

"I love it, and that’s why we have a community that gets together, and I am very grateful we have a community in North Long Beach," Villarrel said.

Long Beach police say they were requested by the Department of Homeland Security and ICE for assistance due to a vehicle vandalism and a person needing medical aid. When officers arrived, they found the handcuffed man detained by ICE bleeding.

Police say they took the man to a nearby fire station, where they removed the handcuffs, and Long Beach Fire personnel took him to a hospital for treatment.

Long Beach police say they were not involved in any immigration enforcement and did not make any arrests.

Long Beach Mayor Rex Richardson posted his reaction to the incident on social media.

“Our residents shouldn’t be put in these situations," Richardson said. "Families shouldn’t have to live in fear in their own neighborhoods. I’ve asked our city team to verify exactly what happened and to document everything."

Congressman Robert Garcia, who represents Long Beach, also condemned the encounter.

“ICE agents brutally attacked and broke the arm of a North Long Beach resident and U.S. citizen," Garcia said in an X post. :The videos are horrific and should concern not just our community but the country. I’m proud of the neighbors who documented and stood up for the family being terrorized by ICE. Donald Trump and his inhumane and illegal deportation machine must be stopped. Long Beach stands with our community and our immigrant families. ICE is not welcome in Long Beach. Abolish ICE.”

U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli responded to Garcia’s message with the following:

“You’re a sitting member of Congress and you’re encouraging people to obstruct immigration agents enforcing laws enacted by Congress? Shame on you. These incidents would be less common if the targets complied with lawful commands. You’re intentionally fanning the flames and increasing danger for the community and officers. I’m proud of the men and women of law enforcement who risk their lives every day to keep us safe. We will not hesitate to arrest and prosecute anyone who assaults them.”

NBCLA reached out to ICE, DHS and CBP regarding the incident but has not received a response.

text:
A resident of Long Beach, California, was injured during an incident involving Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Saturday, according to federal and local officials.

Ricardo Gonzalez, a former Long Beach city employee, was reportedly found by Long Beach police after he and other community members called 911 after becoming concerned about unmarked vehicles, Long Beach Mayor Rex Richardson told CNN on Sunday.

ICE personnel had requested emergency assistance from the Long Beach Police Department in response to vehicle vandalism and a person in need of medical aid, Long Beach police said in a statement Saturday.

When local officers arrived, they found a man handcuffed and bleeding while being detained by ICE, police said, adding a “large group disturbance” involving the agents was taking place.

“(Gonzalez) called 911 when he saw a circumstance escalating, and so he called and asked for assistance,” Richardson said. “When the police arrived, we know that he was detained. He was on a curb. He was injured.”

It’s not yet known what led up to the circumstances or what occurred before Gonzalez was detained.

A GoFundMe created by Gonzalez’s daughter, Leslie Gonzalez, said he was struck by an unmarked vehicle believed to be driven by federal agents while riding an e-bike.

CNN has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security, the city of Long Beach and Long Beach police for more information.

Videos shared by a witness showed Gonzalez handcuffed and lying on the ground while being held down by an agent wearing a “Police ICE” vest. In one video, the man can be heard yelling repeatedly, “Help me, my arm is broken” and “call a paramedic.”

Richardson, who said he was “outraged” over the incident, spoke with Gonzalez, who told him he is a US citizen, and his family following the incident. CNN is working to verify Gonzalez’s citizenship status.

US citizens have been caught up in the Trump administration’s sweeping immigration crackdown, which has featured highly visible enforcement operations and aggressive tactics that have prompted nationwide protests, legal battles and political backlash.

Long Beach police officers took Gonzalez to a nearby fire station, where his handcuffs were removed, police said in the statement. Fire department personnel then transported him to a hospital for medical attention. Richardson declined to comment on Gonzalez’s current condition, citing his privacy.

Meanwhile, officers remained at the scene in an attempt to de-escalate the situation, the police statement said. When Long Beach police left the scene, some ICE agents followed officers to the station’s parking lot, where the federal agents were asked to leave and told they could contact the department to file a vandalism report.

US Rep. Robert Garcia, a Democrat from California, said in a post on X: “ICE agents brutally attacked and broke the arm of a North Long Beach resident and U.S. citizen,” calling the videos “horrific.”

The GoFundMe was created to pay his medical bills, the website said. Leslie Gonzalez said her father is currently receiving treatment for his injuries.

“My Dad is one of the hardest working men out there,” she wrote on the GoFundMe. “Because of him I have a roof over my head and I have all the opportunities around me. Our family is everything because of him.”

Richardson said he attempted to contact ICE through its complaint hotline, but has yet to speak with someone at the agency.

What would have been a safe weekend in North Long Beach “turned into a violent incident with no transparency or accountability, and a lot more questions than answers,” Richardson told CNN.

title: Blunder in, abandon allies and court a dictator: it's the Trump doctrine, now playing out in Myanmar
description:
This sparked a civil war that has now turned into a brutal series of overlapping conflicts between the military, resistance forces and a medley of ethnic militias.
This month the Trump administration decided to upend nearly a decade of united western policy and open direct talks with the Myanmar regime.
The purpose of the talks was not to persuade the military regime to reintroduce democracy or stop its brutal war.
Since the 2021 coup, rare-earth shipments from Myanmar to China have totalled $3.6bn, making up the majority of China’s rare-earth imports.
Many Myanmar resistance figures, including Aung San Suu Kyi, have placed their hope in US help.
text:
Marco Rubio was once adamant that the US had to do everything in its power to end what he described as the “ethnic cleansing” of the Rohingya in Myanmar. In a 2017 letter he signed along with 20 other US senators, Rubio called for “strong multilateral sanctions against specific senior Burmese military officials associated with the gross human rights abuses”. Those responsible for the atrocities should be prosecuted, he argued.

In the years since, the Myanmar military’s crimes have only increased. What was then deemed ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya is now widely viewed, including by the US, as genocide. What little democracy existed in Myanmar was eradicated in 2021 when Aung San Suu Kyi was arrested and imprisoned and her party’s election victory overturned, and the military took full control.

This sparked a civil war that has now turned into a brutal series of overlapping conflicts between the military, resistance forces and a medley of ethnic militias. Around 100,000 people have been killed in the conflict, which has forced 5 million people to flee their homes. The UN estimates that 16 million are now in need of urgent assistance. It is one of the world’s biggest humanitarian disasters – and entirely human-made.

Earlier this year, Myanmar held sham elections, and Min Aung Hlaing – the general most responsible for Myanmar’s genocide and one of the targets of Rubio’s letter – became president.

But Rubio, now the US secretary of state, no longer believes that Min Aung Hlaing should be prosecuted. Instead he’d rather like him to become an ally. This month the Trump administration decided to upend nearly a decade of united western policy and open direct talks with the Myanmar regime. The possibility of lifting sanctions is now being discussed. The move has shocked other western nations – none of which, it appears, was warned.

Inevitably, a Maga figure lingers in the background. This time it’s Roger Stone, the Donald Trump ally who was found guilty in 2019 of lying to Congress, witness tampering and obstructing the investigation into whether the Trump campaign conspired with Russia in the 2016 presidential election.

Stone, who was spared jail after Trump commuted his sentence, recently started working as a lobbyist for the Myanmar regime, helping to “rebuild relations between the Republic of the Union of Myanmar and the United States”.

It seems to be working. Earlier this month Michael Vance, the assistant secretary of ​state for intelligence and research, travelled to Myanmar’s capital Naypyidaw. The trip was supposedly to secure the release of a US citizen, but Vance also held talks with the generals. The purpose of the talks was not to persuade the military regime to reintroduce democracy or stop its brutal war. Instead it appeared to be about securing American access to Myanmar’s rare earth minerals.

In recent years, the race to control a steady supply of rare-earth minerals – elements used in a host of military technology and hi-tech manufacturing applications – has become increasingly fraught. China controls most of the world’s rare-earth mines and almost all of the processing capacity. The Trump administration’s desire to turn the tables has led it to strike one-sided deals with Ukraine and the Democratic Republic of Congo that have placed US business interests over practically everything else.

There are more than 600 rare earth mines in Myanmar, most of which currently supply China. Since the 2021 coup, rare-earth shipments from Myanmar to China have totalled $3.6bn, making up the majority of China’s rare-earth imports. This is the prize the US appears to have its eyes on.

Vance’s trip has handed Myanmar’s generals a propaganda victory at a moment when they are doing everything they can to legitimise the regime. The US, unfortunately, is not the only country welcoming Myanmar’s generals back into the fold. Min Aung Hlaing this month flew to Malaysia, once a strong opponent of the junta, where the prime minister Anwar Imbrahim floated the idea of Myanmar being welcomed back into the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean). Trips to Indonesia and Brunei are also on the cards, while the Philippines has indicated that it too would like to see relations normalised.

The junta’s diplomatic victories follow growing military success. Over the last two and a half years, with the help of more sophisticated drones supplied by Russia and China, and the conscription of another 100,000 young men, the junta has regained control over several towns and pushed the resistance back into the countryside.

For Myanmar’s civilians, the long nightmare continues. Last month more than 50 people were killed when the military bombed a busy market in a rebel-held area. Every week brings fresh atrocities, while the hope of a peaceful, democratic Myanmar slips further into the distance.

The one silver lining that those fighting for Myanmar’s freedom can cling to is that the rest of the west hasn’t given up on it yet. British diplomats are adamant that there will be no change in the UK’s position, while Canada, Australia and the EU are all likely to hold the line too. But even here there are concerns.

Campaigners point to the UK’s recent reduction in aid to Myanmar from £66m a year to £55m. Just half of the $889.6m the UN has requested for Myanmar this year has been provided by international donors. They would also like to see Britain and others engage more directly with Myanmar’s pro-democracy camp, including the resistance.

Trump is not the first president to prioritise resources over democracy, as a cursory glance at US relations with Saudi Arabia since it discovered oil in 1938 shows. But Trump’s rapacious attitude to oil and minerals, his willingness to enrich his friends and family, and his brazen support for dictators makes this a very different America. Myanmar is simply another example of the corrosive nature that Trump’s foreign policy is having in every corner of the globe.

The question is whether Trump will get what he wants. US policy on Myanmar has been driven by Congress, and there remains bipartisan support for keeping it in place. The House of Representatives recently passed a bill that would extend the sanctions regime for another six years. Particularly at a time when his support is waning, Trump is unlikely to have much joy in persuading senators and members of Congress who have long supported Myanmar’s pro-democracy movement to turn a blind eye to genocide and war crimes.

Even if he did, the bigger question is whether Myanmar’s generals can give Trump what he wants. The vast majority of Myanmar’s rare earth mines are near the border with China and many are controlled by militia groups, not the junta. “There is no way China is going to let the US get anywhere near the rare earths,” Joshua Kurlantzick at the Council on Foreign Relations told me.

And yet even if none of this leads to any real change, the Trump administration’s decision to open talks with a genocidal regime responsible for one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises is a disaster for those in Myanmar fighting for their freedom. Many Myanmar resistance figures, including Aung San Suu Kyi, have placed their hope in US help. Like other democrats fighting demagogues, such as Volodymyr Zelenskyy, they have been deserted.

Here is yet another example of the Trump administration blundering into a part of the world where it knows little, offering a prize to an authoritarian and leaving with not much to show for it.
